content.content: \begin{document} \section{Problem statement} In the following, a monoid is an integral, saturated, sharp, commutative, unital semigroup.  Monoids are written additively.  A monoid $M$ induces a translation invariant partial order on its associated group $M^{\rm gp}$ such that $x \geq 0$ if and only if $x \in M$.  A valuative monoid is a monoid in which the associated partial order is a total order. If $M$ is a monoid, $x \in M^{\rm gp}$, and $y \in M$, we write $x \prec y$ to mean that there are integers $m$ and $n$ such that $my \leq x \leq ny$. A monoid homomorphism $f : M \to N$ is called \emph{infinitesimal} if the following condition holds: \begin{enumerate}[label=$\bullet$] \item If there are $x \in M^{\rm gp}$ and $y \in M$ such that $f(x) \in N$ and $x \prec y$ and $f(y) \prec f(x)$ then $x \in M$. \end{enumerate} If $P \xrightarrow f Q \xrightarrow g N$ are monoid homomorphisms, we say that $f$ is \emph{birhizomic} at $g$ if it is of finite presentation in the category of (integral, saturated, sharp) monoids and, for every factorization of $gf$ through monoid homomorphisms $P \xrightarrow h M \xrightarrow p N$ with $p$ infinitesimal, there is a unique monoid homomorphism $u : Q \to M$ with $pu = g$ and $uf = h$. A family of morphisms $P \rightarrow Q_i$ is called a birhizomic cover if, for every valuative monoid $V$ and every homomorphism $v : P \to V$, there is a factorization of $v$ through some $Q_i \to V$ such that $P \to Q_i$ is birhizomic at $Q_i \to V$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  Let $A_P$ be the category of monoid homomorphisms $P \to Q$.  The birhizomic covers form a Grothendieck topology on $A_P^{\rm op}$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  For any $x$ in $P$, there is an initial monoid homomorphism $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$ that sends $x$ to $0$.  Let $B_P$ be the full subcategory of $A_P$ consisting of homomorphisms $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$, for $x \in P$. We have given $A_P^{\rm op}$ the birhizomic topology and $B_P^{\rm op}$ the trivial topology in which all presheaves are sheaves.  The inclusion $B_P^{\rm op} \subset A_P^{\rm op}$ is left exact.  By left Kan extension and sheafification, it extends to a functor $\pi^{-1} : \operatorname{Sh}(B_P) \to \operatorname{Sh}(A_P)$ on the categories of sheaves.   Let $\pi_\ast$ be the right adjoint of $\pi^{-1}$. \paragraph{Question} \em Is it the case that, for all presheaves of abelian groups $F$ on $B_P^{\rm op}$, the morphism $$F \to \mathrm R \pi_\ast \pi^{-1} F$$ is a quasi-isomorphism? \end{document}

\begin{document} \section{Problem statement} In the following, a monoid is an integral, saturated, sharp, commutative, unital semigroup.  Monoids are written additively.  A monoid $M$ induces a translation invariant partial order on its associated group $M^{\rm gp}$ such that $x \geq 0$ if and only if $x \in M$.  A valuative monoid is a monoid in which the associated partial order is a total order. If $M$ is a monoid, $x \in M^{\rm gp}$, and $y \in M$, we write $x \prec y$ to mean that there are integers $m$ and $n$ such that $my \leq x \leq ny$. A monoid homomorphism $f : M \to N$ is called \emph{infinitesimal} if the following condition holds: \begin{enumerate}[label=$\bullet$] \item If there are $x \in M^{\rm gp}$ and $y \in M$ such that $f(x) \in N$ and $x \prec y$ and $f(y) \prec f(x)$ then $x \in M$. \end{enumerate} If $P \xrightarrow f Q \xrightarrow g N$ are monoid homomorphisms, we say that $f$ is \emph{birhizomic} at $g$ if it is of finite presentation in the category of (integral, saturated, sharp) monoids and, for every factorization of $gf$ through monoid homomorphisms $P \xrightarrow h M \xrightarrow p N$ with $p$ infinitesimal, there is a unique monoid homomorphism $u : Q \to M$ with $pu = g$ and $uf = h$. A family of morphisms $P \rightarrow Q_i$ is called a birhizomic cover if, for every valuative monoid $V$ and every homomorphism $v : P \to V$, there is a factorization of $v$ through some $Q_i \to V$ such that $P \to Q_i$ is birhizomic at $Q_i \to V$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  Let $A_P$ be the category of monoid homomorphisms $P \to Q$.  The birhizomic covers form a Grothendieck topology on $A_P^{\rm op}$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  For any $x$ in $P$, there is an initial monoid homomorphism $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$ that sends $x$ to $0$.  Let $B_P$ be the full subcategory of $A_P$ consisting of homomorphisms $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$, for $x \in P$. We have given $A_P^{\rm op}$ the birhizomic topology and $B_P^{\rm op}$ the trivial topology in which all presheaves are sheaves.  The inclusion $B_P^{\rm op} \subset A_P^{\rm op}$ is left exact.  By left Kan extension and sheafification, it extends to a functor $\pi^{-1} : \operatorname{Sh}(B_P) \to \operatorname{Sh}(A_P)$ on the categories of sheaves.   Let $\pi_\ast$ be the right adjoint of $\pi^{-1}$. \paragraph{Question} \em Is it the case that, for all presheaves of abelian groups $F$ on $B_P^{\rm op}$, the morphism $$F \to \mathrm R \pi_\ast \pi^{-1} F$$ is a quasi-isomorphism? \end{document}

\begin{document} \section{Problem statement} In the following, a monoid is an integral, saturated, sharp, commutative, unital semigroup.  Monoids are written additively.  A monoid $M$ induces a translation invariant partial order on its associated group $M^{\rm gp}$ such that $x \geq 0$ if and only if $x \in M$.  A valuative monoid is a monoid in which the associated partial order is a total order. If $M$ is a monoid, $x \in M^{\rm gp}$, and $y \in M$, we write $x \prec y$ to mean that there are integers $m$ and $n$ such that $my \leq x \leq ny$. A monoid homomorphism $f : M \to N$ is called \emph{infinitesimal} if the following condition holds: \begin{enumerate}[label=$\bullet$] \item If there are $x \in M^{\rm gp}$ and $y \in M$ such that $f(x) \in N$ and $x \prec y$ and $f(y) \prec f(x)$ then $x \in M$. \end{enumerate} If $P \xrightarrow f Q \xrightarrow g N$ are monoid homomorphisms, we say that $f$ is \emph{birhizomic} at $g$ if it is of finite presentation in the category of (integral, saturated, sharp) monoids and, for every factorization of $gf$ through monoid homomorphisms $P \xrightarrow h M \xrightarrow p N$ with $p$ infinitesimal, there is a unique monoid homomorphism $u : Q \to M$ with $pu = g$ and $uf = h$. A family of morphisms $P \rightarrow Q_i$ is called a birhizomic cover if, for every valuative monoid $V$ and every homomorphism $v : P \to V$, there is a factorization of $v$ through some $Q_i \to V$ such that $P \to Q_i$ is birhizomic at $Q_i \to V$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  Let $A_P$ be the category of monoid homomorphisms $P \to Q$.  The birhizomic covers form a Grothendieck topology on $A_P^{\rm op}$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  For any $x$ in $P$, there is an initial monoid homomorphism $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$ that sends $x$ to $0$.  Let $B_P$ be the full subcategory of $A_P$ consisting of homomorphisms $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$, for $x \in P$. We have given $A_P^{\rm op}$ the birhizomic topology and $B_P^{\rm op}$ the trivial topology in which all presheaves are sheaves.  The inclusion $B_P^{\rm op} \subset A_P^{\rm op}$ is left exact.  By left Kan extension and sheafification, it extends to a functor $\pi^{-1} : \operatorname{Sh}(B_P) \to \operatorname{Sh}(A_P)$ on the categories of sheaves.   Let $\pi_\ast$ be the right adjoint of $\pi^{-1}$. \paragraph{Question} \em Is it the case that, for all presheaves of abelian groups $F$ on $B_P^{\rm op}$, the morphism $$F \to \mathrm R \pi_\ast \pi^{-1} F$$ is a quasi-isomorphism? \end{document}

Background heuristics from the director (UNVERIFIED -- check anything you use):
(a) A_P^op has a terminal object, id: P -> P (P = P[-0]^sharp lies in B_P). Likewise in B_P^op the object P is terminal, so for any presheaf F on B_P^op, global sections are F(P) and higher cohomology (trivial topology) vanishes. For the object P[-x]^sharp, the relevant comparison is with the same question for the monoid P[-x]^sharp (A_{P[-x]^sharp} is a slice of A_P). So the question amounts to: (i) the counit/unit identifies (pi^{-1}F)(P[-x]^sharp) with F(P[-x]^sharp) on sections, and (ii) H^i(A_P^op-site, pi^{-1}F) evaluated at the terminal object vanishes for i>0 and equals F(P) for i=0 -- for every P (then apply to the localizations).
(b) Saturated + sharp implies P^gp is torsion-free and the partial order on P^gp is isolated, so it extends to a total order; hence there is always a valuation v : P -> V with v^{-1}(0) = 0. So no family of maps P -> P[-x_i]^sharp with all x_i nonzero is a birhizomic cover; the Zariski-type covers inside B_P are trivial (each P[-x]^sharp is sharp, "local").
(c) Expected picture for P finitely generated (fine, saturated, sharp): let sigma = Hom(P, R_{>=0}) be the dual cone. Objects P[-x]^sharp of B_P correspond to faces x^perp of sigma; a presheaf F on B_P^op is a functor on faces with restriction maps from a face to its subfaces. Birhizomic covers should include the covers of P by the charts of a subdivision Sigma of sigma (log blow-ups / log modifications), and points of the topos should be valuations P -> V (possibly of higher rank) up to a suitable equivalence. For a subdivision Sigma with r : Sigma -> faces(sigma) sending a cone to the smallest face containing it, one expects R lim over Sigma^op of c |-> F(r(c)) to equal F(sigma) in degree 0 (a Quillen theorem A / convexity argument: the cones c with r(c) containing a fixed face tau form a poset whose realization is the open star of the relative interior of tau, which is contractible). If the birhizomic cohomology at P is the colimit over subdivisions of these finite-poset cohomologies, the answer would be YES for finitely generated P. Non-finitely-generated P (e.g. irrational cones, P = Q_{>=0}, rank-two monoids with non-principal faces, infinite-rank monoids) and the role of higher-rank valuations / the "infinitesimal" condition are where this picture is least certain.
EOF

1	kind: attempt
2	Open question attempted: the headline question itself -- is F -> R pi_* pi^{-1} F a quasi-isomorphism for every monoid P and every presheaf of abelian groups F on B_P^op? This query asks for a complete, rigorous answer with full proof (or a counterexample with full verification).
3	
4	Suggested route (you may choose another): prove YES via a "points and proper base change" style argument.
5	1. Make the birhizomic topology concrete: characterize infinitesimal homomorphisms (at least those with target a valuative monoid), characterize when P -> Q (finitely presented) is birhizomic at Q -> V for V valuative, and show the birhizomic topos has enough points given by valuations P -> V (or by suitable equivalence classes of them). Compute the stalk of pi^{-1}F at a point v : P -> V (expected: the colimit of F(P[-x]^sharp) over x in v^{-1}(0)).
6	2. Show that pi^{-1}F evaluated at objects of B_P agrees with F (H^0 part), and that the higher cohomology of pi^{-1}F at the terminal object P vanishes, e.g. by identifying cohomology at P with a colimit over subdivisions / finitely presented covers of cohomology of finite posets, and proving the finite-poset statement by a contractibility (convexity) argument.
7	3. Treat general (not finitely generated) P, e.g. by writing P as a filtered colimit of fine saturated sharp monoids and controlling how B_P, covers and cohomology behave in the colimit -- or explain precisely where this fails and give a counterexample.
8	
9	Background heuristics from the director (UNVERIFIED -- check anything you use):
10	(a) A_P^op has a terminal object, id: P -> P (P = P[-0]^sharp lies in B_P). Likewise in B_P^op the object P is terminal, so for any presheaf F on B_P^op, global sections are F(P) and higher cohomology (trivial topology) vanishes. For the object P[-x]^sharp, the relevant comparison is with the same question for the monoid P[-x]^sharp (A_{P[-x]^sharp} is a slice of A_P). So the question amounts to: (i) the counit/unit identifies (pi^{-1}F)(P[-x]^sharp) with F(P[-x]^sharp) on sections, and (ii) H^i(A_P^op-site, pi^{-1}F) evaluated at the terminal object vanishes for i>0 and equals F(P) for i=0 -- for every P (then apply to the localizations).
11	(b) Saturated + sharp implies P^gp is torsion-free and the partial order on P^gp is isolated, so it extends to a total order; hence there is always a valuation v : P -> V with v^{-1}(0) = 0. So no family of maps P -> P[-x_i]^sharp with all x_i nonzero is a birhizomic cover; the Zariski-type covers inside B_P are trivial (each P[-x]^sharp is sharp, "local").
12	(c) Expected picture for P finitely generated (fine, saturated, sharp): let sigma = Hom(P, R_{>=0}) be the dual cone. Objects P[-x]^sharp of B_P correspond to faces x^perp of sigma; a presheaf F on B_P^op is a functor on faces with restriction maps from a face to its subfaces. Birhizomic covers should include the covers of P by the charts of a subdivision Sigma of sigma (log blow-ups / log modifications), and points of the topos should be valuations P -> V (possibly of higher rank) up to a suitable equivalence. For a subdivision Sigma with r : Sigma -> faces(sigma) sending a cone to the smallest face containing it, one expects R lim over Sigma^op of c |-> F(r(c)) to equal F(sigma) in degree 0 (a Quillen theorem A / convexity argument: the cones c with r(c) containing a fixed face tau form a poset whose realization is the open star of the relative interior of tau, which is contractible). If the birhizomic cohomology at P is the colimit over subdivisions of these finite-poset cohomologies, the answer would be YES for finitely generated P. Non-finitely-generated P (e.g. irrational cones, P = Q_{>=0}, rank-two monoids with non-principal faces, infinite-rank monoids) and the role of higher-rank valuations / the "infinitesimal" condition are where this picture is least certain.
13	
14	Deliverable: either a complete proof that the answer is YES (for ALL monoids P in the stated sense, including non-finitely-generated ones), or a complete counterexample showing NO (explicit P and F, with the failure of the quasi-isomorphism verified in a specific degree). If you can only prove part (e.g. finitely generated P, or only degree 0), state exactly what you proved, with full proofs, and isolate precisely the remaining gap as a single lemma.

# Answer to round1_q2 (partial)

## Proved: (L1) infinitesimal maps out of a valuative monoid

**Lemma 1.** Let M be valuative, N any (sharp) monoid, f : M -> N a homomorphism. Then f is infinitesimal iff f^{-1}(0) ∩ M = {0}. (Since M^gp = M ∪ (-M), this is the same as f^gp being injective.) In particular, a homomorphism of valuative monoids V -> W is infinitesimal iff it is injective.

*Proof.* (⇐) Suppose f(x) ∈ N with x ∈ M^gp, and suppose x ∉ M. Since M is totally ordered, -x ∈ M and -x ≠ 0. Then f(x) and f(-x) = -f(x) both lie in N. Because N is sharp, f(x) = 0, so f(-x) = 0 with -x a nonzero element of M. This contradicts the hypothesis. So x ∈ M. (The ≺ hypotheses are not even needed.)

(⇒) Let 0 ≠ h ∈ M with f(h) = 0. Put y = h and x = -h. Then (-1)y ≤ x ≤ 0·y, so x ≺ y. Also f(x) = 0 ∈ N, and f(y) = 0 ≺ 0 = f(x). The infinitesimal condition would then force -h ∈ M, which contradicts sharpness of M. ∎

**Example.** Take Z^2 with the lexicographic order, mapping to Z by the first coordinate, i.e. the quotient by the convex subgroup 0×Z. This map is **not** infinitesimal: use x = (0,-1), y = (0,1). Quotients by nonzero convex subgroups are never infinitesimal. Injective maps, for example Z -> Z^2 lex with n -> (0,n) or n -> (n,0), are infinitesimal. So, among valuative monoids, "infinitesimal" means "injective". It does not mean "quotient by a convex subgroup".

**Consequence for birhizomic maps (partial L2).** Suppose N = V is valuative and M is valuative. Then factorizations P -> M -> V with p injective are exactly the embeddings of valuation monoids into V. So, at least against valuative test objects, "birhizomic at g" is a unique-lifting property along *injective* maps into V. This looks like a valuative-criterion (properness/separatedness) condition rather than an étale one. This motivates the director's guess that covers are log modifications plus localizations at elements with g = 0. **I have not proved this.**

## Not settled
- (L2): the exact criterion for being birhizomic, when M is not valuative (Lemma 1 does not cover a non-valuative source).
- (L3): quasi-compactness and refinement by subdivisions.
- (L4): points of the topos and stalks of π^{-1}F.
- (L5): the degree-0 comparison.

The director's heuristics (a)–(c) are still unverified. Heuristic (b) is consistent with Lemma 1: a valuation v with v^{-1}(0) = 0 exists because the order on the torsion-free group P^gp extends to a total order. I recall this ordering-extension fact from memory and did not prove it here. Given that valuation, a family P -> P[-x_i]^sharp with all x_i ≠ 0 cannot factor v, so it is not a cover.

## Implication for the headline question
Still open. The single statement that would settle it is the following. For every P, the birhizomic cohomology of the terminal object with coefficients π^{-1}F equals the colimit, over subdivisions Σ of the dual cone, of R lim over Σ^op of the functor c ↦ F(r(c)). This should be paired with the contractibility of open stars, which would give F(P) in degree 0 and zero in higher degrees. If both hold, the answer is YES, at least for finitely generated P.

=== END OF ANSWER round1_q2 ===

\begin{document} \section{Problem statement} In the following, a monoid is an integral, saturated, sharp, commutative, unital semigroup.  Monoids are written additively.  A monoid $M$ induces a translation invariant partial order on its associated group $M^{\rm gp}$ such that $x \geq 0$ if and only if $x \in M$.  A valuative monoid is a monoid in which the associated partial order is a total order. If $M$ is a monoid, $x \in M^{\rm gp}$, and $y \in M$, we write $x \prec y$ to mean that there are integers $m$ and $n$ such that $my \leq x \leq ny$. A monoid homomorphism $f : M \to N$ is called \emph{infinitesimal} if the following condition holds: \begin{enumerate}[label=$\bullet$] \item If there are $x \in M^{\rm gp}$ and $y \in M$ such that $f(x) \in N$ and $x \prec y$ and $f(y) \prec f(x)$ then $x \in M$. \end{enumerate} If $P \xrightarrow f Q \xrightarrow g N$ are monoid homomorphisms, we say that $f$ is \emph{birhizomic} at $g$ if it is of finite presentation in the category of (integral, saturated, sharp) monoids and, for every factorization of $gf$ through monoid homomorphisms $P \xrightarrow h M \xrightarrow p N$ with $p$ infinitesimal, there is a unique monoid homomorphism $u : Q \to M$ with $pu = g$ and $uf = h$. A family of morphisms $P \rightarrow Q_i$ is called a birhizomic cover if, for every valuative monoid $V$ and every homomorphism $v : P \to V$, there is a factorization of $v$ through some $Q_i \to V$ such that $P \to Q_i$ is birhizomic at $Q_i \to V$. For any $x$ in $P$, there is an initial monoid homomorphism $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$ that sends $x$ to $0$.  Let $B_P$ be the full subcategory of $A_P$ consisting of homomorphisms $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$, for $x \in P$. We have given $A_P^{\rm op}$ the birhizomic topology and $B_P^{\rm op}$ the trivial topology in which all presheaves are sheaves.  The inclusion $B_P^{\rm op} \subset A_P^{\rm op}$ is left exact. **What is proved:** for P = N, the map N → 0 is birhizomic at any v : 0 → V.

- The map N → 0 is of finite presentation (one relation).

# Answer to round1_q4

## Part A (proved, modulo two standard results quoted from memory)

**Claim.** σ is a strictly convex rational polyhedral cone and Σ is a fan with |Σ| = σ, ordered by c' ≤ c iff c' is a face of c. Let r(c) be the smallest face of σ containing c. Then for every G : Faces(σ)^op → Ab we have R lim_{Σ^op} G∘r = G(σ), concentrated in degree 0.

**Cited results (from memory).**
(Q) Homotopy-initial functors (Quillen's Theorem A, version for limits). Let f : C → D be a functor of small categories. Suppose that for every d the comma category f/d, whose objects are pairs (c, f(c) → d), has a contractible nerve. Then R lim_D G → R lim_C f^*G is an isomorphism for every abelian-group-valued G.
(H) Let K be a regular CW complex (for example a polytopal complex) and L a subcomplex. Then the order complex of the poset of cells of K that are not in L is homotopy equivalent to |K| \ |L|; in fact it is a deformation retract of it inside the barycentric subdivision.

**Step 1: reduction to contractibility.** Write f = r : Σ^op → D := Faces(σ)^op. In D the object σ is initial, because τ ⊆ σ for every face τ. Hence R lim_D G = G(σ) in degree 0. Fix a face τ. A morphism f(c) → τ in D means τ ⊆ r(c). So f/τ is the poset U_τ = {c ∈ Σ : r(c) ⊇ τ}, with the order of Σ reversed, and its nerve is the same as the nerve of U_τ. By (Q) it therefore suffices to show that every U_τ is contractible.

**Step 2: identifying U_τ.**
- Take a cone c ∈ Σ and a face F of σ. If relint c meets F, then c ⊆ F, because F is a face and c is convex. So r(c) is the unique face F of σ with relint c ⊆ relint F. Each face of σ is a union of cones of Σ, so it is a subfan.
- Hence r(c) ⊉ τ iff c ⊆ F for some face F with F ⊉ τ. So U_τ = Σ \ L_τ, where L_τ is the subfan made of the cones lying in the union Z_τ of the faces of σ that do not contain τ.
- If τ = 0, then L_τ = ∅ and U_τ = Σ. This poset has the least element {0}, so it is contractible.
- If τ ≠ 0, then {0} ∈ L_τ. Choose a linear form ℓ that is positive on σ \ 0, and slice at ℓ = 1. The slices give a polytopal complex K subdividing the polytope Δ = σ ∩ {ℓ = 1}, and K has the same poset as Σ \ {0}. The subcomplex L_τ becomes L, the union of the faces of Δ that do not contain τ' = τ ∩ {ℓ = 1} ≠ ∅. By (H), U_τ ≃ Δ \ |L|.

**Step 3: Δ \ |L| is star-shaped, hence contractible.** Choose p ∈ relint τ', and let x ∈ Δ \ |L| and y = (1−t)p + tx with t ∈ [0,1].
- If t = 1, then y = x, which is not in |L|.
- If t < 1 and y lies in a face F of Δ, then p ∈ F. For t = 0 this is because y = p. For 0 < t < 1 it holds because y is an interior point of the segment [p, x] and F is a face.
- Since p ∈ relint τ' ∩ F, we get τ' ⊆ F, so F is not one of the faces making up L. Hence y ∉ |L|.

So Δ \ |L| is star-shaped about p and contractible, which proves the claim. ∎

## Part B: not done

I did not prove the reduction. The following steps are still open:
(i) charts of a subdivision form birhizomic covers of P;
(ii) every birhizomic cover of P is refined by a subdivision cover, possibly combined with localizations;
(iii) a Čech-to-derived comparison, with Čech nerves computed by the finite posets of Part A;
(iv) the values of π^{-1}F on the chart objects after sheafification.

Assuming (i)–(iv), Part A gives that the cohomology at P equals F(P) in degree 0, for P finitely generated.

## Status

- **Proved:** Part A.
- **Not proved:** Part B. So the headline question, even for fine P, depends on the open steps (i)–(iv). Non-finitely-generated P is not touched at all.

=== END OF ANSWER round1_q4 ===

If $M$ is a monoid, $x \in M^{\rm gp}$, and $y \in M$, we write $x \prec y$ to mean that there are integers $m$ and $n$ such that $my \leq x \leq ny$. A monoid homomorphism $f : M \to N$ is called \emph{infinitesimal} if the following condition holds: \begin{enumerate}[label=$\bullet$] \item If there are $x \in M^{\rm gp}$ and $y \in M$ such that $f(x) \in N$ and $x \prec y$ and $f(y) \prec f(x)$ then $x \in M$. \end{enumerate} If $P \xrightarrow f Q \xrightarrow g N$ are monoid homomorphisms, we say that $f$ is \emph{birhizomic} at $g$ if it is of finite presentation in the category of (integral, saturated, sharp) monoids and, for every factorization of $gf$ through monoid homomorphisms $P \xrightarrow h M \xrightarrow p N$ with $p$ infinitesimal, there is a unique monoid homomorphism $u : Q \to M$ with $pu = g$ and $uf = h$. A family of morphisms $P \rightarrow Q_i$ is called a birhizomic cover if, for every valuative monoid $V$ and every homomorphism $v : P \to V$, there is a factorization of $v$ through some $Q_i \to V$ such that $P \to Q_i$ is birhizomic at $Q_i \to V$. Let $B_P$ be the full subcategory of $A_P$ consisting of homomorphisms $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$, for $x \in P$. We have given $A_P^{\rm op}$ the birhizomic topology and $B_P^{\rm op}$ the trivial topology in which all presheaves are sheaves.  The inclusion $B_P^{\rm op} \subset A_P^{\rm op}$ is left exact. Let $\pi_\ast$ be the right adjoint of $\pi^{-1}$. \paragraph{Question} \em Is it the case that, for all presheaves of abelian groups $F$ on $B_P^{\rm op}$, the morphism $$F \to \mathrm R \pi_\ast \pi^{-1} F$$ is a quasi-isomorphism? \end{document}

I proved Part A, which is the combinatorial core. I did not do Part B, the reduction of birhizomic cohomology to Part A. So the headline question is not settled here, even for finitely generated P.

**Part A (proved, using two standard results quoted from memory).** Let Σ be a fan subdividing a strictly convex rational cone σ, and r(c) the smallest face of σ containing the cone c. Then for every G : Faces(σ)^op → Ab, the derived limit of c ↦ G(r(c)) over Σ^op is G(σ), concentrated in degree 0.

The two cited results are:
- **Quillen's Theorem A, limit version:** if every comma category f/d has a contractible nerve, then derived limits along f agree.
- **Cell complexes:** for a regular cell complex K with subcomplex L, the poset of cells of K not in L is homotopy equivalent to |K| \ |L|.

The proof has three steps:
1. In Faces(σ)^op the face σ is initial, so the derived limit there is G(σ). The comma category over a face τ is U_τ = {c : r(c) ⊇ τ}, so it is enough to show each U_τ is contractible.
2. U_τ is Σ with a subfan removed: the cones lying in faces of σ that do not contain τ. If τ = 0, U_τ has a least element and is contractible. Otherwise, slicing σ by a positive linear form turns U_τ into a polytope Δ minus the union of its faces not containing τ.
3. That set is star-shaped about any point in the relative interior of τ ∩ Δ, hence contractible.

**Still open (Part B):**
1. Charts of a subdivision form birhizomic covers of P.
2. Every birhizomic cover of P is refined by a subdivision cover, possibly with localizations.
3. A Čech-to-derived comparison whose Čech nerves are the finite posets of Part A.
4. How sheafification in π^{-1} affects the values on chart objects.

If those four steps hold, Part A gives the answer yes for finitely generated P. Monoids that are not finitely generated are not addressed at all.

\begin{document} \section{Problem statement} In the following, a monoid is an integral, saturated, sharp, commutative, unital semigroup.  Monoids are written additively.  A monoid $M$ induces a translation invariant partial order on its associated group $M^{\rm gp}$ such that $x \geq 0$ if and only if $x \in M$.  A valuative monoid is a monoid in which the associated partial order is a total order. If $M$ is a monoid, $x \in M^{\rm gp}$, and $y \in M$, we write $x \prec y$ to mean that there are integers $m$ and $n$ such that $my \leq x \leq ny$. A monoid homomorphism $f : M \to N$ is called \emph{infinitesimal} if the following condition holds: \begin{enumerate}[label=$\bullet$] \item If there are $x \in M^{\rm gp}$ and $y \in M$ such that $f(x) \in N$ and $x \prec y$ and $f(y) \prec f(x)$ then $x \in M$. \end{enumerate} If $P \xrightarrow f Q \xrightarrow g N$ are monoid homomorphisms, we say that $f$ is \emph{birhizomic} at $g$ if it is of finite presentation in the category of (integral, saturated, sharp) monoids and, for every factorization of $gf$ through monoid homomorphisms $P \xrightarrow h M \xrightarrow p N$ with $p$ infinitesimal, there is a unique monoid homomorphism $u : Q \to M$ with $pu = g$ and $uf = h$. A family of morphisms $P \rightarrow Q_i$ is called a birhizomic cover if, for every valuative monoid $V$ and every homomorphism $v : P \to V$, there is a factorization of $v$ through some $Q_i \to V$ such that $P \to Q_i$ is birhizomic at $Q_i \to V$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  Let $A_P$ be the category of monoid homomorphisms $P \to Q$.  The birhizomic covers form a Grothendieck topology on $A_P^{\rm op}$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  For any $x$ in $P$, there is an initial monoid homomorphism $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$ that sends $x$ to $0$.  Let $B_P$ be the full subcategory of $A_P$ consisting of homomorphisms $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$, for $x \in P$. We have given $A_P^{\rm op}$ the birhizomic topology and $B_P^{\rm op}$ the trivial topology in which all presheaves are sheaves.  The inclusion $B_P^{\rm op} \subset A_P^{\rm op}$ is left exact.  By left Kan extension and sheafification, it extends to a functor $\pi^{-1} : \operatorname{Sh}(B_P) \to \operatorname{Sh}(A_P)$ on the categories of sheaves.   Let $\pi_\ast$ be the right adjoint of $\pi^{-1}$. \paragraph{Question} \em Is it the case that, for all presheaves of abelian groups $F$ on $B_P^{\rm op}$, the morphism $$F \to \mathrm R \pi_\ast \pi^{-1} F$$ is a quasi-isomorphism? \end{document}

\begin{document} \section{Problem statement} In the following, a monoid is an integral, saturated, sharp, commutative, unital semigroup.  Monoids are written additively.  A monoid $M$ induces a translation invariant partial order on its associated group $M^{\rm gp}$ such that $x \geq 0$ if and only if $x \in M$.  A valuative monoid is a monoid in which the associated partial order is a total order. If $M$ is a monoid, $x \in M^{\rm gp}$, and $y \in M$, we write $x \prec y$ to mean that there are integers $m$ and $n$ such that $my \leq x \leq ny$. A monoid homomorphism $f : M \to N$ is called \emph{infinitesimal} if the following condition holds: \begin{enumerate}[label=$\bullet$] \item If there are $x \in M^{\rm gp}$ and $y \in M$ such that $f(x) \in N$ and $x \prec y$ and $f(y) \prec f(x)$ then $x \in M$. \end{enumerate} If $P \xrightarrow f Q \xrightarrow g N$ are monoid homomorphisms, we say that $f$ is \emph{birhizomic} at $g$ if it is of finite presentation in the category of (integral, saturated, sharp) monoids and, for every factorization of $gf$ through monoid homomorphisms $P \xrightarrow h M \xrightarrow p N$ with $p$ infinitesimal, there is a unique monoid homomorphism $u : Q \to M$ with $pu = g$ and $uf = h$. A family of morphisms $P \rightarrow Q_i$ is called a birhizomic cover if, for every valuative monoid $V$ and every homomorphism $v : P \to V$, there is a factorization of $v$ through some $Q_i \to V$ such that $P \to Q_i$ is birhizomic at $Q_i \to V$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  Let $A_P$ be the category of monoid homomorphisms $P \to Q$.  The birhizomic covers form a Grothendieck topology on $A_P^{\rm op}$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  For any $x$ in $P$, there is an initial monoid homomorphism $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$ that sends $x$ to $0$.  Let $B_P$ be the full subcategory of $A_P$ consisting of homomorphisms $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$, for $x \in P$. We have given $A_P^{\rm op}$ the birhizomic topology and $B_P^{\rm op}$ the trivial topology in which all presheaves are sheaves.  The inclusion $B_P^{\rm op} \subset A_P^{\rm op}$ is left exact.  By left Kan extension and sheafification, it extends to a functor $\pi^{-1} : \operatorname{Sh}(B_P) \to \operatorname{Sh}(A_P)$ on the categories of sheaves.   Let $\pi_\ast$ be the right adjoint of $\pi^{-1}$. \paragraph{Question} \em Is it the case that, for all presheaves of abelian groups $F$ on $B_P^{\rm op}$, the morphism $$F \to \mathrm R \pi_\ast \pi^{-1} F$$ is a quasi-isomorphism? \end{document}

75	## Proved: (L1) infinitesimal maps out of a valuative monoid
76	
77	**Lemma 1.** Let M be valuative, N any (sharp) monoid, f : M -> N a homomorphism. Then f is infinitesimal iff f^{-1}(0) ∩ M = {0}. (Since M^gp = M ∪ (-M), this is the same as f^gp being injective.) In particular, a homomorphism of valuative monoids V -> W is infinitesimal iff it is injective.
78	
79	*Proof.* (⇐) Suppose f(x) ∈ N with x ∈ M^gp, and suppose x ∉ M. Since M is totally ordered, -x ∈ M and -x ≠ 0. Then f(x) and f(-x) = -f(x) both lie in N. Because N is sharp, f(x) = 0, so f(-x) = 0 with -x a nonzero element of M. This contradicts the hypothesis. So x ∈ M. (The ≺ hypotheses are not even needed.)
80	
81	(⇒) Let 0 ≠ h ∈ M with f(h) = 0. Put y = h and x = -h. Then (-1)y ≤ x ≤ 0·y, so x ≺ y. Also f(x) = 0 ∈ N, and f(y) = 0 ≺ 0 = f(x). The infinitesimal condition would then force -h ∈ M, which contradicts sharpness of M. ∎
82	
83	**Example.** Take Z^2 with the lexicographic order, mapping to Z by the first coordinate, i.e. the quotient by the convex subgroup 0×Z. This map is **not** infinitesimal: use x = (0,-1), y = (0,1). Quotients by nonzero convex subgroups are never infinitesimal. Injective maps, for example Z -> Z^2 lex with n -> (0,n) or n -> (n,0), are infinitesimal. So, among valuative monoids, "infinitesimal" means "injective". It does not mean "quotient by a convex subgroup".

150	
151	**Claim.** σ is a strictly convex rational polyhedral cone and Σ is a fan with |Σ| = σ, ordered by c' ≤ c iff c' is a face of c. Let r(c) be the smallest face of σ containing c. Then for every G : Faces(σ)^op → Ab we have R lim_{Σ^op} G∘r = G(σ), concentrated in degree 0.

153	**Cited results (from memory).**
154	(Q) Homotopy-initial functors (Quillen's Theorem A, version for limits). Let f : C → D be a functor of small categories. Suppose that for every d the comma category f/d, whose objects are pairs (c, f(c) → d), has a contractible nerve. Then R lim_D G → R lim_C f^*G is an isomorphism for every abelian-group-valued G.
155	(H) Let K be a regular CW complex (for example a polytopal complex) and L a subcomplex. Then the order complex of the poset of cells of K that are not in L is homotopy equivalent to |K| \ |L|; in fact it is a deformation retract of it inside the barycentric subdivision.
156	
157	**Step 1: reduction to contractibility.** Write f = r : Σ^op → D := Faces(σ)^op. In D the object σ is initial, because τ ⊆ σ for every face τ. Hence R lim_D G = G(σ) in degree 0. Fix a face τ. A morphism f(c) → τ in D means τ ⊆ r(c). So f/τ is the poset U_τ = {c ∈ Σ : r(c) ⊇ τ}, with the order of Σ reversed, and its nerve is the same as the nerve of U_τ. By (Q) it therefore suffices to show that every U_τ is contractible.
158	
159	**Step 2: identifying U_τ.**
160	- Take a cone c ∈ Σ and a face F of σ. If relint c meets F, then c ⊆ F, because F is a face and c is convex. So r(c) is the unique face F of σ with relint c ⊆ relint F. Each face of σ is a union of cones of Σ, so it is a subfan.
161	- Hence r(c) ⊉ τ iff c ⊆ F for some face F with F ⊉ τ. So U_τ = Σ \ L_τ, where L_τ is the subfan made of the cones lying in the union Z_τ of the faces of σ that do not contain τ.
162	- If τ = 0, then L_τ = ∅ and U_τ = Σ. This poset has the least element {0}, so it is contractible.
163	- If τ ≠ 0, then {0} ∈ L_τ. Choose a linear form ℓ that is positive on σ \ 0, and slice at ℓ = 1. The slices give a polytopal complex K subdividing the polytope Δ = σ ∩ {ℓ = 1}, and K has the same poset as Σ \ {0}. The subcomplex L_τ becomes L, the union of the faces of Δ that do not contain τ' = τ ∩ {ℓ = 1} ≠ ∅. By (H), U_τ ≃ Δ \ |L|.

165	**Step 3: Δ \ |L| is star-shaped, hence contractible.** Choose p ∈ relint τ', and let x ∈ Δ \ |L| and y = (1−t)p + tx with t ∈ [0,1].

168	- Since p ∈ relint τ' ∩ F, we get τ' ⊆ F, so F is not one of the faces making up L. Hence y ∉ |L|.
169	
170	So Δ \ |L| is star-shaped about p and contractible, which proves the claim. ∎

178	(iv) the values of π^{-1}F on the chart objects after sheafification.

184	- **Proved:** Part A.
185	- **Not proved:** Part B. So the headline question, even for fine P, depends on the open steps (i)–(iv). Non-finitely-generated P is not touched at all.

=== Background: what earlier work on this problem established (proofs included; re-check anything you use) ===

Notation. For a monoid P (integral, saturated, sharp, possibly not finitely generated) a "valuation" is a homomorphism v : P -> V with V valuative. For P fine, sigma = Hom(P, R_{>=0}) is the dual cone; a face of P is a submonoid F with a+b in F <=> a,b in F; P[-x]^sharp is P localized at x and then sharpened, i.e. the quotient of P[-x] by the subgroup generated by the face spanned by x.

R0 (reduction; standard). id_P is terminal in A_P^op and in B_P^op. For y = P[-x]^sharp, the slice A_P^op/y is A_y^op and B_P^op/y is B_y^op (an object P[-x']^sharp under y is y[-x']^sharp), and restriction to slices commutes with pi^{-1}, pi_*, R pi_*. Since B_P^op has the trivial topology and terminal object P, the question is equivalent to: for EVERY monoid P and every F, (i) H^0(A_P, pi^{-1}F) = F(P) via the natural map, and (ii) H^i(A_P, pi^{-1}F) = 0 for i > 0 (cohomology of the site A_P^op with the birhizomic topology, at the terminal object).

R1 (proved). If y in M, p : M -> N is infinitesimal and p(y) = 0, then y = 0. Proof: put x = -y. Then p(x) = 0 in N, -y <= x <= 0*y so x prec y, and p(y) = 0 prec 0 = p(x). Infinitesimality gives -y in M; M sharp gives y = 0. Consequently, for M valuative, f : M -> N is infinitesimal iff f^{-1}(0) = {0} (iff f^gp injective): if the kernel is trivial and f(x) in N with x notin M, then -x in M, f(-x) = -f(x) in N, N sharp forces f(x)=0, so -x = 0, contradiction. So among valuative monoids "infinitesimal" = "injective"; the quotient Z^2_lex -> Z by the convex subgroup 0 x Z is NOT infinitesimal.

R2 (proved). For every finitely presented f : P -> Q and every V, f is birhizomic at the zero map Q -> V: in a factorization P -h-> M -p-> V of 0 with p infinitesimal, R1 gives h = 0, and any u : Q -> M with pu = 0 is 0 by R1; so u = 0 exists and is unique. Likewise, P -> P[-x]^sharp is birhizomic at every g : P[-x]^sharp -> V: p(h(x)) = g(0) = 0 forces h(x) = 0, so h factors uniquely through P[-x]^sharp by its universal property (and pu = g follows by uniqueness of maps out of P[-x]^sharp). In particular the zero valuation factors birhizomically through every object of A_P.

R3 (proved; corrects an earlier heuristic). Closed charts of a subdivision of the dual cone are NOT birhizomic at valuations lying on the walls. Example: P = N^2 (basis e1,e2), Q = <e2, e1-e2> subset Z^2 (the chart of the cone spanned by (1,0),(1,1) in the subdivision of R_{>=0}^2 by the ray (1,1)), g : Q -> N with g(e2) = 1, g(e1-e2) = 0 (so v(e1) = v(e2) = 1). Let M = {x in Z^2 : x1+x2 > 0} union {0} (integral, saturated, sharp, M^gp = Z^2), h : P -> M the inclusion, p : M -> N, p(x) = x1+x2. Then ph = gf. p is infinitesimal: if p(x) >= 0, x prec y, p(y) prec p(x): when p(x) > 0, x in M; when p(x) = 0, p(y) prec 0 forces p(y) = 0, so y = 0, and x prec 0 forces x = 0. But a u : Q -> M with uf = h must send e1-e2 to e1-e2 notin M. So P -> Q is not birhizomic at g. Hence birhizomic covers are NOT (refinements of) subdivision covers by closed charts.

R4 (proved). "Open-cone" neighbourhoods are birhizomic. Let v : P -> V be a valuation, a_1,...,a_k in P^gp with v(a_i) > 0, and suppose each a_i = b_i - c_i with b_i, c_i in P and v(b_i + c_i) prec v(a_i) in V (i.e. m v(a_i) <= v(b_i+c_i) <= n v(a_i); automatic if V is archimedean, e.g. V subset R_{>=0}). Let Q be the saturation in P^gp of the submonoid generated by P and the a_i, and g : Q -> V the extension of v. Then Q is sharp (if q, -q in Q then v(q) = 0, and nq = p + sum m_i a_i with v = 0 forces all m_i = 0, so nq, -nq in P, so q = 0), and P -> Q is birhizomic at g, provided it is of finite presentation (clear if P is finitely generated). Proof: given P -h-> M -p-> V infinitesimal, x = h^gp(a_i), y = h(b_i + c_i): y - x = 2h(c_i) >= 0 and y + x = 2h(b_i) >= 0, so x prec y; p(x) = v(a_i) in V; p(y) prec p(x) by hypothesis; so x in M. M saturated gives h^gp(Q) subset M; u = h^gp|_Q works, and is unique because Q^gp = P^gp (and M^gp is torsion-free). So for a rank-one valuation v with v^{-1}(0) = 0 on fine P, the birhizomic neighbourhoods include the monoids dual to rational polyhedral cones containing v in their INTERIOR.

R5 (director's heuristic, UNVERIFIED). Picture: the birhizomic topos should be the sheaf topos of a space X_P of valuations (up to equivalence), with open sets U_Q = {v : v factors through Q and P -> Q is birhizomic there}; the stalk of pi^{-1}F at v should be colim over x in P with v(x) = 0 of F(P[-x]^sharp) (the left Kan extension to an object Q is colim over the face {x : f(x) = 0} of F(P[-x]^sharp)). The zero valuation lies in every nonempty U_Q (R2). Each face object P[-x]^sharp is an open U containing the valuations killing x. For N^2, a rank-two valuation such as v(e1) = 1, v(e2) = eps (eps infinitely small relative to 1) seems to have only neighbourhoods Q generated by P and elements a with v(a) in the archimedean class of 1 (elements whose value is infinitesimal fail the prec condition of R4), and every such neighbourhood also contains the boundary valuation w(e1) = 1, w(e2) = 0; such higher-rank points would "glue" each face to the interior. This picture (and the role of the prec condition for higher-rank valuations) has NOT been checked.

R6 (proved, may or may not be needed). Finite-poset lemma: for a fan Sigma subdividing a rational cone sigma and r(c) = smallest face of sigma containing c, R lim over Sigma^op of G o r equals G(sigma) in degree 0 for every G : Faces(sigma)^op -> Ab (Quillen's Theorem A; the relevant comma posets {c : r(c) contains tau} are homotopy equivalent to Delta minus the faces not containing tau, which is star-shaped about a point of relint tau). Note that by R3 the closed-chart covers are not birhizomic covers, so this lemma is not directly applicable.

Expected answer so far (nobody has proved it): YES. No counterexample has been found; the cases most at risk are non-finitely-generated P (non-principal faces, e.g. P = N^(infinity) where faces like the span of infinitely many basis vectors are not of the form "face of x", irrational cones, P = Q_{>=0}^2, P valuative of rank >= 2) and the effect of higher-rank valuations.
=== End of background ===
EOF

\begin{document} \section{Problem statement} In the following, a monoid is an integral, saturated, sharp, commutative, unital semigroup.  Monoids are written additively.  A monoid $M$ induces a translation invariant partial order on its associated group $M^{\rm gp}$ such that $x \geq 0$ if and only if $x \in M$.  A valuative monoid is a monoid in which the associated partial order is a total order. If $M$ is a monoid, $x \in M^{\rm gp}$, and $y \in M$, we write $x \prec y$ to mean that there are integers $m$ and $n$ such that $my \leq x \leq ny$. A monoid homomorphism $f : M \to N$ is called \emph{infinitesimal} if the following condition holds: \begin{enumerate}[label=$\bullet$] \item If there are $x \in M^{\rm gp}$ and $y \in M$ such that $f(x) \in N$ and $x \prec y$ and $f(y) \prec f(x)$ then $x \in M$. \end{enumerate} If $P \xrightarrow f Q \xrightarrow g N$ are monoid homomorphisms, we say that $f$ is \emph{birhizomic} at $g$ if it is of finite presentation in the category of (integral, saturated, sharp) monoids and, for every factorization of $gf$ through monoid homomorphisms $P \xrightarrow h M \xrightarrow p N$ with $p$ infinitesimal, there is a unique monoid homomorphism $u : Q \to M$ with $pu = g$ and $uf = h$. A family of morphisms $P \rightarrow Q_i$ is called a birhizomic cover if, for every valuative monoid $V$ and every homomorphism $v : P \to V$, there is a factorization of $v$ through some $Q_i \to V$ such that $P \to Q_i$ is birhizomic at $Q_i \to V$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  Let $A_P$ be the category of monoid homomorphisms $P \to Q$.  The birhizomic covers form a Grothendieck topology on $A_P^{\rm op}$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  For any $x$ in $P$, there is an initial monoid homomorphism $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$ that sends $x$ to $0$.  Let $B_P$ be the full subcategory of $A_P$ consisting of homomorphisms $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$, for $x \in P$. We have given $A_P^{\rm op}$ the birhizomic topology and $B_P^{\rm op}$ the trivial topology in which all presheaves are sheaves.  The inclusion $B_P^{\rm op} \subset A_P^{\rm op}$ is left exact.  By left Kan extension and sheafification, it extends to a functor $\pi^{-1} : \operatorname{Sh}(B_P) \to \operatorname{Sh}(A_P)$ on the categories of sheaves.   Let $\pi_\ast$ be the right adjoint of $\pi^{-1}$. \paragraph{Question} \em Is it the case that, for all presheaves of abelian groups $F$ on $B_P^{\rm op}$, the morphism $$F \to \mathrm R \pi_\ast \pi^{-1} F$$ is a quasi-isomorphism? \end{document}

2	Open question attempted (flagged open by this run): what exactly are the birhizomic morphisms and covers, and what is the birhizomic topos on A_P^op concretely -- its points and the stalks of pi^{-1}F? Settle this with proofs, then use it to decide the headline question if you can.
3	
4	=== Background: what earlier work on this problem established (proofs included; re-check anything you use) ===
5	
6	Notation. For a monoid P (integral, saturated, sharp, possibly not finitely generated) a "valuation" is a homomorphism v : P -> V with V valuative. For P fine, sigma = Hom(P, R_{>=0}) is the dual cone; a face of P is a submonoid F with a+b in F <=> a,b in F; P[-x]^sharp is P localized at x and then sharpened, i.e. the quotient of P[-x] by the subgroup generated by the face spanned by x.
7	
8	R0 (reduction; standard). id_P is terminal in A_P^op and in B_P^op. For y = P[-x]^sharp, the slice A_P^op/y is A_y^op and B_P^op/y is B_y^op (an object P[-x']^sharp under y is y[-x']^sharp), and restriction to slices commutes with pi^{-1}, pi_*, R pi_*. Since B_P^op has the trivial topology and terminal object P, the question is equivalent to: for EVERY monoid P and every F, (i) H^0(A_P, pi^{-1}F) = F(P) via the natural map, and (ii) H^i(A_P, pi^{-1}F) = 0 for i > 0 (cohomology of the site A_P^op with the birhizomic topology, at the terminal object).
9	
10	R1 (proved). If y in M, p : M -> N is infinitesimal and p(y) = 0, then y = 0. Proof: put x = -y. Then p(x) = 0 in N, -y <= x <= 0*y so x prec y, and p(y) = 0 prec 0 = p(x). Infinitesimality gives -y in M; M sharp gives y = 0. Consequently, for M valuative, f : M -> N is infinitesimal iff f^{-1}(0) = {0} (iff f^gp injective): if the kernel is trivial and f(x) in N with x notin M, then -x in M, f(-x) = -f(x) in N, N sharp forces f(x)=0, so -x = 0, contradiction. So among valuative monoids "infinitesimal" = "injective"; the quotient Z^2_lex -> Z by the convex subgroup 0 x Z is NOT infinitesimal.
11	
12	R2 (proved). For every finitely presented f : P -> Q and every V, f is birhizomic at the zero map Q -> V: in a factorization P -h-> M -p-> V of 0 with p infinitesimal, R1 gives h = 0, and any u : Q -> M with pu = 0 is 0 by R1; so u = 0 exists and is unique. Likewise, P -> P[-x]^sharp is birhizomic at every g : P[-x]^sharp -> V: p(h(x)) = g(0) = 0 forces h(x) = 0, so h factors uniquely through P[-x]^sharp by its universal property (and pu = g follows by uniqueness of maps out of P[-x]^sharp). In particular the zero valuation factors birhizomically through every object of A_P.
13	
14	R3 (proved; corrects an earlier heuristic). Closed charts of a subdivision of the dual cone are NOT birhizomic at valuations lying on the walls. Example: P = N^2 (basis e1,e2), Q = <e2, e1-e2> subset Z^2 (the chart of the cone spanned by (1,0),(1,1) in the subdivision of R_{>=0}^2 by the ray (1,1)), g : Q -> N with g(e2) = 1, g(e1-e2) = 0 (so v(e1) = v(e2) = 1). Let M = {x in Z^2 : x1+x2 > 0} union {0} (integral, saturated, sharp, M^gp = Z^2), h : P -> M the inclusion, p : M -> N, p(x) = x1+x2. Then ph = gf. p is infinitesimal: if p(x) >= 0, x prec y, p(y) prec p(x): when p(x) > 0, x in M; when p(x) = 0, p(y) prec 0 forces p(y) = 0, so y = 0, and x prec 0 forces x = 0. But a u : Q -> M with uf = h must send e1-e2 to e1-e2 notin M. So P -> Q is not birhizomic at g. Hence birhizomic covers are NOT (refinements of) subdivision covers by closed charts.
15	
16	R4 (proved). "Open-cone" neighbourhoods are birhizomic. Let v : P -> V be a valuation, a_1,...,a_k in P^gp with v(a_i) > 0, and suppose each a_i = b_i - c_i with b_i, c_i in P and v(b_i + c_i) prec v(a_i) in V (i.e. m v(a_i) <= v(b_i+c_i) <= n v(a_i); automatic if V is archimedean, e.g. V subset R_{>=0}). Let Q be the saturation in P^gp of the submonoid generated by P and the a_i, and g : Q -> V the extension of v. Then Q is sharp (if q, -q in Q then v(q) = 0, and nq = p + sum m_i a_i with v = 0 forces all m_i = 0, so nq, -nq in P, so q = 0), and P -> Q is birhizomic at g, provided it is of finite presentation (clear if P is finitely generated). Proof: given P -h-> M -p-> V infinitesimal, x = h^gp(a_i), y = h(b_i + c_i): y - x = 2h(c_i) >= 0 and y + x = 2h(b_i) >= 0, so x prec y; p(x) = v(a_i) in V; p(y) prec p(x) by hypothesis; so x in M. M saturated gives h^gp(Q) subset M; u = h^gp|_Q works, and is unique because Q^gp = P^gp (and M^gp is torsion-free). So for a rank-one valuation v with v^{-1}(0) = 0 on fine P, the birhizomic neighbourhoods include the monoids dual to rational polyhedral cones containing v in their INTERIOR.
17	
18	R5 (director's heuristic, UNVERIFIED). Picture: the birhizomic topos should be the sheaf topos of a space X_P of valuations (up to equivalence), with open sets U_Q = {v : v factors through Q and P -> Q is birhizomic there}; the stalk of pi^{-1}F at v should be colim over x in P with v(x) = 0 of F(P[-x]^sharp) (the left Kan extension to an object Q is colim over the face {x : f(x) = 0} of F(P[-x]^sharp)). 19	
20	R6 (proved, may or may not be needed). Finite-poset lemma: for a fan Sigma subdividing a rational cone sigma and r(c) = smallest face of sigma containing c, R lim over Sigma^op of G o r equals G(sigma) in degree 0 for every G : Faces(sigma)^op -> Ab (Quillen's Theorem A; the relevant comma posets {c : r(c) contains tau} are homotopy equivalent to Delta minus the faces not containing tau, which is star-shaped about a point of relint tau). Note that by R3 the closed-chart covers are not birhizomic covers, so this lemma is not directly applicable.
21	
22	Expected answer so far (nobody has proved it): YES. No counterexample has been found; the cases most at risk are non-finitely-generated P (non-principal faces, e.g. P = N^(infinity) where faces like the span of infinitely many basis vectors are not of the form "face of x", irrational cones, P = Q_{>=0}^2, P valuative of rank >= 2) and the effect of higher-rank valuations.
23	=== End of background ===
24	
25	Task.
26	(1) Give a necessary and sufficient criterion for "f : P -> Q is birhizomic at g : Q -> V" (V valuative), at least for P finitely generated, and then for arbitrary P. Natural candidates to test: (a) f^gp is injective with Q^gp/f(P^gp) torsion, or f is a localization-and-sharpening P -> P[-x]^sharp followed by a map of the R4 type; (b) every element of Q^gp beyond P^gp is "controlled" by the prec condition at g. Find the correct statement; decide whether non-injective-on-groups f other than localizations can be birhizomic; decide what the prec condition demands at higher-rank valuations (prove or refute the claim in R5 about the rank-two valuation of N^2). Use test objects M like the one in R3 (M = {x : p(x) > 0} union {0}, and its higher-rank analogues) to obtain necessary conditions.
27	(2) Describe the covers: show that every birhizomic cover of P is refined by one of an explicit type, and say whether finite subcovers exist (quasi-compactness) for P finitely generated and for P arbitrary.
28	(3) Construct a topological space X_P (or a locale) of equivalence classes of valuations with Sh(A_P^op, birhizomic) equivalent to Sh(X_P) -- or show enough points exist in some other form -- and compute the stalks of pi^{-1}F (prove or correct the formula in R5).
29	(4) With (1)-(3), compute H^0 and H^1(A_P, pi^{-1}F) for P = N^2 and arbitrary F on its four faces, and state what your description implies for the headline question.
30	
31	Deliverable: precise statements with complete proofs; mark clearly anything you could not prove. If you find that some statement in the background is wrong, say so with a proof.

# round2_q2: partial answer

## Proved: Step 1 (devissage) for fine P

**Structure of B_P.** Let P be fine. Every face of P is generated by finitely many elements, so it is the face spanned by one element x (take the sum of the generators). For faces Phi(x), Phi(x'), there is a morphism P[-x]^sharp -> P[-x']^sharp under P exactly when x maps to a unit in P[-x']^sharp. Because P[-x']^sharp is sharp, this means x maps to 0, i.e. x lies in Phi(x'). Such a morphism is unique, by the universal property. So B_P is equivalent to the finite poset Faces(P), ordered by inclusion. A presheaf F on B_P^op is a covariant functor on this poset: there are maps F(Phi) -> F(Phi') when Phi ⊂ Phi'. The smallest face {0} corresponds to P.

**Filtration.** Let U be an upward-closed set of faces. Define F_U to equal F on U and 0 elsewhere. This is a subfunctor of F: a transition map leaving U would have to go downward, which is impossible, so all transition maps out of U stay in U. List the faces in a linear extension Phi_1, ..., Phi_r of the order, starting with the largest. The sets U_k = {Phi_1, ..., Phi_k} are upward closed. They give a finite filtration 0 = F_{U_0} ⊂ ... ⊂ F_{U_r} = F. Each graded piece F_{U_k}/F_{U_{k-1}} is concentrated at the single face Phi_k, with value F(Phi_k), and is again a functor on B_P^op.

**Reduction.** pi^{-1} is exact: it is the left adjoint of a geometric morphism, and the inclusion is left exact. R pi_* is a triangulated functor. So F -> R pi_* pi^{-1} F is a natural transformation between exact functors on bounded complexes. By induction along the filtration, using the five lemma on the long exact sequences, it is a quasi-isomorphism for every F if it is one for every F concentrated at a single face. By R0, it is enough to check H^*(A_P, pi^{-1} F) for such F, for all fine P.

## Not proved

- **Step 2 (P = N^2).** I did not do the computation. Its key ingredient is the claimed description of the neighbourhoods of rank-two valuations in background item R5. I have not verified that description.
- **Step 3 (general fine P).** Not done.

## Open

The remaining lemma, still open, is this. For fine P and F concentrated at a single face Phi with value A:
- H^0(A_P, pi^{-1}F) = A if Phi = {0}, and 0 otherwise;
- H^i(A_P, pi^{-1}F) = 0 for all i > 0.

So the headline question is unresolved. The expected answer is YES, but this file proves only the reduction above.

- P ⊂ M, by the hypothesis on v.

- p is infinitesimal. Suppose x ∈ P^gp, y ∈ M, p(x) ∈ V, x ≺ y and p(y) ≺ p(x). If v(x) > 0 then x ∈ M. Otherwise v(x) = 0, so p(y) ≺ 0, so p(y) = 0, so y = 0. Then x ≺ 0 forces x = 0 ∈ M.

- id_V;

# round2_q4: attempt at the structural route

## Status
This is NOT RESOLVED. I do not have a proof of YES for all P, and I have no counterexample.

## What I checked
- R1, R2 and R4 from the background: I re-checked the arguments. They are correct as stated; R4 needs the finite-presentation hypothesis.
- Step (a), the injective resolution: for a presheaf F on the poset of principal faces, the map F -> prod_tau I_{tau,F(tau)} is a monomorphism. Here I_{tau,A}(b) = A when tau is a localization of b, and 0 otherwise. Its tau-component is the evaluation at tau, so it is injective objectwise. I_{tau,A} is injective when A is injective, because Hom(G, I_{tau,A}) = Hom(G(tau), A). This step is fine.
- Step (a)(1) is open: does pi^{-1} commute with infinite products? Sheafification does not commute with infinite products in general. Unless the birhizomic site is shown to be coherent (finitary covers), this step fails. Finite presentation of each P -> Q_i does not by itself bound the number of members in a cover.
- Step (b) is open: identify pi^{-1} I_{tau,A} as the pushforward of a constant sheaf from the slice A_tau. This needs a computation of the left Kan extension followed by sheafification, and I did not carry it out. It also needs the acyclicity of the constant sheaf on the birhizomic site, which nobody has proved. R2 (the zero valuation factors birhizomically everywhere) does not give a splitting of covers, so it does not give flasqueness.

## Open questions, stated precisely
1. Is the birhizomic site of every monoid coherent? Does pi^{-1} commute with products?
2. Is pi^{-1} I_{tau,A} equal to j_* of the constant sheaf A on A_tau^op?
3. Does the constant sheaf A on A_{P'}^op satisfy H^0 = A and H^{>0} = 0, for every monoid P'?

A YES answer to 1, 2 and 3 would give YES to the main question. 3 alone does not.

\begin{document} \section{Problem statement} In the following, a monoid is an integral, saturated, sharp, commutative, unital semigroup.  Monoids are written additively.  A monoid $M$ induces a translation invariant partial order on its associated group $M^{\rm gp}$ such that $x \geq 0$ if and only if $x \in M$.  A valuative monoid is a monoid in which the associated partial order is a total order. If $M$ is a monoid, $x \in M^{\rm gp}$, and $y \in M$, we write $x \prec y$ to mean that there are integers $m$ and $n$ such that $my \leq x \leq ny$. A monoid homomorphism $f : M \to N$ is called \emph{infinitesimal} if the following condition holds: \begin{enumerate}[label=$\bullet$] \item If there are $x \in M^{\rm gp}$ and $y \in M$ such that $f(x) \in N$ and $x \prec y$ and $f(y) \prec f(x)$ then $x \in M$. \end{enumerate} If $P \xrightarrow f Q \xrightarrow g N$ are monoid homomorphisms, we say that $f$ is \emph{birhizomic} at $g$ if it is of finite presentation in the category of (integral, saturated, sharp) monoids and, for every factorization of $gf$ through monoid homomorphisms $P \xrightarrow h M \xrightarrow p N$ with $p$ infinitesimal, there is a unique monoid homomorphism $u : Q \to M$ with $pu = g$ and $uf = h$. A family of morphisms $P \rightarrow Q_i$ is called a birhizomic cover if, for every valuative monoid $V$ and every homomorphism $v : P \to V$, there is a factorization of $v$ through some $Q_i \to V$ such that $P \to Q_i$ is birhizomic at $Q_i \to V$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  Let $A_P$ be the category of monoid homomorphisms $P \to Q$.  The birhizomic covers form a Grothendieck topology on $A_P^{\rm op}$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  For any $x$ in $P$, there is an initial monoid homomorphism $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$ that sends $x$ to $0$.  Let $B_P$ be the full subcategory of $A_P$ consisting of homomorphisms $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$, for $x \in P$. We have given $A_P^{\rm op}$ the birhizomic topology and $B_P^{\rm op}$ the trivial topology in which all presheaves are sheaves.  The inclusion $B_P^{\rm op} \subset A_P^{\rm op}$ is left exact.  By left Kan extension and sheafification, it extends to a functor $\pi^{-1} : \operatorname{Sh}(B_P) \to \operatorname{Sh}(A_P)$ on the categories of sheaves.   Let $\pi_\ast$ be the right adjoint of $\pi^{-1}$. \paragraph{Question} \em Is it the case that, for all presheaves of abelian groups $F$ on $B_P^{\rm op}$, the morphism $$F \to \mathrm R \pi_\ast \pi^{-1} F$$ is a quasi-isomorphism? \end{document}

# round2_q1: partial answer

## Proved: a criterion for birhizomic maps in one case

**Setting.** P is fine. f : P -> Q has f^gp an isomorphism, so Q is a fine saturated monoid with P ⊂ Q ⊂ P^gp. g : Q -> V, V is valuative, and v := g^gp : P^gp -> V^gp. Assume v(x) ≠ 0 for every x ∈ P \ {0}.

**Lemma A (necessary condition).** If f is birhizomic at g, then g(q) > 0 for every q ∈ Q \ {0}.

*Proof.* Let M = {x ∈ P^gp : v(x) > 0} ∪ {0}.
- M is a sharp, integral submonoid of P^gp. It is saturated: V^gp is a totally ordered torsion-free group, so v(nx) > 0 implies v(x) > 0.
- P ⊂ M, by the hypothesis on v.
- Let h : P -> M be the inclusion and p = v|_M : M -> V. Then ph = gf.
- p is infinitesimal. Suppose x ∈ P^gp, y ∈ M, p(x) ∈ V, x ≺ y and p(y) ≺ p(x). If v(x) > 0 then x ∈ M. Otherwise v(x) = 0, so p(y) ≺ 0, so p(y) = 0, so y = 0. Then x ≺ 0 forces x = 0 ∈ M.

So there is a u : Q -> M with uf = h. Because Q^gp = P^gp, u must be the inclusion (u^gp agrees with h^gp, which is the identity). Hence Q ⊂ M, i.e. v > 0 on Q \ {0}. ∎

This generalises R3: there v(e1 − e2) = 0 with e1 − e2 ∈ Q.

**Proposition B (rank one).** Suppose in addition that V is archimedean (rank one). Then f is birhizomic at g if and only if g^{-1}(0) = {0}.

*Proof.*
- (⇒) This is Lemma A.
- (⇐) Q is finitely generated, so Q is the saturation of P + ⟨a_1, …, a_k⟩ with a_i ∈ Q \ {0}, and g(a_i) > 0. Write each a_i = b_i − c_i with b_i, c_i ∈ P. Since V is archimedean and v(a_i) > 0, we have v(b_i + c_i) ≺ v(a_i). R4 then applies; I re-checked its proof and it is correct. Finite presentation holds because P and Q are fine. ∎

In words: for a rank-one valuation that is injective on P, the birhizomic neighbourhoods with f^gp an isomorphism are exactly the charts whose dual cone contains v in its interior. These are open-cone neighbourhoods, not the closed charts of a subdivision.

## Status of the remaining items (not done)

- **Higher rank.** Lemma A holds for every V. Sufficiency at higher rank needs the ≺ condition of R4, and I have not proved that it is necessary. So the R5 claim about the rank-two valuation of N^2 is still unverified. The test monoid M of Lemma A does not settle it.
- **Non-injective f^gp.** I have not classified birhizomic maps f with f^gp not injective (beyond the localizations P -> P[-x]^♯) or with nontrivial ker v on P.
- **Covers, quasi-compactness, the space X_P and stalk formulas.** Open; nothing beyond the background.
- **Headline question.** Undecided. The expected answer is YES, but it is not proved here.

=== END OF ANSWER round2_q1 ===

# round2_q2: partial answer

## Proved: Step 1 (devissage) for fine P

**Structure of B_P.** Let P be fine. Every face of P is generated by finitely many elements, so it is the face spanned by one element x (take the sum of the generators). For faces Phi(x), Phi(x'), there is a morphism P[-x]^sharp -> P[-x']^sharp under P exactly when x maps to a unit in P[-x']^sharp. Because P[-x']^sharp is sharp, this means x maps to 0, i.e. x lies in Phi(x'). Such a morphism is unique, by the universal property. So B_P is equivalent to the finite poset Faces(P), ordered by inclusion. A presheaf F on B_P^op is a covariant functor on this poset: there are maps F(Phi) -> F(Phi') when Phi ⊂ Phi'. The smallest face {0} corresponds to P.

**Filtration.** Let U be an upward-closed set of faces. Define F_U to equal F on U and 0 elsewhere. This is a subfunctor of F: a transition map leaving U would have to go downward, which is impossible, so all transition maps out of U stay in U. List the faces in a linear extension Phi_1, ..., Phi_r of the order, starting with the largest. The sets U_k = {Phi_1, ..., Phi_k} are upward closed. They give a finite filtration 0 = F_{U_0} ⊂ ... ⊂ F_{U_r} = F. Each graded piece F_{U_k}/F_{U_{k-1}} is concentrated at the single face Phi_k, with value F(Phi_k), and is again a functor on B_P^op.

**Reduction.** pi^{-1} is exact: it is the left adjoint of a geometric morphism, and the inclusion is left exact. R pi_* is a triangulated functor. So F -> R pi_* pi^{-1} F is a natural transformation between exact functors on bounded complexes. By induction along the filtration, using the five lemma on the long exact sequences, it is a quasi-isomorphism for every F if it is one for every F concentrated at a single face. By R0, it is enough to check H^*(A_P, pi^{-1} F) for such F, for all fine P.

## Not proved

- **Step 2 (P = N^2).** I did not do the computation. Its key ingredient is the claimed description of the neighbourhoods of rank-two valuations in background item R5. I have not verified that description.
- **Step 3 (general fine P).** Not done.

## Open

The remaining lemma, still open, is this. For fine P and F concentrated at a single face Phi with value A:
- H^0(A_P, pi^{-1}F) = A if Phi = {0}, and 0 otherwise;
- H^i(A_P, pi^{-1}F) = 0 for all i > 0.

So the headline question is unresolved. The expected answer is YES, but this file proves only the reduction above.

=== END OF ANSWER round2_q2 ===

# round2_q3: partial answer (little progress made)

I did not settle any of the test cases. Everything below is either a small observation or a plan.

## Observation 1 (proved): the identity valuation of a valuative P
Let P = V be valuative, and suppose a covering family contains a member f : V -> Q that is birhizomic at g : Q -> V with gf = id_V. Take the factorization V -id-> V -id-> V. Here id is infinitesimal, since it is injective (R1). So there is a unique u : Q -> V with u f = id and u = g. Hence **g = u is a retraction of f.** In particular f is injective and V is a retract of Q.

This does not by itself show that the family can be refined to {id}. That step also needs control of the valuations to V that are not injective.

## Observation 2 (proved): B_P for a valuative V of rank one
Take V = Q_{>=0}, or Z[sqrt2] intersected with R_{>=0}. The only faces are 0 and V. So B_V has two objects:
- id_V;
- V -> 0, which equals V[-x]^sharp for every x != 0.

A presheaf F on B_V^op is therefore just a map F(V) -> F(0). The left Kan extension of F to an object f : V -> Q of A_V is F(V) if f is injective, and F(0) if f = 0. Since V has rank one, ker f is either 0 or all of V, so these are the only two cases.

## Open
- The claim for every test case (1)-(3), in particular H^0 and H^1.
- Whether every birhizomic cover of N^(infinity) can be refined to a finite cover.

My guess, which I have not proved, is that the expected answer YES is correct.

=== END OF ANSWER round2_q3 ===

# round2_q4: attempt at the structural route

## Status
This is NOT RESOLVED. I do not have a proof of YES for all P, and I have no counterexample.

## What I checked
- R1, R2 and R4 from the background: I re-checked the arguments. They are correct as stated; R4 needs the finite-presentation hypothesis.
- Step (a), the injective resolution: for a presheaf F on the poset of principal faces, the map F -> prod_tau I_{tau,F(tau)} is a monomorphism. Here I_{tau,A}(b) = A when tau is a localization of b, and 0 otherwise. Its tau-component is the evaluation at tau, so it is injective objectwise. I_{tau,A} is injective when A is injective, because Hom(G, I_{tau,A}) = Hom(G(tau), A). This step is fine.
- Step (a)(1) is open: does pi^{-1} commute with infinite products? Sheafification does not commute with infinite products in general. Unless the birhizomic site is shown to be coherent (finitary covers), this step fails. Finite presentation of each P -> Q_i does not by itself bound the number of members in a cover.
- Step (b) is open: identify pi^{-1} I_{tau,A} as the pushforward of a constant sheaf from the slice A_tau. This needs a computation of the left Kan extension followed by sheafification, and I did not carry it out. It also needs the acyclicity of the constant sheaf on the birhizomic site, which nobody has proved. R2 (the zero valuation factors birhizomically everywhere) does not give a splitting of covers, so it does not give flasqueness.

## Open questions, stated precisely
1. Is the birhizomic site of every monoid coherent? Does pi^{-1} commute with products?
2. Is pi^{-1} I_{tau,A} equal to j_* of the constant sheaf A on A_tau^op?
3. Does the constant sheaf A on A_{P'}^op satisfy H^0 = A and H^{>0} = 0, for every monoid P'?

A YES answer to 1, 2 and 3 would give YES to the main question. 3 alone does not.

Conclusion: the answer is conjecturally YES, as in the background, but this is unproved.

=== END OF ANSWER round2_q4 ===

\begin{document} \section{Problem statement} In the following, a monoid is an integral, saturated, sharp, commutative, unital semigroup.  Monoids are written additively.  A monoid $M$ induces a translation invariant partial order on its associated group $M^{\rm gp}$ such that $x \geq 0$ if and only if $x \in M$.  A valuative monoid is a monoid in which the associated partial order is a total order. If $M$ is a monoid, $x \in M^{\rm gp}$, and $y \in M$, we write $x \prec y$ to mean that there are integers $m$ and $n$ such that $my \leq x \leq ny$. A monoid homomorphism $f : M \to N$ is called \emph{infinitesimal} if the following condition holds: \begin{enumerate}[label=$\bullet$] \item If there are $x \in M^{\rm gp}$ and $y \in M$ such that $f(x) \in N$ and $x \prec y$ and $f(y) \prec f(x)$ then $x \in M$. \end{enumerate} If $P \xrightarrow f Q \xrightarrow g N$ are monoid homomorphisms, we say that $f$ is \emph{birhizomic} at $g$ if it is of finite presentation in the category of (integral, saturated, sharp) monoids and, for every factorization of $gf$ through monoid homomorphisms $P \xrightarrow h M \xrightarrow p N$ with $p$ infinitesimal, there is a unique monoid homomorphism $u : Q \to M$ with $pu = g$ and $uf = h$. A family of morphisms $P \rightarrow Q_i$ is called a birhizomic cover if, for every valuative monoid $V$ and every homomorphism $v : P \to V$, there is a factorization of $v$ through some $Q_i \to V$ such that $P \to Q_i$ is birhizomic at $Q_i \to V$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  Let $A_P$ be the category of monoid homomorphisms $P \to Q$.  The birhizomic covers form a Grothendieck topology on $A_P^{\rm op}$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  For any $x$ in $P$, there is an initial monoid homomorphism $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$ that sends $x$ to $0$.  Let $B_P$ be the full subcategory of $A_P$ consisting of homomorphisms $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$, for $x \in P$. We have given $A_P^{\rm op}$ the birhizomic topology and $B_P^{\rm op}$ the trivial topology in which all presheaves are sheaves.  The inclusion $B_P^{\rm op} \subset A_P^{\rm op}$ is left exact.  By left Kan extension and sheafification, it extends to a functor $\pi^{-1} : \operatorname{Sh}(B_P) \to \operatorname{Sh}(A_P)$ on the categories of sheaves.   Let $\pi_\ast$ be the right adjoint of $\pi^{-1}$. \paragraph{Question} \em Is it the case that, for all presheaves of abelian groups $F$ on $B_P^{\rm op}$, the morphism $$F \to \mathrm R \pi_\ast \pi^{-1} F$$ is a quasi-isomorphism? \end{document}

=== Background: what earlier work on this problem established (proofs included; re-check anything you use) ===

Notation. For a monoid P (integral, saturated, sharp, possibly not finitely generated) a "valuation" is a homomorphism v : P -> V with V valuative. For P fine, sigma = Hom(P, R_{>=0}) is the dual cone; a face of P is a submonoid F with a+b in F <=> a,b in F; P[-x]^sharp is P localized at x and then sharpened, i.e. the quotient of P[-x] by the subgroup generated by the face spanned by x.

R0 (reduction; standard). id_P is terminal in A_P^op and in B_P^op. For y = P[-x]^sharp, the slice A_P^op/y is A_y^op and B_P^op/y is B_y^op (an object P[-x']^sharp under y is y[-x']^sharp), and restriction to slices commutes with pi^{-1}, pi_*, R pi_*. Since B_P^op has the trivial topology and terminal object P, the question is equivalent to: for EVERY monoid P and every F, (i) H^0(A_P, pi^{-1}F) = F(P) via the natural map, and (ii) H^i(A_P, pi^{-1}F) = 0 for i > 0 (cohomology of the site A_P^op with the birhizomic topology, at the terminal object).

=== Background B: a proof outline for finitely generated P (written by the director of this attempt; NOT yet checked by anyone — every step must be re-verified) ===

Conventions. "Monoid" = integral, saturated, sharp, commutative. Presheaves on A_P^op are covariant functors A_P -> Ab (Q |-> G(Q), with G(Q) -> G(Q') for each map Q -> Q' under P). The covering families of an object (P -> Q) of A_P^op are taken to be the families {Q -> Q_i} (maps under P) that are birhizomic covers of Q in the sense of the problem (with Q in the role of P). Fibre products in A_P^op are pushouts in A_P, computed in the category of integral saturated sharp monoids (pushout of monoids, then integralization, saturation, sharpening). A valuation of Q is a homomorphism Q -> V with V valuative; R_{>=0} is a valuative monoid. "f.p." = of finite presentation in the category of integral saturated sharp monoids under the source. For a monoid Q write Q^v_R = Hom(Q, R_{>=0}) (real valuations).

Step 0 (the comparison functor). Let P be fine. For an object f : P -> Q of A_P let Phi_Q = f^{-1}(0), a face of P; since P is finitely generated, Phi_Q is the face generated by one element x_Q (the sum of the generators of P lying in Phi_Q). A morphism P[-x]^sharp -> Q under P exists iff f(x) = 0, and is then unique; so B_P is a preorder equivalent to the finite poset of faces of P, and the comma category {(b in B_P, b -> Q)} has the terminal object b(Q) := P[-x_Q]^sharp. Hence the left Kan extension of F along B_P^op -> A_P^op is (Lan F)(Q) = F(Phi_Q) =: (F o b)(Q), the transition maps being those of F. pi^{-1}F is the sheafification of F o b.

Step 1 (kernel faces via real valuations). If Q is fine (f.p. objects over a fine P are finitely generated, hence fine), then for x in P, f(x) = 0 iff w(f(x)) = 0 for all w in Q^v_R (a fine saturated sharp monoid has a strictly positive real functional, which is positive on every nonzero element). So Phi_Q = { x in P : w(f(x)) = 0 for all w in Q^v_R }. For a covering {Q -> Q_i}_{i in I} of a fine object Q and a finite sigma subset I, let Q_sigma be the pushout over Q of the Q_i, i in sigma (repetitions allowed), and T_i = image of Q_i^v_R -> Q^v_R (a closed polyhedral convex cone). By the universal property of the pushout (R_{>=0} is a monoid of our kind), the image of Q_sigma^v_R in Q^v_R is the intersection T_sigma of the T_i, i in sigma. So Phi_{Q_sigma} = { x in P : w(x) = 0 for all w in T_sigma } (w(x) meaning w(f(x))).

Step 2 (covers are covers of the real dual cone; finite subfamilies). Every w in Q^v_R factors through some Q_i, so the union of the T_i is all of Q^v_R. Lemma K (claimed): there is a FINITE J_0 subset I with union over J_0 of T_i = Q^v_R. Sketch: let W = Q^gp (x) Q (rationals). Let Omega be the set of positive cones Pi of total preorders on the Q-vector space W compatible with addition and positive rational scaling, with Q subset Pi; Omega is closed in {0,1}^W, hence compact (Tychonoff; the "patch" topology). Each Pi gives an ordered Q-vector space V_Pi = W/(Pi cap -Pi) and a valuation v_Pi : Q -> V_Pi^{>=0}; every valuation v : Q -> V is equivalent to one of these (Pi = {x : v(x) >= 0}). Writing Q_i as a retract of (Q (+) N^k / finitely many relations)^{int,sat,sharp}, "v_Pi factors through Q_i" says that a finite system of linear equations and inequalities y_j >= 0 with integer coefficients and constants in v_Pi(Q^gp) has a solution in V_Pi; by Fourier–Motzkin elimination (quantifier elimination for ordered divisible abelian groups) this is a finite Boolean combination of sign conditions on finitely many elements of W, so E_i = {Pi : v_Pi factors through Q_i} is clopen. The E_i cover Omega (cover property applied to v_Pi), so finitely many do; for a real w, V_{Pi_w} embeds in R, giving the claim.

Step 3 (Cech complexes of injective-type presheaves are nerves). For a face tau of P and an abelian group A let I_{tau,A} be the presheaf on B_P^op with I_{tau,A}(b) = A if Phi_b subset Phi_tau and 0 otherwise (identity transition maps where both are A). Then Hom(F, I_{tau,A}) = Hom(F(tau), A), so I_{tau,A} is injective when A is, and every F embeds into the finite product over tau of I_{tau, E(F(tau))} (E = injective hull); so every F has an injective resolution by finite products of such. For G = I_{tau,A} o b and a covering {Q -> Q_i}_{i in I} of a fine object Q, G(Q_sigma) = A iff Phi_{Q_sigma} subset Phi_tau, else 0. Let C = { w in Q^v_R : w(x) > 0 for all x in P \ Phi_tau } (convex: it suffices to impose it on the finitely many generators of P outside Phi_tau). Then Phi_{Q_sigma} subset Phi_tau iff T_sigma meets C (take w = sum of generators of the polyhedral cone T_sigma, whose kernel on P is exactly Phi_{Q_sigma}). So the Cech complex of G for this covering is the ordered cochain complex, with coefficients A, of the simplicial complex N_tau = { finite sigma : T_sigma cap C nonempty } = nerve of the family {T_i cap C}.

Step 4 (the nerves are contractible). If C is empty, G(Q) = 0 and N_tau is empty. Otherwise: every finite subcomplex L of N_tau lies in the full subcomplex N_tau(J') on J' = vertices(L) union J_0. Choose one witness point of T_sigma cap C for each simplex sigma of N_tau(J') and let D be the convex hull of the witnesses: a compact convex subset of C. The sets T_i cap D (i in J') are compact convex, cover D (because the T_i, i in J_0, cover Q^v_R), and have nerve exactly N_tau(J'). By the nerve theorem for finite families of compact convex sets, N_tau(J') is homotopy equivalent to D, hence contractible. So |N_tau| is contractible, its cohomology is A in degree 0 and 0 above; thus the Cech cohomology of I_{tau,A} o b on every covering of every fine object is A (resp. 0) in degree 0 when C is nonempty (resp. empty) — equal to G(Q) — and 0 in positive degrees.

Step 5 (sheaf property). Degree 0 of Step 4 says I_{tau,A} o b satisfies the sheaf condition for all coverings of f.p. objects. For general F, embed F into an injective I^0 as in Step 3 and use left exactness of equalizers and exactness of F |-> F o b: F o b satisfies the sheaf condition for all coverings of f.p. objects. Since coverings and their fibre products of f.p. objects only involve f.p. objects, the sheafification of F o b agrees with F o b on f.p. objects: pi^{-1}F(Q) = F(Phi_Q) for all f.p. Q, in particular pi_* pi^{-1} F = F via the unit.

Step 6 (higher vanishing). Cartan's criterion (Stacks Project, Lemma 21.10.9 [tag 03F7]): let B be the set of f.p. objects of A_P^op and Cov the set of all coverings of objects of B (members and all fibre products are again in B). If a sheaf G has vanishing Cech cohomology in positive degrees on every covering in Cov, then H^p(U, G) = 0 for p > 0 and all U in B. Apply to G = (I_{tau,A} o b)^sheafified (Steps 4–5); then for general F use the resolution F o b -> I^. o b, which is exact objectwise, by sheaves that are acyclic on B: H^p(U, pi^{-1}F) = 0 for p > 0 and U in B. Finally R^p pi_* G is the (trivial-topology) sheaf b |-> H^p(b, G) on B_P^op (pi is induced by the continuous left exact inclusion of sites), and every b = P[-x]^sharp is f.p. So R pi_* pi^{-1} F = F, i.e. the answer is YES for every finitely generated P.

Remark. This outline uses about the birhizomic topology only that covering families consist of f.p. objects and that every valuation factors through some member. For non-finitely-generated P the outline breaks at Step 0 (are kernel faces principal?), at Step 1 (real valuations no longer detect kernel faces: e.g. for P = {x in Z^3 : x3 > 0, or x3 = 0 and x1, x2 >= 0} every real valuation kills e1 and e2), and at Step 4 (the analogous sets of higher-rank valuations, E_i cap C below, are convex in Hom(Q^gp, H) for a large Hahn group H but not closed, and the nerve theorem fails for non-closed convex sets: [0,1) and [1,2] have disconnected nerve). For general Q (f.p. over arbitrary P) one still has: N_tau = nerve of {E_i cap C_Omega} where E_i = valuations factoring through Q_i and C_Omega = valuations v with v(x) > 0 for all x in P \ Phi_tau (using that every monoid has an injective valuation by the order-extension theorem for torsion-free abelian groups, and that a valuation into V factors through Q_i into V iff it does so into the divisible hull, by model completeness of ordered divisible abelian groups); and Lemma K holds verbatim.
=== End of background B ===
