# Running summary after round 3 planning

## Goal
The problem fixes the claim (ledger #1, OPEN [GOAL]). For every monoid P (integral, saturated, sharp, and NOT assumed finitely generated) and every presheaf of abelian groups F on B_P^op, the map F -> R pi_* pi^{-1} F is a quasi-isomorphism. Answer YES = PROVED; a counterexample = REFUTED.

## Established so far (worker results)
- round1_q1 (#2): reduction. id_P is terminal in A_P^op and in B_P^op, and slices are the sites of the localizations. So the claim is equivalent to H^0(A_P, pi^{-1}F) = F(P) and H^{>0} = 0 for all P and F. The director's Step 6 below gives a cleaner route that needs no slicing.
- round1_q2 (#3): a map M -> N with M valuative is infinitesimal iff it kills no nonzero element. Every infinitesimal map kills no nonzero element of its source.
- round1_q3 (#4): the claim for P = N, at the level of valuations.
- round1_q4 (#5): the finite-poset lemma for subdivisions. It is not directly needed now.
- round2_q4 (#9): re-checked R1, R2 and R4. R2: every f.p. map is birhizomic at the zero map, and localizations are birhizomic everywhere. R4: open-cone extensions sat(P + <a_i>) are birhizomic when v(a_i) > 0 under the prec-control, given finite presentation. It also checked that I_{tau,A} (the co-skyscrapers on the face poset) are injective and that F embeds into their product. It flagged that pi^{-1} might not commute with infinite products; this is irrelevant for fine P, where the products are finite.
- round2_q1 (#10, #11): Lemma A and Proposition B.
  - Lemma A: let P be fine, P ⊂ Q ⊂ P^gp, and v nonzero on P\0. If P -> Q is birhizomic at g, then g > 0 on Q\0. The test object is M = {v > 0} ∪ {0}. In particular, closed subdivision charts are not birhizomic at wall valuations.
  - Proposition B: at rank one with v injective on P, the map is birhizomic iff g^{-1}(0) = 0.
  - Open there: whether the prec condition is necessary at higher rank, and maps that are not injective on groups.
- round2_q2 (#12): for fine P, B_P is the finite face poset. A filtration by up-sets plus the five lemma reduces the claim to F concentrated at one face.
- round2_q3: proved only two small observations; nothing load-bearing. (Its "Observation 1", that g is a retraction of f, is tautological because gf = id is assumed.)

## NEW: the director's proof outline for finitely generated P (ledger #13, OPEN until a worker writes it out and it is verified)
The full text is "Background B", reproduced verbatim inside round3_q1..q4.md. In summary:
- **Step 0.** For fine P, every kernel face Phi_Q = f^{-1}(0) is principal. The comma category for the left Kan extension has a terminal object b(Q) = P[-x_Q]^sharp. So Lan F = F∘b, with (F∘b)(Q) = F(Phi_Q). Presheaves on A_P^op are covariant functors on A_P.
- **Step 1.** For fine Q, Phi_Q = P ∩ T_Q^⊥, where T_Q is the cone of real valuations. Real valuations of a pushout are the compatible tuples, so T_sigma = ∩ T_i.
- **Step 2 (Lemma K).** Every birhizomic covering has a finite subfamily whose real cones T_i cover Q^v_R. Proof sketch: compactness of the patch space of total preorders on Q^gp⊗Q, plus Fourier–Motzkin/quantifier elimination, which makes the sets "factors through Q_i" clopen. Lemma K holds for arbitrary Q.
- **Step 3.** Every F has a finite injective resolution by products of I_{tau,A}. The Čech complex of I_{tau,A}∘b on a covering is the ordered cochain complex of N_tau = nerve of {T_i ∩ C}, where C = {w : w > 0 on P \ Phi_tau} is convex.
- **Step 4.** Every finite subcomplex of N_tau lies in a full subcomplex on J' ⊇ J_0, whose nerve is that of a finite compact convex cover of a compact convex set D, hence contractible. So N_tau is contractible.
- **Step 5.** Hence F∘b satisfies the sheaf condition on all coverings of f.p. objects, and pi^{-1}F = F∘b on f.p. objects. This gives pi_* pi^{-1} F = F.
- **Step 6.** Cartan's criterion (Stacks 03F7), with B = the f.p. objects and Cov = all their coverings, gives H^{>0}(U, pi^{-1}F) = 0 for all f.p. U, including the objects of B_P. R^p pi_* is computed objectwise, so the answer is YES for fine P.
- **Notable feature:** the outline uses only two properties of coverings: their members are f.p., and every valuation factors through some member. Birhizomicity itself is not used for fine P.

## Dead ends
- Covers by closed charts of subdivisions are not birhizomic (R3, Lemma A). The finite-poset lemma (#5) is not the mechanism.
- Exactness of pi_! = Lan along b fails in general: the comma categories are not filtered. So the "pi^{-1} preserves injectives" route is not available.
- The topological-space picture (R5: open-cone neighbourhoods, generic zero valuation, rank-two points gluing faces to the interior) is consistent with the outline but no longer needed for fine P.

## Open gaps
1. **(#13)** A complete rigorous write-up of the fine-P outline, especially:
   - Lemma K, in full;
   - the nerve theorem for compact convex sets and the passage to infinite complexes;
   - Cartan's criterion and its hypotheses (f.p. objects are closed under pushouts, and f.p. objects over fine P are fine);
   - the formula for R^p pi_*;
   - the interpretation that coverings of a non-terminal object Q are the birhizomic covers of Q.
2. **(#14)** Arbitrary P. Three issues:
   - (a) Are kernel faces of f.p. maps principal? A sketch says yes: the face generated by Y ∩ P, with Y a finitely generated monoid, is principal, using rational points of rational polyhedra and saturation.
   - (b) Real valuations do not detect faces. Example: P = {x3 > 0} ∪ (N^2 × 0) in Z^3.
   - (c) The nerve N_tau equals the nerve of {E_i ∩ C_Omega} for higher-rank valuations. These sets are convex in Hom(Q^gp, H) for a Hahn group H but not closed, so the convex nerve theorem fails. This is where the birhizomic prec condition may be essential: covers by "closed" sign splits are not birhizomic. A counterexample to the headline claim would need a birhizomic covering with disconnected or acyclicity-failing N_tau.
   - Observation: for a sign split by a, the overlap has kernel 0 whenever injective valuations of both signs exist (an order-extension argument). So sign splits cannot produce disconnection.
3. A reduction route for #14: P is a filtered union of fine P_S. Two caveats: valuations of P_S need not extend to P (example: P = N^2, S = {e1, e1+2e2}), and descending covers needs Lemma K.

## Next round (round 3 wave: 4 attempt queries, all carrying Background A (R1–R4, Lemma A/Prop B) and Background B verbatim)
- q1: a complete rigorous proof for fine P along Background B (target #13), with an N^2 sanity check.
- q2: a positive proof for arbitrary P: principal kernels, plus the property of birhizomic loci that makes N_tau contractible (target #14).
- q3: a counterexample hunt among non-fg P for a birhizomic covering with non-contractible N_tau, with birhizomicity rigorously verified; also an adversarial check of Background B.
- q4: reduce arbitrary P to fine P via filtered unions, descent of f.p. objects and coverings, and limits of topoi.

Afterwards: once q1 returns a complete fine-P proof, send it to two verify queries. If q2 or q4 yields arbitrary P, that becomes the [GOAL] proof. If only fine P is proved, the posed goal still covers all P; keep #14 as the target (escalation round 4).

For any $x$ in $P$, there is an initial monoid homomorphism $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$ that sends $x$ to $0$.  Let $B_P$ be the full subcategory of $A_P$ consisting of homomorphisms $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$, for $x \in P$. I did not conclude this round. I wrote 4 query files, and all 4 are attempt queries.

The target is the gap between finitely generated P and arbitrary P. I drafted my own proof outline for the finitely generated case (ledger #13, OPEN). Its core facts are:
- π⁻¹F agrees with F evaluated at the kernel face, on finitely presented objects.
- Čech complexes of the co-skyscraper presheaves are nerves of convex real dual cones.
- These nerves are contractible, via a finite real subcover and the convex nerve theorem.
- Cartan's criterion then gives the higher vanishing.

No worker has checked this outline yet.

- **q1:** write the finitely generated proof out in full and check every step.
- **q2:** prove the claim for arbitrary P. The weak points are that real valuations stop detecting faces, and that higher-rank sets are not closed.
- **q3:** look for a counterexample among non-finitely-generated P.
- **q4:** reduce arbitrary P to the finitely generated case through filtered unions.

Let $B_P$ be the full subcategory of $A_P$ consisting of homomorphisms $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$, for $x \in P$. By left Kan extension and sheafification, it extends to a functor $\pi^{-1} : \operatorname{Sh}(B_P) \to \operatorname{Sh}(A_P)$ on the categories of sheaves.   Let $\pi_\ast$ be the right adjoint of $\pi^{-1}$. \paragraph{Question} \em Is it the case that, for all presheaves of abelian groups $F$ on $B_P^{\rm op}$, the morphism $$F \to \mathrm R \pi_\ast \pi^{-1} F$$ is a quasi-isomorphism? \end{document}

Problem statement (verbatim, for reference):
\begin{document} \section{Problem statement} In the following, a monoid is an integral, saturated, sharp, commutative, unital semigroup.  Monoids are written additively.  A monoid $M$ induces a translation invariant partial order on its associated group $M^{\rm gp}$ such that $x \geq 0$ if and only if $x \in M$.  A valuative monoid is a monoid in which the associated partial order is a total order. If $M$ is a monoid, $x \in M^{\rm gp}$, and $y \in M$, we write $x \prec y$ to mean that there are integers $m$ and $n$ such that $my \leq x \leq ny$. A monoid homomorphism $f : M \to N$ is called \emph{infinitesimal} if the following condition holds: \begin{enumerate}[label=$\bullet$] \item If there are $x \in M^{\rm gp}$ and $y \in M$ such that $f(x) \in N$ and $x \prec y$ and $f(y) \prec f(x)$ then $x \in M$. \end{enumerate} If $P \xrightarrow f Q \xrightarrow g N$ are monoid homomorphisms, we say that $f$ is \emph{birhizomic} at $g$ if it is of finite presentation in the category of (integral, saturated, sharp) monoids and, for every factorization of $gf$ through monoid homomorphisms $P \xrightarrow h M \xrightarrow p N$ with $p$ infinitesimal, there is a unique monoid homomorphism $u : Q \to M$ with $pu = g$ and $uf = h$. A family of morphisms $P \rightarrow Q_i$ is called a birhizomic cover if, for every valuative monoid $V$ and every homomorphism $v : P \to V$, there is a factorization of $v$ through some $Q_i \to V$ such that $P \to Q_i$ is birhizomic at $Q_i \to V$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  Let $A_P$ be the category of monoid homomorphisms $P \to Q$.  The birhizomic covers form a Grothendieck topology on $A_P^{\rm op}$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  For any $x$ in $P$, there is an initial monoid homomorphism $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$ that sends $x$ to $0$.  Let $B_P$ be the full subcategory of $A_P$ consisting of homomorphisms $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$, for $x \in P$. We have given $A_P^{\rm op}$ the birhizomic topology and $B_P^{\rm op}$ the trivial topology in which all presheaves are sheaves.  The inclusion $B_P^{\rm op} \subset A_P^{\rm op}$ is left exact.  By left Kan extension and sheafification, it extends to a functor $\pi^{-1} : \operatorname{Sh}(B_P) \to \operatorname{Sh}(A_P)$ on the categories of sheaves.   Let $\pi_\ast$ be the right adjoint of $\pi^{-1}$. \paragraph{Question} \em Is it the case that, for all presheaves of abelian groups $F$ on $B_P^{\rm op}$, the morphism $$F \to \mathrm R \pi_\ast \pi^{-1} F$$ is a quasi-isomorphism? \end{document}

2	Open question attempted (flagged open by this run): is there a counterexample among NON-finitely-generated monoids P? Concretely: does some birhizomic covering of some f.p. object over a non-finitely-generated P have a non-contractible (e.g. disconnected) "kernel nerve" N_tau, so that the answer to the headline question is NO?
3	
4	=== Background A: earlier results of this run (proofs included; re-check anything you use) ===
5	
6	Notation. For a monoid P (integral, saturated, sharp, possibly not finitely generated) a "valuation" is a homomorphism v : P -> V with V valuative. For P fine, sigma = Hom(P, R_{>=0}) is the dual cone; a face of P is a submonoid F with a+b in F <=> a,b in F; P[-x]^sharp is P localized at x and then sharpened, i.e. the quotient of P[-x] by the subgroup generated by the face spanned by x.
7	
8	R1 (proved). If y in M, p : M -> N is infinitesimal and p(y) = 0, then y = 0. Proof: put x = -y. Then p(x) = 0 in N, -y <= x <= 0*y so x prec y, and p(y) = 0 prec 0 = p(x). Infinitesimality gives -y in M; M sharp gives y = 0. Consequently, for M valuative, f : M -> N is infinitesimal iff f^{-1}(0) = {0} (iff f^gp injective): if the kernel is trivial and f(x) in N with x notin M, then -x in M, f(-x) = -f(x) in N, N sharp forces f(x)=0, so -x = 0, contradiction. So among valuative monoids "infinitesimal" = "injective"; the quotient Z^2_lex -> Z by the convex subgroup 0 x Z is NOT infinitesimal.
9	
10	R2 (proved). For every finitely presented f : P -> Q and every V, f is birhizomic at the zero map Q -> V: in a factorization P -h-> M -p-> V of 0 with p infinitesimal, R1 gives h = 0, and any u : Q -> M with pu = 0 is 0 by R1; so u = 0 exists and is unique. Likewise, P -> P[-x]^sharp is birhizomic at every g : P[-x]^sharp -> V: p(h(x)) = g(0) = 0 forces h(x) = 0, so h factors uniquely through P[-x]^sharp by its universal property (and pu = g follows by uniqueness of maps out of P[-x]^sharp). In particular the zero valuation factors birhizomically through every object of A_P.
11	
12	R3 (proved; corrects an earlier heuristic). Closed charts of a subdivision of the dual cone are NOT birhizomic at valuations lying on the walls. Example: P = N^2 (basis e1,e2), Q = <e2, e1-e2> subset Z^2 (the chart of the cone spanned by (1,0),(1,1) in the subdivision of R_{>=0}^2 by the ray (1,1)), g : Q -> N with g(e2) = 1, g(e1-e2) = 0 (so v(e1) = v(e2) = 1). Let M = {x in Z^2 : x1+x2 > 0} union {0} (integral, saturated, sharp, M^gp = Z^2), h : P -> M the inclusion, p : M -> N, p(x) = x1+x2. Then ph = gf. p is infinitesimal: if p(x) >= 0, x prec y, p(y) prec p(x): when p(x) > 0, x in M; when p(x) = 0, p(y) prec 0 forces p(y) = 0, so y = 0, and x prec 0 forces x = 0. But a u : Q -> M with uf = h must send e1-e2 to e1-e2 notin M. So P -> Q is not birhizomic at g. Hence birhizomic covers are NOT (refinements of) subdivision covers by closed charts.
13	
14	R4 (proved). "Open-cone" neighbourhoods are birhizomic. Let v : P -> V be a valuation, a_1,...,a_k in P^gp with v(a_i) > 0, and suppose each a_i = b_i - c_i with b_i, c_i in P and v(b_i + c_i) prec v(a_i) in V (i.e. m v(a_i) <= v(b_i+c_i) <= n v(a_i); automatic if V is archimedean, e.g. V subset R_{>=0}). Let Q be the saturation in P^gp of the submonoid generated by P and the a_i, and g : Q -> V the extension of v. Then Q is sharp (if q, -q in Q then v(q) = 0, and nq = p + sum m_i a_i with v = 0 forces all m_i = 0, so nq, -nq in P, so q = 0), and P -> Q is birhizomic at g, provided it is of finite presentation (clear if P is finitely generated). Proof: given P -h-> M -p-> V infinitesimal, x = h^gp(a_i), y = h(b_i + c_i): y - x = 2h(c_i) >= 0 and y + x = 2h(b_i) >= 0, so x prec y; p(x) = v(a_i) in V; p(y) prec p(x) by hypothesis; so x in M. M saturated gives h^gp(Q) subset M; u = h^gp|_Q works, and is unique because Q^gp = P^gp (and M^gp is torsion-free). So for a rank-one valuation v with v^{-1}(0) = 0 on fine P, the birhizomic neighbourhoods include the monoids dual to rational polyhedral cones containing v in their INTERIOR.
15	
16	Lemma A / Proposition B (proved in an earlier round; text verbatim):
17	
18	**Setting.** P is fine. f : P -> Q has f^gp an isomorphism, so Q is a fine saturated monoid with P ⊂ Q ⊂ P^gp. g : Q -> V, V is valuative, and v := g^gp : P^gp -> V^gp. Assume v(x) ≠ 0 for every x ∈ P \ {0}.
19	
20	**Lemma A (necessary condition).** If f is birhizomic at g, then g(q) > 0 for every q ∈ Q \ {0}.
21	
22	*Proof.* Let M = {x ∈ P^gp : v(x) > 0} ∪ {0}.
23	- M is a sharp, integral submonoid of P^gp. It is saturated: V^gp is a totally ordered torsion-free group, so v(nx) > 0 implies v(x) > 0.
24	- P ⊂ M, by the hypothesis on v.
25	- Let h : P -> M be the inclusion and p = v|_M : M -> V. Then ph = gf.
26	- p is infinitesimal. Suppose x ∈ P^gp, y ∈ M, p(x) ∈ V, x ≺ y and p(y) ≺ p(x). If v(x) > 0 then x ∈ M. Otherwise v(x) = 0, so p(y) ≺ 0, so p(y) = 0, so y = 0. Then x ≺ 0 forces x = 0 ∈ M.
27	
28	So there is a u : Q -> M with uf = h. Because Q^gp = P^gp, u must be the inclusion (u^gp agrees with h^gp, which is the identity). Hence Q ⊂ M, i.e. v > 0 on Q \ {0}. ∎
29	
30	This generalises R3: there v(e1 − e2) = 0 with e1 − e2 ∈ Q.
31	
32	**Proposition B (rank one).** Suppose in addition that V is archimedean (rank one). Then f is birhizomic at g if and only if g^{-1}(0) = {0}.
33	
34	*Proof.*
35	- (⇒) This is Lemma A.
36	- (⇐) Q is finitely generated, so Q is the saturation of P + ⟨a_1, …, a_k⟩ with a_i ∈ Q \ {0}, and g(a_i) > 0. Write each a_i = b_i − c_i with b_i, c_i ∈ P. Since V is archimedean and v(a_i) > 0, we have v(b_i + c_i) ≺ v(a_i). R4 then applies; I re-checked its proof and it is correct. Finite presentation holds because P and Q are fine. ∎
37	
38	In words: for a rank-one valuation that is injective on P, the birhizomic neighbourhoods with f^gp an isomorphism are exactly the charts whose dual cone contains v in its interior. These are open-cone neighbourhoods, not the closed charts of a subdivision.
39	
40	=== End of background A ===
41	
42	=== Background B: a proof outline for finitely generated P (written by the director of this attempt; NOT yet checked by anyone — every step must be re-verified) ===
43	
44	Conventions. "Monoid" = integral, saturated, sharp, commutative. Presheaves on A_P^op are covariant functors A_P -> Ab (Q |-> G(Q), with G(Q) -> G(Q') for each map Q -> Q' under P). The covering families of an object (P -> Q) of A_P^op are taken to be the families {Q -> Q_i} (maps under P) that are birhizomic covers of Q in the sense of the problem (with Q in the role of P). Fibre products in A_P^op are pushouts in A_P, computed in the category of integral saturated sharp monoids (pushout of monoids, then integralization, saturation, sharpening). A valuation of Q is a homomorphism Q -> V with V valuative; R_{>=0} is a valuative monoid. "f.p." = of finite presentation in the category of integral saturated sharp monoids under the source. For a monoid Q write Q^v_R = Hom(Q, R_{>=0}) (real valuations).
45	
46	Step 0 (the comparison functor). Let P be fine. For an object f : P -> Q of A_P let Phi_Q = f^{-1}(0), a face of P; since P is finitely generated, Phi_Q is the face generated by one element x_Q (the sum of the generators of P lying in Phi_Q). A morphism P[-x]^sharp -> Q under P exists iff f(x) = 0, and is then unique; so B_P is a preorder equivalent to the finite poset of faces of P, and the comma category {(b in B_P, b -> Q)} has the terminal object b(Q) := P[-x_Q]^sharp. Hence the left Kan extension of F along B_P^op -> A_P^op is (Lan F)(Q) = F(Phi_Q) =: (F o b)(Q), the transition maps being those of F. pi^{-1}F is the sheafification of F o b.
47	
48	Step 1 (kernel faces via real valuations). If Q is fine (f.p. objects over a fine P are finitely generated, hence fine), then for x in P, f(x) = 0 iff w(f(x)) = 0 for all w in Q^v_R (a fine saturated sharp monoid has a strictly positive real functional, which is positive on every nonzero element). So Phi_Q = { x in P : w(f(x)) = 0 for all w in Q^v_R }. For a covering {Q -> Q_i}_{i in I} of a fine object Q and a finite sigma subset I, let Q_sigma be the pushout over Q of the Q_i, i in sigma (repetitions allowed), and T_i = image of Q_i^v_R -> Q^v_R (a closed polyhedral convex cone). By the universal property of the pushout (R_{>=0} is a monoid of our kind), the image of Q_sigma^v_R in Q^v_R is the intersection T_sigma of the T_i, i in sigma. So Phi_{Q_sigma} = { x in P : w(x) = 0 for all w in T_sigma } (w(x) meaning w(f(x))).
49	
50	Step 2 (covers are covers of the real dual cone; finite subfamilies). Every w in Q^v_R factors through some Q_i, so the union of the T_i is all of Q^v_R. Lemma K (claimed): there is a FINITE J_0 subset I with union over J_0 of T_i = Q^v_R. Sketch: let W = Q^gp (x) Q (rationals). Let Omega be the set of positive cones Pi of total preorders on the Q-vector space W compatible with addition and positive rational scaling, with Q subset Pi; Omega is closed in {0,1}^W, hence compact (Tychonoff; the "patch" topology). Each Pi gives an ordered Q-vector space V_Pi = W/(Pi cap -Pi) and a valuation v_Pi : Q -> V_Pi^{>=0}; every valuation v : Q -> V is equivalent to one of these (Pi = {x : v(x) >= 0}). Writing Q_i as a retract of (Q (+) N^k / finitely many relations)^{int,sat,sharp}, "v_Pi factors through Q_i" says that a finite system of linear equations and inequalities y_j >= 0 with integer coefficients and constants in v_Pi(Q^gp) has a solution in V_Pi; by Fourier–Motzkin elimination (quantifier elimination for ordered divisible abelian groups) this is a finite Boolean combination of sign conditions on finitely many elements of W, so E_i = {Pi : v_Pi factors through Q_i} is clopen. The E_i cover Omega (cover property applied to v_Pi), so finitely many do; for a real w, V_{Pi_w} embeds in R, giving the claim.
51	
52	Step 3 (Cech complexes of injective-type presheaves are nerves). For a face tau of P and an abelian group A let I_{tau,A} be the presheaf on B_P^op with I_{tau,A}(b) = A if Phi_b subset Phi_tau and 0 otherwise (identity transition maps where both are A). Then Hom(F, I_{tau,A}) = Hom(F(tau), A), so I_{tau,A} is injective when A is, and every F embeds into the finite product over tau of I_{tau, E(F(tau))} (E = injective hull); so every F has an injective resolution by finite products of such. For G = I_{tau,A} o b and a covering {Q -> Q_i}_{i in I} of a fine object Q, G(Q_sigma) = A iff Phi_{Q_sigma} subset Phi_tau, else 0. Let C = { w in Q^v_R : w(x) > 0 for all x in P \ Phi_tau } (convex: it suffices to impose it on the finitely many generators of P outside Phi_tau). Then Phi_{Q_sigma} subset Phi_tau iff T_sigma meets C (take w = sum of generators of the polyhedral cone T_sigma, whose kernel on P is exactly Phi_{Q_sigma}). So the Cech complex of G for this covering is the ordered cochain complex, with coefficients A, of the simplicial complex N_tau = { finite sigma : T_sigma cap C nonempty } = nerve of the family {T_i cap C}.
53	
54	Step 4 (the nerves are contractible). If C is empty, G(Q) = 0 and N_tau is empty. Otherwise: every finite subcomplex L of N_tau lies in the full subcomplex N_tau(J') on J' = vertices(L) union J_0. Choose one witness point of T_sigma cap C for each simplex sigma of N_tau(J') and let D be the convex hull of the witnesses: a compact convex subset of C. The sets T_i cap D (i in J') are compact convex, cover D (because the T_i, i in J_0, cover Q^v_R), and have nerve exactly N_tau(J'). By the nerve theorem for finite families of compact convex sets, N_tau(J') is homotopy equivalent to D, hence contractible. So |N_tau| is contractible, its cohomology is A in degree 0 and 0 above; thus the Cech cohomology of I_{tau,A} o b on every covering of every fine object is A (resp. 0) in degree 0 when C is nonempty (resp. empty) — equal to G(Q) — and 0 in positive degrees.
55	
56	Step 5 (sheaf property). Degree 0 of Step 4 says I_{tau,A} o b satisfies the sheaf condition for all coverings of f.p. objects. For general F, embed F into an injective I^0 as in Step 3 and use left exactness of equalizers and exactness of F |-> F o b: F o b satisfies the sheaf condition for all coverings of f.p. objects. Since coverings and their fibre products of f.p. objects only involve f.p. objects, the sheafification of F o b agrees with F o b on f.p. objects: pi^{-1}F(Q) = F(Phi_Q) for all f.p. Q, in particular pi_* pi^{-1} F = F via the unit.
57	
58	Step 6 (higher vanishing). Cartan's criterion (Stacks Project, Lemma 21.10.9 [tag 03F7]): let B be the set of f.p. objects of A_P^op and Cov the set of all coverings of objects of B (members and all fibre products are again in B). If a sheaf G has vanishing Cech cohomology in positive degrees on every covering in Cov, then H^p(U, G) = 0 for p > 0 and all U in B. Apply to G = (I_{tau,A} o b)^sheafified (Steps 4–5); then for general F use the resolution F o b -> I^. o b, which is exact objectwise, by sheaves that are acyclic on B: H^p(U, pi^{-1}F) = 0 for p > 0 and U in B. Finally R^p pi_* G is the (trivial-topology) sheaf b |-> H^p(b, G) on B_P^op (pi is induced by the continuous left exact inclusion of sites), and every b = P[-x]^sharp is f.p. So R pi_* pi^{-1} F = F, i.e. the answer is YES for every finitely generated P.
59	
60	Remark. This outline uses about the birhizomic topology only that covering families consist of f.p. objects and that every valuation factors through some member. For non-finitely-generated P the outline breaks at Step 0 (are kernel faces principal?), at Step 1 (real valuations no longer detect kernel faces: e.g. for P = {x in Z^3 : x3 > 0, or x3 = 0 and x1, x2 >= 0} every real valuation kills e1 and e2), and at Step 4 (the analogous sets of higher-rank valuations, E_i cap C below, are convex in Hom(Q^gp, H) for a large Hahn group H but not closed, and the nerve theorem fails for non-closed convex sets: [0,1) and [1,2] have disconnected nerve). For general Q (f.p. over arbitrary P) one still has: N_tau = nerve of {E_i cap C_Omega} where E_i = valuations factoring through Q_i and C_Omega = valuations v with v(x) > 0 for all x in P \ Phi_tau (using that every monoid has an injective valuation by the order-extension theorem for torsion-free abelian groups, and that a valuation into V factors through Q_i into V iff it does so into the divisible hull, by model completeness of ordered divisible abelian groups); and Lemma K holds verbatim.
61	=== End of background B ===
62	
63	Task (counterexample hunt with rigorous checks). By Background B, for finitely generated P the answer appears to be YES and the whole question reduces to the contractibility of the complexes N_tau = { finite sigma : Phi_{Q_sigma} subset Phi_tau } attached to birhizomic coverings {Q -> Q_i} (Q_sigma = pushout over Q of the Q_i, i in sigma; Phi = kernel face in P). For general P, N_tau is the nerve of the sets E_i cap C_Omega of valuations (Remark in Background B), and these sets are convex but not closed in higher rank, so a covering like "E_1 = valuations along a segment with t < 1, E_2 = those with t >= 1" could make N_tau disconnected. If N_tau is disconnected for some covering of id_P with tau = the face {0} and F = I_{{0},A} (i.e. F(P) = A and F(b) = 0 for b != P), then F o b is not a sheaf and pi_* pi^{-1} F(P) is strictly bigger than F(P) = A: answer NO.
64	(1) Try to build such a covering for specific non-finitely-generated P: P = V x N with V = (Z^2, lex)_{>=0}; P = {x in Z^3 : x3 > 0, or x3 = 0 and (x1,x2) in N^2}; P valuative of infinite rank; P = N^(infinity); P = Q_{>=0}^2; irrational cones in Z^2 and Z^3; P = (Z^2,lex)_{>=0} x (Z^2,lex)_{>=0}. For each candidate covering you MUST verify that it is a birhizomic covering: every valuation v of P (all ranks) must factor through some member Q_i with P -> Q_i birhizomic at the factorization. Use R2 and R4 for sufficiency and Lemma A, R1 and test objects M = {x : v(x) > 0} cup {0} (and higher-rank analogues) for necessity. Note the obstruction: for a sign split {sat(P + <a>), sat(P + <-a>)} the overlap has kernel face 0 whenever injective valuations with v(a) > 0 and with v(a) < 0 both exist, so N_{0} is connected for sign splits; and sign splits are typically not birhizomic coverings anyway (R3).
65	(2) If no counterexample arises, identify the structural reason (e.g. a property of birhizomic loci such as closure under coarsening and "openness" with respect to the prec relation) and prove it in as much generality as you can; this is exactly what a positive proof for general P needs.
66	(3) Also check the finitely generated outline itself for hidden failures on a small example (P = N^2 with a non-obvious birhizomic covering, e.g. one using a rank-two valuation's neighbourhoods), and report any step of Background B that is wrong.
67	Deliverable: either an explicit counterexample (P, covering, tau, F) with complete verification of birhizomicity and of the failure of F -> R pi_* pi^{-1} F, or complete proofs of whatever partial results you obtain; mark anything unproved.

**Reduction to a finite presentation.** Q is a retract under P of Q' = (P (+) N^k / R)^{int,sat,sharp} with R finite. This is the standard description of compact objects in the under-category, which I cite from memory rather than prove. If maps Q -> Q' -> Q compose to id_Q under P, then ker(P->Q) = ker(P->Q'). Indeed, x killed in Q' implies x killed in Q. Conversely, if x is killed in Q, its image in Q' is the image of 0, which is 0.

**Kernel of P -> Q'.** Let G = (P^gp (+) Z^k)/L, where L is generated by l_j = r_j - s_j, j = 1..J. Let M0 be the image of P (+) N^k in G, and let M1 = {g : ng in M0 for some n >= 1} be its saturation. Then Q' = M1/M1^*. So x in P is killed iff its image is a unit of M1. This happens iff -nx in M0 for some n >= 1, i.e. iff -nx - p - m in L for some p in P and m in N^k (all taken in P^gp (+) Z^k). Write the element of L as sum c_j l_j with c in Z^J. The Z^k-component condition says c lies in K = {c in Z^J : Z^k-part of sum c_j l_j lies in -N^k}. K is the set of lattice points of a rational polyhedral cone, so it is a finitely generated monoid (Gordan). Let psi : K -> P^gp be the P^gp-part of c |-> -sum c_j l_j, and let Y = psi(K), a finitely generated submonoid of P^gp. Then x is killed iff nx + p in Y for some n >= 1 and p in P. Such an element y = nx + p lies in S := Y ∩ P, and nx <= y. Conversely, if nx <= y in S, then p := y - nx is in P. Hence

- So the ranks of the G_i strictly increase.

What remains open: for a birhizomic covering {Q -> Q_i} of an f.p. Q over arbitrary P, and a principal face tau, is N_tau = {sigma : Phi_{Q_sigma} ⊂ Phi_tau} contractible or empty?

The cover property refers to valuations of P, and the infinitesimality test maps change. So this reduction is unproved. This is exactly the gap.

Proved here: Step 0 extends to all P (Part 1).

Open:
- (a) the contractibility of N_tau for non-finitely-generated P;
- hence (b) the headline claim (answer YES) for arbitrary P.

The claim holds for finitely generated P only conditionally on Background B, whose outline I have not re-verified. I found no counterexample.

# round3_q4: reducing to finitely generated P

Plan: (1) descent of f.p. objects, and a proof that kernel faces are principal for arbitrary P. This fixes Step 0 of Background B. (2) What goes wrong with valuations and covers. (3) Where the cohomological reduction stands. (4) Summary.

Conventions are those of Background B. P_S is the saturation, in <S>^gp, of the submonoid generated by the finite set S ⊂ P. These P_S are fine, and P is their filtered union.

## 1. Filtered colimits and kernel faces

**1.1 Filtered colimits stay in the category (proved).** Let (M_j) be a filtered system of integral, saturated, sharp monoids, and let M be its colimit as commutative monoids. Each of the three properties is witnessed by finitely many elements, so each can be checked at a finite stage:
- If a+c = b+c in M, then this already holds at some stage, where integrality gives a = b.
- If nx = ny in M^gp, this holds at some stage, so x = y there.
- If nx ∈ M, then nx lies in M_j at some stage, and saturation of M_j gives x ∈ M_j.
- If x+y = 0, this holds at some stage, so x = 0.

So M is again an object, and it is the colimit in our category.

In particular P = colim_S P_S. Pushouts (pushout, then integralize, saturate, sharpen) commute with this colimit, because they are colimits.

**1.2 Descent of f.p. objects (sketched; standard argument).** Let Q be f.p. under P. Then Q is the filtered colimit, over pairs (S, finite T ⊂ Q), of the images R_{S,T} of P ⊕_{P_S} Q'_{S,T}, where Q'_{S,T} is the saturated sharp image of P_S ⊕ N^T. Because Q is f.p., id_Q factors through some stage. So Q is a retract of R = P ⊕_{P_S} Q' with Q' fine over P_S.

The idempotent e of R is determined by finitely many data. After enlarging S, it therefore descends to an idempotent e_S of a fine R_S over P_S, with R = P ⊕_{P_S} R_S. Then:
- Q is the coequalizer of (e, id).
- Coequalizers commute with base change.
- The image of an idempotent on a fine monoid is fine.

Hence Q ≅ P ⊕_{P_S} Q_S with Q_S = image(e_S) fine. Morphisms and pushouts between f.p. objects descend in the same way, after enlarging S. The point is that Hom_P(P ⊕_{P_S} Q_S, X) = Hom_{P_S}(Q_S, X), and Q_S is finitely presented over P_S. (Sketch only: the bookkeeping of "enlarge S" is routine and is not written out.)

*Proof.*

Setup. Write Q = P ⊕_{P_0} Q_0 with P_0 = P_{S_0} and Q_0 fine, using f_0 : P_0 → Q_0. Put G = (P^gp ⊕ Q_0^gp)/P_0^gp modulo torsion. The pushout is Q = R/R^×, where R is the saturation in G of the image of P ⊕ Q_0.

Characterizing the kernel. Let x ∈ P. Then f(x) = 0 iff x is a unit of R. That holds iff there are n ≥ 1, p ∈ P and q ∈ Q_0 with
- -nx = p + q in G,
- i.e. (−nx − p, −q) lies in the image of P_0^gp, up to torsion,
- i.e. there are m ≥ 1 and a ∈ L := P_0^gp with m(nx + p) = −a in P^gp and mq = f_0^gp(a).

Hence Φ_Q is the face generated by the set −K, where
K = { a ∈ L : f_0^gp(a) ∈ Q_0 and −a ∈ P }.

Here we used saturation of Q_0: f_0^gp(a) = mq ∈ Q_0. Conversely, every −a with a ∈ K lies in the kernel: −a + a = 0 in R, and a ∈ R.

Describing K by cones. L is a lattice of finite rank. For any saturated monoid N, the intersection N ∩ L equals L ∩ cone_R(N ∩ L). Proof of this claim: if x ∈ L lies in the real cone, Carathéodory writes x as a nonnegative combination of linearly independent elements of N ∩ L. The coefficients are then rational, so kx ∈ N for some k ≥ 1, and saturation gives x ∈ N.

Apply this to (f_0^gp)^{-1}(Q_0) and to (−P) ∩ L. Writing C(·) for the real cone spanned:
K = L ∩ C(A) ∩ C(−P ∩ L), with A = (f_0^gp)^{-1}(Q_0).
So K = L ∩ D for a convex cone D ⊃ C(K).

Choosing a generator. Pick finitely many elements of K that span the linear span of K, and let e be their sum. Then e lies in the relative interior of C(K). Now take any c ∈ K. For t ≫ 0 we have te − c ∈ C(K) ∩ L ⊂ K. So −c = −te + (te − c) with −(te − c) ∈ P, which gives −c ≤ t(−e) in P.

Conclusion. Every element of Φ_Q is ≤ a multiple of −e: if x ∈ Φ_Q, then x ≤ −a ≤ t(−e) for some a ∈ K. Also −e ∈ Φ_Q. So Φ_Q is the face generated by x_Q := −e.

Descent. Finally take S ⊃ S_0 ∪ {−e}. Then −e ∈ P_S, and −e already becomes a unit in P_S ⊕_{P_0} Q_0, since e ∈ L maps into Q_0. ∎

- B_P is a preorder, equivalent to the poset of principal faces.
- (Lan F)(Q) = F(P[−x_Q]^♯) for f.p. Q.
- π^{-1}F is the sheafification of F∘b on f.p. objects.

## 2. Valuations and covers

**Extension can fail (proved).** A valuation w of P_S need not extend to P. Take P = N^2, S = {e1, e1+2e2}, and w with w(e1+2e2) = 0 < w(e1). Any extension would need 2w(e2) = −w(e1) < 0.

**What survives (proved).** Every valuation v of P restricts to valuations of the P_S. Conversely, by Theorem 1.3, kernel faces are detected at finite level. But a birhizomic cover {Q → Q_i} of Q over P only needs to cover valuations of Q. Its descended family {Q_S → Q_{i,S}}, after Lemma K and enlarging S, covers exactly the valuations of Q_S that extend to Q. Valuations of Q_S that do not extend need not be covered. So **covers do not descend to covers over P_S**, and the topos Sh(A_P) is *not* naively the limit of the Sh(A_{P_S}).

A further unchecked point: birhizomy of P → Q_i at g is also not obviously inherited by P_S → Q_{i,S}. Test factorizations through infinitesimal maps over P_S do not come from P.

Proposed replacement (not carried out): use instead the site of f.p. objects over P_S, with the topology generated by families that cover the closed subset Val(P)|_{P_S} ⊂ Val(P_S). Then Sh(A_P) would be the limit of these modified sites. For SGA 4 VI 8.7 one would need these sites to be coherent with transition maps that preserve coverings. Lemma K provides finite subcovers, so quasi-compactness is plausible. However, the analogue of Background B's Step 4 (contractible nerves) must then be proved for the restricted valuation sets. Those sets are defined by infinitely many strict inequalities, so they are neither closed nor polyhedral, and the closed-convex nerve theorem does not apply directly.

## 3. Cohomology

A direct Čech approach needs the following. Take a finite subcomplex L of N_τ (the nerve of {E_i ∩ C_Ω}). One must find S such that L lies inside a contractible complex, computed from real (or finite-rank) valuations of Q_S that extend to P.

The witnesses for the simplices of L are finitely many valuations of P. Their restrictions to P_S are valuations of Q_S. For them, convex-hull arguments would work only if the sets E_{i,S} were closed in a common finite-dimensional space. For rank > 1 valuations they are not: this is the [0,1) ∪ [1,2] obstruction noted in Background B. I could not close this gap.

## 4. Summary of status

Proved:
- Filtered colimits stay in the category (1.1).
- Kernel faces of f.p. maps out of an arbitrary P are principal, and they are detected at a finite stage (1.3).
- Hence Step 0 (the Kan extension formula) holds for all P.
- Covers do not naively descend to P_S, because valuations of P_S need not extend (§2, with explicit examples).

Sketched: descent of f.p. objects, morphisms and pushouts (1.2).

Not established (open):
- (a) Whether a birhizomic cover over P descends to a family over some P_S that covers Val(P)|_{P_S} and consists of maps that are birhizomic in a suitable relative sense.
- (b) Contractibility of the kernel nerves N_τ for non-finitely-generated P. This needs a nerve theorem for the non-closed convex valuation sets.
- (c) Therefore whether R π_* π^{-1} F ≅ F holds for arbitrary P. The reduction yields no new case beyond finitely generated P. Not even the case where P^gp has finite rank is settled: that case still faces obstacle (b), via the example P = {x ∈ Z^3 : x3 > 0, or x3 = 0 and x1, x2 ≥ 0}.

Used without proof: the Background B result for fine P (taken as the black box).

# Answer to round3_q1: the question for finitely generated P

**Result.** For every fine monoid P (finitely generated, saturated, sharp) and every presheaf of abelian groups F on B_P^op, the unit F -> R pi_* pi^{-1} F is a quasi-isomorphism. The proof follows Background B, with every step checked. Lemma K gets a new proof by induction on dimension using tangent cones and flag valuations; the Tychonoff / quantifier-elimination sketch is not used. All steps are proved below; I found no false step. Steps 2–6 rely on standard facts quoted from memory: Borsuk's nerve theorem, Cartan's criterion, and the local conic structure of polyhedra. The case of P not finitely generated is not treated and remains open.

Conventions are those of Background B. Presheaves on A_P^op are covariant functors A_P -> Ab. Objects are maps under P. Fibre products in A_P^op are pushouts in the category of integral saturated sharp monoids.

## Step 0: the Kan extension and the unit

**B_P is a preorder.**
- Let f : P -> Q be in A_P. A map P[-x]^sharp -> Q under P exists iff f(x) = 0, and it is then unique, by the universal property.
- Phi_Q := f^{-1}(0) is a face of P, because Q is sharp and integral.
- P is finitely generated, so Phi_Q is generated as a face by x_Q, the sum of the generators of P lying in Phi_Q. Hence f(x) = 0 iff x lies in Phi_Q iff the face of x is contained in Phi_Q.
- So B_P is equivalent to the finite poset of faces of P.
- The category of pairs (b, b -> Q) has the terminal object b(Q) = P[-x_Q]^sharp.

**The left Kan extension.** Let u : B_P^op -> A_P^op be the inclusion. The left Kan extension of presheaves is
(u_p F)(Q) = colim over the pairs (b, b -> Q in A_P) of F(b).
Because there is a terminal object, this equals F(b(Q)) = F(Phi_Q). So u_p F = F∘b, and u_p is exact, being evaluation at an object.
Hence pi^{-1} F = (F∘b)^sh, and pi^{-1} is exact.

**pi_* is restriction to B_P.** We have Hom(pi^{-1}F, G) = Hom_psh(F∘b, G) = Hom(F, G|_B). So pi_* G = G|_B.
For b in B_P we have b(b) = b. The unit F(b) -> (F∘b)(b) = F(b) is therefore the identity, and it remains so after sheafification once Step 5 shows that sheafification does not change values on f.p. objects.

## Step 1: kernel faces via real valuations

**f.p. objects over fine P are fine.**
- Every object Q is the filtered union of the saturations sat(S), taken in S^gp, of the finitely generated submonoids S ⊂ Q containing f(P).
- Such an sat(S) lies in Q, because Q is saturated: if x is in S^gp ⊂ Q^gp and nx is in Q, then x is in Q. It is sharp, being a submonoid of Q. It is finitely generated by Gordan's lemma.
- Filtered unions of integral saturated sharp monoids are again of that kind, and they are the colimit in this category.
- If Q is f.p., the identity of Q factors through some sat(S). So Q is a retract of a fine monoid, i.e. an image of a finitely generated one, hence fine.
- Pushouts and compositions of f.p. maps are f.p. So all the Q_sigma below are fine.

**Strictly positive functional.** A fine saturated sharp Q has a strictly positive functional w in Q^v_R, with w(q) > 0 for every q ≠ 0. Indeed, sharpness means that the dual cone has nonempty interior; take w in that interior. Hence
Phi_Q = {x in P : w(f x) = 0 for all w in Q^v_R}.

**Real valuations of a pushout.** R_{>=0} is a monoid of our kind. By the universal property, Hom(Q_sigma, R_{>=0}) is the set of compatible tuples of maps Q_i -> R_{>=0}. So the image of Q_sigma^v_R in Q^v_R is T_sigma, the intersection over i in sigma of the T_i.
Each T_i is a closed polyhedral cone, being the linear image of a polyhedral cone. Applying the formula above to Q_sigma gives
Phi_{Q_sigma} = {x in P : w(x) = 0 for all w in T_sigma}.

## Step 2: Lemma K (proved)

Put S = Q^v_R, a closed polyhedral cone in Hom(Q^gp, R) = R^n.

**Definition.** A flag (d_0, ..., d_m) of vectors *lies in* a closed polyhedral cone C if the sum over k of δ^k d_k lies in C for all sufficiently small δ > 0. Writing C = {ℓ_j >= 0}, this is equivalent to: for every j, the tuple (ℓ_j(d_0), ..., ℓ_j(d_m)) is >= 0 in the lexicographic order. Indeed, a polynomial in δ is >= 0 for all small δ > 0 iff its lowest nonzero coefficient is positive.

**Hypothesis (H): every flag lying in S lies in some T_i.** Proof of (H) from the cover property:
- Let V be the nonnegative part of R^{m+1} with the lexicographic order. V is a valuative monoid.
- A flag lying in S defines a valuation v : Q -> V, q ↦ (d_0(q), ..., d_m(q)).
- By the cover property, v factors through some Q_i -> V. The components of this lift give a flag (d'_k) in Hom(Q_i^gp, R) lying in Q_i^v_R. Its image is (d_k), so the sum of δ^k d_k lies in T_i for small δ.

**Local conic structure (standard).** Let C be a polyhedral set and w a point of C. Then TC_C(w) := {d : w + δd ∈ C for small δ > 0} is a closed polyhedral cone, cut out by the constraints active at w. There is a ball N around w with C ∩ N = (w + TC_C(w)) ∩ N.

**Lemma K.** Let S be a closed polyhedral cone in R^n and {T_i} a family of closed polyhedral cones T_i ⊂ S satisfying (H). Then finitely many T_i cover S.

*Proof.* Induction on n.

*Base case n = 0.* The flag (0) gives some T_i containing 0, so T_i = S.

*Reduction to a local statement.* Since everything is conic, and 0 is covered by the case m = 0, it suffices to cover a neighbourhood in S of each point w with |w| = 1. Compactness of S ∩ (unit sphere) then finishes the proof.

*The local cover at w.*
1. Let I_w = {i : w ∈ T_i}. Every cone TC_S(w) and TC_i(w), for i in I_w, contains the line Rw.
2. Put S' = TC_S(w)/Rw and T_i' = TC_i(w)/Rw in R^n/Rw, which has dimension n-1. These are closed polyhedral cones, T_i' ⊂ S'.
3. *(H) holds for S' and the T_i'.*
   - Take a flag (e_0, ..., e_m) lying in S', with lifts d_1, ..., d_{m+1}. Because TC_S(w) contains Rw, the flag (d_1, ..., d_{m+1}) lies in TC_S(w).
   - Put x_δ = sum of δ^{k-1} d_k. It lies in TC_S(w) and stays bounded. By local conic structure, w + δ x_δ lies in S for small δ. So the flag (w, d_1, ..., d_{m+1}) lies in S.
   - By (H) it lies in some T_i. Letting δ -> 0 gives w ∈ T_i, so i is in I_w.
   - By local conic structure of T_i, δ x_δ lies in TC_i(w), hence x_δ lies in TC_i(w). So the flag (e_k) lies in T_i'.
4. By induction, a finite set F ⊂ I_w of the T_i' covers S'. Hence the TC_i(w), i in F, cover TC_S(w).
5. Choose a ball N around w on which local conic structure holds for S and for the T_i, i in F. If x lies in S ∩ N, then x - w lies in TC_S(w), so x - w lies in TC_i(w) for some i in F, so x lies in (w + TC_i(w)) ∩ N ⊂ T_i. ∎

This yields a finite J_0 ⊂ I with the union of the T_i, i in J_0, equal to Q^v_R. (Note that Lemma A shows the cover property, not just covering of S by the T_i, is essential: S can be covered by infinitely many rays with no finite subcover.)

## Step 3: the Čech complex of I_{tau,A}∘b

**The presheaf I_{tau,A}.** Define I_{tau,A}(b) = A if Phi_b ⊂ tau, and 0 otherwise, with identity transition maps when both values are A.
- This is a functor: if b -> b', then Phi_b ⊂ Phi_b'. So a value A at b' forces the value A at b.
- A map F -> I_{tau,A} amounts to compatible maps F(b) -> A for Phi_b ⊂ tau. These are determined by their component at tau, since F(b) -> F(tau) -> A. Hence Hom(F, I_{tau,A}) = Hom(F(tau), A), and I_{tau,A} is injective when A is.
- F embeds into the product over the finitely many faces tau of I_{tau, E(F(tau))}, where E denotes the injective hull. Iterating this embedding on cokernels gives injective resolutions by finite products of such presheaves.

**Identification of the Čech complex.** Let G = I_{tau,A}∘b and let {Q -> Q_i} be a covering of an f.p. object Q.
- G(Q_sigma) = A iff Phi_{Q_sigma} ⊂ tau.
- This holds iff T_sigma meets C := {w ∈ S : w(x) > 0 for all x ∈ P \ tau}.
  - (⇐) A point of T_sigma ∩ C kills nothing outside tau.
  - (⇒) Let w_0 be the sum of the generators of the polyhedral cone T_sigma. Then ker(w_0) ∩ P = Phi_{Q_sigma} ⊂ tau, so w_0 lies in C.
- C is convex: it suffices to impose w(x) > 0 on the finitely many generators of P outside tau.
- Transition maps between nonzero terms are identities.

So the Čech complex of G on the covering is the ordered cochain complex, with coefficients A, of N_tau = {finite tuples sigma : T_sigma ∩ C ≠ ∅}, the nerve of {T_i ∩ C}. (The empty tuple corresponds to Q itself.) The ordered cochain complex computes the simplicial cohomology of N_tau (standard).

## Step 4: N_tau is contractible

**If C ∩ S is empty**, then N_tau is empty and G(Q) = 0, so all Čech groups vanish.

**Otherwise:**
1. Take a finite subcomplex L of N_tau, and let J' = vertices(L) ∪ J_0, which is finite.
2. Choose a witness point in T_sigma ∩ C for each simplex sigma of N_tau(J'). Let D be their convex hull. D is compact, convex, nonempty and contained in C.
3. The sets T_i ∩ D, i in J', are compact and convex. They cover D, because D ⊂ S is covered by the T_i, i in J_0.
4. Their nerve is exactly N_tau(J'): it is contained in N_tau(J') because D ⊂ C, and it contains N_tau(J') because of the witnesses.
5. **Nerve theorem (Borsuk 1948; Leray), quoted from memory:** the nerve of a finite family of compact convex sets in R^n is homotopy equivalent to their union. Hence N_tau(J') ≃ D, which is contractible.
6. So every finite subcomplex lies in a contractible finite subcomplex. Therefore the reduced homology of N_tau vanishes, since homology commutes with this direct limit.
7. The augmented chain complex is then a free acyclic complex, so it is split exact. Applying Hom(-, A) gives cohomology A in degree 0 and 0 in degrees > 0.

**Conclusion.** The Čech cohomology of G on every covering of every f.p. object is G(Q) in degree 0 and 0 in positive degrees.

## Step 5: the sheaf property

1. Take 0 -> F -> I^0 -> I^1 with I^0, I^1 finite products of injectives of the form I_{tau,A}.
2. Composing with b is exact. The Čech H^0 is left exact.
3. By Step 4, I^0∘b and I^1∘b satisfy the sheaf condition on all coverings of f.p. objects. Hence so does F∘b, as a kernel.
4. Coverings of f.p. objects, and all their fibre products, consist of f.p. objects, because birhizomic maps are f.p. by definition.
5. So the plus construction does not change values on f.p. objects: pi^{-1}F(Q) = F(Phi_Q) for f.p. Q, and pi_* pi^{-1} F = F via the unit, which is the identity by Step 0.

## Step 6: higher vanishing

**Cartan's criterion** (Stacks Project, tag 03F7, from memory). Let B be a set of objects of a site and Cov a set of coverings such that:
- every covering in Cov is a covering of an object of B and has its members in B;
- all fibre products U_{i_0} × ... × U_{i_p} of a covering in Cov lie in B;
- for U in B, the coverings of U in Cov are cofinal among all coverings of U.

If a sheaf G has Ȟ^p(𝒰, G) = 0 for all 𝒰 in Cov and all p > 0, then H^p(U, G) = 0 for all U in B and all p > 0.

**Application.**
- Take B = f.p. objects and Cov = all coverings of objects in B. The hypotheses hold: cofinality is trivial, and the members and fibre products are f.p.
- G = pi^{-1}I_{tau,A} agrees with I_{tau,A}∘b on B by Step 5, so Step 4 gives the required Čech vanishing. Finite products of such G are acyclic as well.
- Since pi^{-1} is exact, pi^{-1}F -> pi^{-1}I^• is a resolution by sheaves acyclic on B.
- For U in B, H^p(U, pi^{-1}F) is therefore the p-th cohomology of I^•(Phi_U), which is exact in degrees > 0. So H^p(U, pi^{-1}F) = 0 for p > 0.

**R^p pi_*.** pi_* is right adjoint to the exact functor pi^{-1}, so it preserves injectives. It is restriction to B. Hence R^p pi_* G is the presheaf b ↦ H^p(b, G). Every P[-x]^sharp is f.p., so R^p pi_* pi^{-1} F = 0 for p > 0, and R^0 pi_* pi^{-1} F = F.

**Answer: YES for finitely generated P.**

## Sanity check: P = N^2

The faces are 0, ⟨e1⟩, ⟨e2⟩ and N^2, so S = R_{>=0}^2 and C is respectively:
- tau = 0: the open quadrant;
- tau = ⟨e1⟩: {w_1 = 0, w_2 > 0};
- tau = ⟨e2⟩: {w_1 > 0, w_2 = 0};
- tau = N^2: all of S.

Consider a cover made of the three localizations P[-e1]^sharp, P[-e2]^sharp, P[-e1-e2]^sharp, together with finitely many R4-type open cones. Here T for P[-e1]^sharp is the ray {w_1 = 0}.

Coverage must include the flag valuations at the boundary rays. For example, the flag (w, d) = ((0,1), (1,0)) must lie in some T_i, so some T_i is a 2-dimensional cone containing the ray w_1 = 0. For tau = ⟨e1⟩, the members meeting C are the localization at e1 and the cones containing that ray. They pairwise meet along that ray inside C, so N_tau is a full simplex, which is contractible. The other three faces behave the same way. This is consistent with the general proof.

## Status

- **Proved:** the full statement for fine P (Steps 0–6 and Lemma K, the latter via a new tangent-cone induction).
- **Quoted from memory:** Borsuk's nerve theorem, Cartan's criterion (Stacks tag 03F7), and the local conic structure of polyhedra.
- **Open:** non-finitely-generated P. There Step 0 (principal kernel faces), Step 1 (real valuations detecting kernels) and the nerve theorem for non-closed convex sets all fail or are unverified; see the Remark in Background B.

=== END OF ANSWER round3_q1 ===

\begin{document} \section{Problem statement} In the following, a monoid is an integral, saturated, sharp, commutative, unital semigroup.  Monoids are written additively.  A monoid $M$ induces a translation invariant partial order on its associated group $M^{\rm gp}$ such that $x \geq 0$ if and only if $x \in M$.  A valuative monoid is a monoid in which the associated partial order is a total order. If $M$ is a monoid, $x \in M^{\rm gp}$, and $y \in M$, we write $x \prec y$ to mean that there are integers $m$ and $n$ such that $my \leq x \leq ny$. A monoid homomorphism $f : M \to N$ is called \emph{infinitesimal} if the following condition holds: \begin{enumerate}[label=$\bullet$] \item If there are $x \in M^{\rm gp}$ and $y \in M$ such that $f(x) \in N$ and $x \prec y$ and $f(y) \prec f(x)$ then $x \in M$. \end{enumerate} If $P \xrightarrow f Q \xrightarrow g N$ are monoid homomorphisms, we say that $f$ is \emph{birhizomic} at $g$ if it is of finite presentation in the category of (integral, saturated, sharp) monoids and, for every factorization of $gf$ through monoid homomorphisms $P \xrightarrow h M \xrightarrow p N$ with $p$ infinitesimal, there is a unique monoid homomorphism $u : Q \to M$ with $pu = g$ and $uf = h$. A family of morphisms $P \rightarrow Q_i$ is called a birhizomic cover if, for every valuative monoid $V$ and every homomorphism $v : P \to V$, there is a factorization of $v$ through some $Q_i \to V$ such that $P \to Q_i$ is birhizomic at $Q_i \to V$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  Let $A_P$ be the category of monoid homomorphisms $P \to Q$.  The birhizomic covers form a Grothendieck topology on $A_P^{\rm op}$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  For any $x$ in $P$, there is an initial monoid homomorphism $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$ that sends $x$ to $0$.  Let $B_P$ be the full subcategory of $A_P$ consisting of homomorphisms $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$, for $x \in P$. \begin{document} \section{Problem statement} In the following, a monoid is an integral, saturated, sharp, commutative, unital semigroup.  Monoids are written additively.  A monoid $M$ induces a translation invariant partial order on its associated group $M^{\rm gp}$ such that $x \geq 0$ if and only if $x \in M$.  A valuative monoid is a monoid in which the associated partial order is a total order. If $M$ is a monoid, $x \in M^{\rm gp}$, and $y \in M$, we write $x \prec y$ to mean that there are integers $m$ and $n$ such that $my \leq x \leq ny$. A monoid homomorphism $f : M \to N$ is called \emph{infinitesimal} if the following condition holds: \begin{enumerate}[label=$\bullet$] \item If there are $x \in M^{\rm gp}$ and $y \in M$ such that $f(x) \in N$ and $x \prec y$ and $f(y) \prec f(x)$ then $x \in M$. \end{enumerate} If $P \xrightarrow f Q \xrightarrow g N$ are monoid homomorphisms, we say that $f$ is \emph{birhizomic} at $g$ if it is of finite presentation in the category of (integral, saturated, sharp) monoids and, for every factorization of $gf$ through monoid homomorphisms $P \xrightarrow h M \xrightarrow p N$ with $p$ infinitesimal, there is a unique monoid homomorphism $u : Q \to M$ with $pu = g$ and $uf = h$. A family of morphisms $P \rightarrow Q_i$ is called a birhizomic cover if, for every valuative monoid $V$ and every homomorphism $v : P \to V$, there is a factorization of $v$ through some $Q_i \to V$ such that $P \to Q_i$ is birhizomic at $Q_i \to V$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  Let $A_P$ be the category of monoid homomorphisms $P \to Q$.  The birhizomic covers form a Grothendieck topology on $A_P^{\rm op}$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  For any $x$ in $P$, there is an initial monoid homomorphism $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$ that sends $x$ to $0$.  Let $B_P$ be the full subcategory of $A_P$ consisting of homomorphisms $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$, for $x \in P$. We have given $A_P^{\rm op}$ the birhizomic topology and $B_P^{\rm op}$ the trivial topology in which all presheaves are sheaves.  The inclusion $B_P^{\rm op} \subset A_P^{\rm op}$ is left exact.  By left Kan extension and sheafification, it extends to a functor $\pi^{-1} : \operatorname{Sh}(B_P) \to \operatorname{Sh}(A_P)$ on the categories of sheaves.   Let $\pi_\ast$ be the right adjoint of $\pi^{-1}$. \paragraph{Question} \em Is it the case that, for all presheaves of abelian groups $F$ on $B_P^{\rm op}$, the morphism $$F \to \mathrm R \pi_\ast \pi^{-1} F$$ is a quasi-isomorphism? \end{document}

\begin{document} \section{Problem statement} In the following, a monoid is an integral, saturated, sharp, commutative, unital semigroup.  Monoids are written additively.  A monoid $M$ induces a translation invariant partial order on its associated group $M^{\rm gp}$ such that $x \geq 0$ if and only if $x \in M$.  A valuative monoid is a monoid in which the associated partial order is a total order. If $M$ is a monoid, $x \in M^{\rm gp}$, and $y \in M$, we write $x \prec y$ to mean that there are integers $m$ and $n$ such that $my \leq x \leq ny$. A monoid homomorphism $f : M \to N$ is called \emph{infinitesimal} if the following condition holds: \begin{enumerate}[label=$\bullet$] \item If there are $x \in M^{\rm gp}$ and $y \in M$ such that $f(x) \in N$ and $x \prec y$ and $f(y) \prec f(x)$ then $x \in M$. \end{enumerate} If $P \xrightarrow f Q \xrightarrow g N$ are monoid homomorphisms, we say that $f$ is \emph{birhizomic} at $g$ if it is of finite presentation in the category of (integral, saturated, sharp) monoids and, for every factorization of $gf$ through monoid homomorphisms $P \xrightarrow h M \xrightarrow p N$ with $p$ infinitesimal, there is a unique monoid homomorphism $u : Q \to M$ with $pu = g$ and $uf = h$. A family of morphisms $P \rightarrow Q_i$ is called a birhizomic cover if, for every valuative monoid $V$ and every homomorphism $v : P \to V$, there is a factorization of $v$ through some $Q_i \to V$ such that $P \to Q_i$ is birhizomic at $Q_i \to V$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  Let $A_P$ be the category of monoid homomorphisms $P \to Q$.  The birhizomic covers form a Grothendieck topology on $A_P^{\rm op}$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  For any $x$ in $P$, there is an initial monoid homomorphism $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$ that sends $x$ to $0$.  Let $B_P$ be the full subcategory of $A_P$ consisting of homomorphisms $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$, for $x \in P$. We have given $A_P^{\rm op}$ the birhizomic topology and $B_P^{\rm op}$ the trivial topology in which all presheaves are sheaves.  The inclusion $B_P^{\rm op} \subset A_P^{\rm op}$ is left exact.  By left Kan extension and sheafification, it extends to a functor $\pi^{-1} : \operatorname{Sh}(B_P) \to \operatorname{Sh}(A_P)$ on the categories of sheaves.   Let $\pi_\ast$ be the right adjoint of $\pi^{-1}$. \paragraph{Question} \em Is it the case that, for all presheaves of abelian groups $F$ on $B_P^{\rm op}$, the morphism $$F \to \mathrm R \pi_\ast \pi^{-1} F$$ is a quasi-isomorphism? \end{document}

A monoid $M$ induces a translation invariant partial order on its associated group $M^{\rm gp}$ such that $x \geq 0$ if and only if $x \in M$.  A valuative monoid is a monoid in which the associated partial order is a total order. If $M$ is a monoid, $x \in M^{\rm gp}$, and $y \in M$, we write $x \prec y$ to mean that there are integers $m$ and $n$ such that $my \leq x \leq ny$. A monoid homomorphism $f : M \to N$ is called \emph{infinitesimal} if the following condition holds: \begin{enumerate}[label=$\bullet$] \item If there are $x \in M^{\rm gp}$ and $y \in M$ such that $f(x) \in N$ and $x \prec y$ and $f(y) \prec f(x)$ then $x \in M$. \end{enumerate} If $P \xrightarrow f Q \xrightarrow g N$ are monoid homomorphisms, we say that $f$ is \emph{birhizomic} at $g$ if it is of finite presentation in the category of (integral, saturated, sharp) monoids and, for every factorization of $gf$ through monoid homomorphisms $P \xrightarrow h M \xrightarrow p N$ with $p$ infinitesimal, there is a unique monoid homomorphism $u : Q \to M$ with $pu = g$ and $uf = h$. A family of morphisms $P \rightarrow Q_i$ is called a birhizomic cover if, for every valuative monoid $V$ and every homomorphism $v : P \to V$, there is a factorization of $v$ through some $Q_i \to V$ such that $P \to Q_i$ is birhizomic at $Q_i \to V$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  Let $A_P$ be the category of monoid homomorphisms $P \to Q$.  The birhizomic covers form a Grothendieck topology on $A_P^{\rm op}$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  For any $x$ in $P$, there is an initial monoid homomorphism $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$ that sends $x$ to $0$.  Let $B_P$ be the full subcategory of $A_P$ consisting of homomorphisms $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$, for $x \in P$. We have given $A_P^{\rm op}$ the birhizomic topology and $B_P^{\rm op}$ the trivial topology in which all presheaves are sheaves.  The inclusion $B_P^{\rm op} \subset A_P^{\rm op}$ is left exact.  By left Kan extension and sheafification, it extends to a functor $\pi^{-1} : \operatorname{Sh}(B_P) \to \operatorname{Sh}(A_P)$ on the categories of sheaves.   Let $\pi_\ast$ be the right adjoint of $\pi^{-1}$. \paragraph{Question} \em Is it the case that, for all presheaves of abelian groups $F$ on $B_P^{\rm op}$, the morphism $$F \to \mathrm R \pi_\ast \pi^{-1} F$$ is a quasi-isomorphism? \end{document}

# Running summary after round 3 planning

## Goal
The problem fixes the claim (ledger #1, OPEN [GOAL]). For every monoid P (integral, saturated, sharp, and NOT assumed finitely generated) and every presheaf of abelian groups F on B_P^op, the map F -> R pi_* pi^{-1} F is a quasi-isomorphism. Answer YES = PROVED; a counterexample = REFUTED.

## Established so far (worker results)
- round1_q1 (#2): reduction. id_P is terminal in A_P^op and in B_P^op, and slices are the sites of the localizations. So the claim is equivalent to H^0(A_P, pi^{-1}F) = F(P) and H^{>0} = 0 for all P and F. The director's Step 6 below gives a cleaner route that needs no slicing.
- round1_q2 (#3): a map M -> N with M valuative is infinitesimal iff it kills no nonzero element. Every infinitesimal map kills no nonzero element of its source.
- round1_q3 (#4): the claim for P = N, at the level of valuations.
- round1_q4 (#5): the finite-poset lemma for subdivisions. It is not directly needed now.
- round2_q4 (#9): re-checked R1, R2 and R4. R2: every f.p. map is birhizomic at the zero map, and localizations are birhizomic everywhere. R4: open-cone extensions sat(P + <a_i>) are birhizomic when v(a_i) > 0 under the prec-control, given finite presentation. It also checked that I_{tau,A} (the co-skyscrapers on the face poset) are injective and that F embeds into their product. It flagged that pi^{-1} might not commute with infinite products; this is irrelevant for fine P, where the products are finite.
- round2_q1 (#10, #11): Lemma A and Proposition B.
  - Lemma A: let P be fine, P ⊂ Q ⊂ P^gp, and v nonzero on P\0. If P -> Q is birhizomic at g, then g > 0 on Q\0. The test object is M = {v > 0} ∪ {0}. In particular, closed subdivision charts are not birhizomic at wall valuations.
  - Proposition B: at rank one with v injective on P, the map is birhizomic iff g^{-1}(0) = 0.
  - Open there: whether the prec condition is necessary at higher rank, and maps that are not injective on groups.
- round2_q2 (#12): for fine P, B_P is the finite face poset. A filtration by up-sets plus the five lemma reduces the claim to F concentrated at one face.
- round2_q3: proved only two small observations; nothing load-bearing. (Its "Observation 1", that g is a retraction of f, is tautological because gf = id is assumed.)

## NEW: the director's proof outline for finitely generated P (ledger #13, OPEN until a worker writes it out and it is verified)
The full text is "Background B", reproduced verbatim inside round3_q1..q4.md. In summary:
- **Step 0.** For fine P, every kernel face Phi_Q = f^{-1}(0) is principal. The comma category for the left Kan extension has a terminal object b(Q) = P[-x_Q]^sharp. So Lan F = F∘b, with (F∘b)(Q) = F(Phi_Q). Presheaves on A_P^op are covariant functors on A_P.
- **Step 1.** For fine Q, Phi_Q = P ∩ T_Q^⊥, where T_Q is the cone of real valuations. Real valuations of a pushout are the compatible tuples, so T_sigma = ∩ T_i.
- **Step 2 (Lemma K).** Every birhizomic covering has a finite subfamily whose real cones T_i cover Q^v_R. Proof sketch: compactness of the patch space of total preorders on Q^gp⊗Q, plus Fourier–Motzkin/quantifier elimination, which makes the sets "factors through Q_i" clopen. Lemma K holds for arbitrary Q.
- **Step 3.** Every F has a finite injective resolution by products of I_{tau,A}. The Čech complex of I_{tau,A}∘b on a covering is the ordered cochain complex of N_tau = nerve of {T_i ∩ C}, where C = {w : w > 0 on P \ Phi_tau} is convex.
- **Step 4.** Every finite subcomplex of N_tau lies in a full subcomplex on J' ⊇ J_0, whose nerve is that of a finite compact convex cover of a compact convex set D, hence contractible. So N_tau is contractible.
- **Step 5.** Hence F∘b satisfies the sheaf condition on all coverings of f.p. objects, and pi^{-1}F = F∘b on f.p. objects. This gives pi_* pi^{-1} F = F.
- **Step 6.** Cartan's criterion (Stacks 03F7), with B = the f.p. objects and Cov = all their coverings, gives H^{>0}(U, pi^{-1}F) = 0 for all f.p. U, including the objects of B_P. R^p pi_* is computed objectwise, so the answer is YES for fine P.
- **Notable feature:** the outline uses only two properties of coverings: their members are f.p., and every valuation factors through some member. Birhizomicity itself is not used for fine P.

## Dead ends
- Covers by closed charts of subdivisions are not birhizomic (R3, Lemma A). The finite-poset lemma (#5) is not the mechanism.
- Exactness of pi_! = Lan along b fails in general: the comma categories are not filtered. So the "pi^{-1} preserves injectives" route is not available.
- The topological-space picture (R5: open-cone neighbourhoods, generic zero valuation, rank-two points gluing faces to the interior) is consistent with the outline but no longer needed for fine P.

## Open gaps
1. **(#13)** A complete rigorous write-up of the fine-P outline, especially:
   - Lemma K, in full;
   - the nerve theorem for compact convex sets and the passage to infinite complexes;
   - Cartan's criterion and its hypotheses (f.p. objects are closed under pushouts, and f.p. objects over fine P are fine);
   - the formula for R^p pi_*;
   - the interpretation that coverings of a non-terminal object Q are the birhizomic covers of Q.
2. **(#14)** Arbitrary P. Three issues:
   - (a) Are kernel faces of f.p. maps principal? A sketch says yes: the face generated by Y ∩ P, with Y a finitely generated monoid, is principal, using rational points of rational polyhedra and saturation.
   - (b) Real valuations do not detect faces. Example: P = {x3 > 0} ∪ (N^2 × 0) in Z^3.
   - (c) The nerve N_tau equals the nerve of {E_i ∩ C_Omega} for higher-rank valuations. These sets are convex in Hom(Q^gp, H) for a Hahn group H but not closed, so the convex nerve theorem fails. This is where the birhizomic prec condition may be essential: covers by "closed" sign splits are not birhizomic. A counterexample to the headline claim would need a birhizomic covering with disconnected or acyclicity-failing N_tau.
   - Observation: for a sign split by a, the overlap has kernel 0 whenever injective valuations of both signs exist (an order-extension argument). So sign splits cannot produce disconnection.
3. A reduction route for #14: P is a filtered union of fine P_S. Two caveats: valuations of P_S need not extend to P (example: P = N^2, S = {e1, e1+2e2}), and descending covers needs Lemma K.

## Next round (round 3 wave: 4 attempt queries, all carrying Background A (R1–R4, Lemma A/Prop B) and Background B verbatim)
- q1: a complete rigorous proof for fine P along Background B (target #13), with an N^2 sanity check.
- q2: a positive proof for arbitrary P: principal kernels, plus the property of birhizomic loci that makes N_tau contractible (target #14).
- q3: a counterexample hunt among non-fg P for a birhizomic covering with non-contractible N_tau, with birhizomicity rigorously verified; also an adversarial check of Background B.
- q4: reduce arbitrary P to fine P via filtered unions, descent of f.p. objects and coverings, and limits of topoi.

Afterwards: once q1 returns a complete fine-P proof, send it to two verify queries. If q2 or q4 yields arbitrary P, that becomes the [GOAL] proof. If only fine P is proved, the posed goal still covers all P; keep #14 as the target (escalation round 4).
