153	- (ii) For 𝒰 ∈ Cov, every member Q_i, and every iterated fibre product Q_{i_0...i_p} := Q_{i_0} ⊔_Q ... ⊔_Q Q_{i_p} (a pushout in Mon), lies in 𝔅.
154	- (iii) For Q ∈ 𝔅 and every covering sieve R of Q, there is 𝒰 ∈ Cov all of whose members lie in R. In particular, every covering family of Q is refined by a member of Cov.
155	- (iv) In 𝒰 ∈ Cov, every valuation of Q factors through some member.
156	
157	*Proof.*
158	- (i) Immediate from the definition of J.
159	- (ii) Lemma 0.1(a)(b).
160	- (iii) By (★), R contains the sieve of a birhizomic cover 𝒰' of Q. By Lemma 3.2, its witness subfamily 𝒰 lies in Cov. Each member of 𝒰 is a member of 𝒰', so it lies in R. If R is generated by a covering family {V_j -> Q}, each member of 𝒰 factors through some V_j. Choosing such factorizations gives the refinement map.
161	- (iv) Each 𝒰 ∈ Cov is a birhizomic cover. ∎
162	
163	So the coverings of f.p. objects with all members f.p. are cofinal among all coverings of f.p. objects, and their iterated fibre products are f.p.
164	
165	## §4 Čech complexes on Cov
166	
167	**Conventions.**
168	- For a presheaf G on A_P^op and 𝒰 = {Q -> Q_i}_{i ∈ I}, the Čech complex is that of Stacks, with *all* ordered tuples, repetitions allowed:
169	  Č^p(𝒰, G) = ∏_{t = (i_0..i_p) ∈ I^{p+1}} G(Q_t),  (ds)_{i_0..i_{p+1}} = Σ_j (-1)^j s_{i_0..î_j..i_{p+1}}|_{Q_{i_0..i_{p+1}}}.
170	- The *augmented* complex puts G(Q) in degree -1, with the restriction maps as augmentation.
171	- For a tuple t, write set(t) for its underlying set and Phi_t := ker(P -> Q_t).
172	
173	**Lemma 4.1 (repeated indices).** Phi_t = Phi_{set(t)}, where for a finite set σ ⊂ I, Q_σ is the pushout over Q of the Q_i, i ∈ σ, as in Result D.
174	
175	*Proof.* There are maps under P (indeed under Q) in both directions between Q_σ and Q_t:
176	- Q_σ -> Q_t sends the factor Q_i to the first slot of t equal to i.
177	- Q_t -> Q_σ sends the slot j to the coprojection of Q_{i_j}. Thus a repeated factor is mapped by the codiagonal.
178	
179	By 1.1 the kernels are contained in each other. ∎
180	
181	So for σ ⊂ σ' we have Phi_σ ⊂ Phi_{σ'}, and the sets N_tau = {σ : Phi_σ ⊂ tau} of Result D are simplicial complexes.
182	
183	**Proposition 4.2.** Let Q ∈ 𝔅, 𝒰 ∈ Cov a covering of Q, tau ∈ Pr(P), A an abelian group, and G = Lan I_{tau,A}.
184	- (a) If Phi_Q ⊄ tau, the augmented Čech complex of G on 𝒰 is zero.
185	- (b) If Phi_Q ⊂ tau, it is isomorphic to the augmented ordered cochain complex of N_tau with coefficients A.
186	
187	In both cases it is exact.
188	
189	*Proof.* All the objects Q, Q_t lie in 𝔅 (Lemma 3.5(ii)). By Lemma 1.5, G(Q_t) ≅ I_{tau,A}(Phi_t). This is A if Phi_t ⊂ tau and 0 otherwise. Restriction maps between two nonzero terms are id_A.
190	
191	(a) Each Q_t receives a map from Q under P, so Phi_Q ⊂ Phi_t ⊄ tau. Hence every term is 0.
192	
193	(b) By Lemma 4.1, Č^p ≅ ∏_{t ∈ I^{p+1}, set(t) ∈ N_tau} A. With the differential above, this is exactly the ordered cochain complex C^p_ord(N_tau; A) = Hom(C^ord_p(N_tau), A). Here C^ord_p is free on the ordered (p+1)-tuples of vertices, repetitions allowed, spanning a simplex. The degree -1 term is G(Q) = A, and the augmentation is the diagonal A -> ∏_i A, i.e. the dual of the augmentation C^ord_0 -> Z.
194	
195	*Exactness.* Result D applies:
196	- the members of 𝒰 are f.p. maps Q -> Q_i;
197	- every valuation of Q factors through one of them (Lemma 3.5(iv));
198	- tau ⊃ Phi_Q.
199	
200	Result D's Q_σ and Phi_σ are ours. So the augmented ordered cochain complex of N_tau with coefficients A is exact.
201	
202	*If "ordered" in Result D means tuples without repetition, or the oriented complex:* the ordered chain complex with repetitions and the oriented chain complex of a simplicial complex are naturally chain homotopy equivalent, compatibly with augmentations (Spanier, *Algebraic Topology*, Thm. 4.3.8, quoted from memory). So exactness of one augmented chain complex gives exactness of the other.
203	- An exact augmented chain complex of free abelian groups, bounded below, is split exact.
204	- Hence its Hom into A is exact.
205	
206	So in every reading, (b) is exact. ∎
207	
208	**Corollary 4.3.** Let 0 -> F -> I^0 -> I^1 -> ... be the resolution of Lemma 2.2. For Q ∈ 𝔅 and 𝒰 ∈ Cov over Q, the augmented Čech complex of each Lan I^k on 𝒰 is exact.
209	
210	*Proof.* On 𝔅, Lan I^k ≅ ∏_tau Lan I_{tau,A_{k,tau}} naturally (Lemma 1.5), and only objects of 𝔅 occur in the complex. So the augmented Čech complex is the product of the complexes of Prop. 4.2, and a product of exact complexes of abelian groups is exact. ∎
211	
212	## §5 Sheafification does not change values on f.p. objects
213	
214	**5.0 Sieve facts.** These are standard (SGA4 II; Stacks, Sites), quoted from memory, and each is easily checked.
215	- Let R be the sieve on U generated by a family {U_i -> U} whose pairwise fibre products exist. Then Hom_PSh(R, G) is the equalizer of ∏_i G(U_i) ⇉ ∏_{(i,j)} G(U_i ×_U U_j). (A map R -> G is determined by its values on the generators. A compatible family defines one: given V -> U in R, factor it as V -> U_i -> U and take s_i|_V. Two factorizations yield a map V -> U_i ×_U U_j, so the value is well defined.)
216	- The plus construction is G^+(U) = colim_{R ∈ J(U)} Hom(R, G), over J(U) ordered by reverse inclusion.
217	- G^# = G^{++}, and G -> G^+ is natural.
218	- A sheaf satisfies the equalizer condition for every covering family.
219	
220	**Lemma 5.1.** Let G be a presheaf on A_P^op such that, for every Q ∈ 𝔅 and every 𝒰 ∈ Cov over Q, the sequence
221	 0 -> G(Q) -> ∏_i G(Q_i) -> ∏_{(i,j)} G(Q_{ij})
222	is exact. Then:
223	- G(Q) -> G^+(Q) is an isomorphism for all Q ∈ 𝔅;
224	- G^+ satisfies the same hypothesis;
225	- hence G(Q) -> G^#(Q) is an isomorphism for all Q ∈ 𝔅.
226	
227	*Proof.*
228	- By Lemma 3.5(iii), the sieves generated by members of Cov over Q are cofinal in J(Q). By 5.0 and the hypothesis, G(Q) -> Hom(R, G) is an isomorphism for each such R, compatibly with the transition maps (all are restrictions of the same element). So G(Q) -> G^+(Q) = colim Hom(R, G) is an isomorphism.
229	- For 𝒰 ∈ Cov over Q ∈ 𝔅, all the objects Q, Q_i, Q_{ij} lie in 𝔅 (Lemma 3.5(ii)). The natural map G -> G^+ is an isomorphism on all of them. So the sequence for G^+ is isomorphic to the one for G, and is exact.
230	- Apply the first point to G^+. ∎
231	
232	**Corollary 5.2.** For every presheaf F on B_P^op, Lan F satisfies the hypothesis of Lemma 5.1.
233	
234	*Proof.* Exactness of Lan gives an exact sequence 0 -> Lan F -> Lan I^0 -> Lan I^1 of presheaves.
235	- Lan I^0 and Lan I^1 satisfy the hypothesis of 5.1, by Cor. 4.3 in degrees -1, 0, 1.
236	- The functor G ↦ [the kernel of G(Q) -> ∏ G(Q_i) -> ∏ G(Q_ij), viewed as an equalizer] commutes with kernels of presheaves, since limits commute with limits.
237	- A diagram chase finishes the proof. Take s ∈ Lan F(Q) with all restrictions 0. Its image in Lan I^0(Q) has all restrictions 0, so it is 0, and hence s = 0. Next take a compatible family (s_i) for Lan F.
238	  - Its image in Lan I^0 glues to some t ∈ Lan I^0(Q).
239	  - The image of t in Lan I^1(Q) restricts to 0 on every Q_i, so it is 0.
240	  - Hence t comes from some s ∈ Lan F(Q), and s restricts to s_i by injectivity of Lan F(Q_i) -> Lan I^0(Q_i). ∎
241	
242	**Corollary 5.3.**
243	- For Q ∈ 𝔅, F(Phi_Q) ≅ Lan F(Q) -> pi^{-1}F(Q) is an isomorphism, natural in F and in Q ∈ 𝔅.
244	- In particular the unit F -> pi_* pi^{-1} F is an isomorphism, since every b ∈ B_P is in 𝔅 (1.2, 1.6).
245	- For the same reason, pi^{-1}I^k(Q) ≅ Lan I^k(Q) ≅ I^k(Phi_Q) for Q ∈ 𝔅, naturally in k.
246	- Hence the Čech complexes of pi^{-1}I^k on members of Cov are those of Cor. 4.3. So **Ȟ^p(𝒰, pi^{-1} I^k) = 0 for p > 0 and every 𝒰 ∈ Cov.**
247	
248	## §6 Cartan's criterion
249	
250	**Statement.** This is Stacks Project, Cohomology on Sites, the lemma at tag 03F7, quoted from memory.
251	- *Setting.* Let C be a site with fibre products of the needed objects, 𝔅 a set of objects, and Cov a set of covering families such that:
252	  - (1) every 𝒰 = {U_i -> U} ∈ Cov has U, U_i and all U_{i_0} ×_U ... ×_U U_{i_p} in 𝔅;
253	  - (2) for each U ∈ 𝔅, the members of Cov covering U are cofinal: every covering of U is refined by one of them.
254	- *Conclusion.* If an abelian sheaf G has Ȟ^p(𝒰, G) = 0 for all p > 0 and all 𝒰 ∈ Cov, then H^p(U, G) = 0 for all p > 0 and all U ∈ 𝔅.
255	
256	Here H^p(U, -) = R^pΓ(U, -) on Ab(C), with Γ(U, G) = G(U).
257	
258	To be self-contained I prove it, using only the version (2') of (2) that I verified in Lemma 3.5(iii): every covering sieve of U ∈ 𝔅 contains all members of some 𝒰 ∈ Cov over U.
259	
260	**Fact 6.1.** If I is an injective abelian sheaf and 𝒰 = {U_i -> U} is any family whose fibre products exist, then Ȟ^p(𝒰, I) = 0 for p > 0.
261	
262	*Proof.*
263	- Let Z_V be the free abelian presheaf on h_V, and set K_p = ⊕_{t ∈ I^{p+1}} Z_{U_t}, with the alternating face differential. Then Hom_PSh(K_•, G) = Č^•(𝒰, G).
264	- Evaluate at W. Hom(W, U_t) is the set of tuples (φ_0..φ_p), φ_j : W -> U_{i_j}, with a common composite ψ : W -> U. So K_•(W) = ⊕_ψ Z[T_ψ^{•+1}], where T_ψ = {(i, φ) : φ : W -> U_i over ψ}.
265	- Each summand is the chain complex of the full simplex on T_ψ, with repetitions. It is acyclic in positive degrees: when T_ψ ≠ ∅, prepending a fixed element gives a contracting homotopy of the augmented complex. Its H_0 is Z if T_ψ ≠ ∅ and 0 otherwise.
266	- So K_• is a presheaf resolution of Z_R, where R is the sieve generated by 𝒰.
267	- Sheafification is exact, so K_•^# is a resolution of Z_R^#.
268	- Hence Č^•(𝒰, I) = Hom_PSh(K_•, I) = Hom_Sh(K_•^#, I) is exact in positive degrees, because Hom_Sh(-, I) is exact. ∎
269	
270	**Proof of Cartan.** Let G satisfy the hypothesis. Choose an embedding G ↪ I with I an injective sheaf (Ab(C) is a Grothendieck category), and let Q = I/G be the sheaf quotient. Sections are left exact, so G(W) = ker(I(W) -> Q(W)) for every W.
271	
272	*(a) I(V) -> Q(V) is onto for V ∈ 𝔅.*
273	- Take s ∈ Q(V). Since I -> Q is an epimorphism of sheaves, s lifts locally on some covering sieve R of V.
274	- By (2'), pick 𝒱 = {V_i -> V} ∈ Cov with members in R, and lifts t_i ∈ I(V_i) of s|_{V_i}.
275	- Put c_{ij} = t_j|_{V_ij} - t_i|_{V_ij}. It lies in G(V_ij), since it maps to s - s = 0 in Q. As c = dt in Č^•(𝒱, I), and Č^•(𝒱, G) ⊂ Č^•(𝒱, I), we get dc = 0 in Č^2(𝒱, G).
276	- Since Ȟ^1(𝒱, G) = 0, c = dg for some g ∈ Č^0(𝒱, G). Then (t_i - g_i) is compatible on all V_ij.
277	- I is a sheaf and 𝒱 is a covering family, so the family glues to t ∈ I(V). The image of t and s agree on every V_i, hence they are equal, because Q is a sheaf.
278	
279	*(b) Q again satisfies the hypothesis.*
280	- For 𝒰 ∈ Cov, all the U_t lie in 𝔅 by (1). So 0 -> Č^•(𝒰, G) -> Č^•(𝒰, I) -> Č^•(𝒰, Q) -> 0 is exact, by (a) and since products are exact.
281	- By Fact 6.1, Ȟ^p(𝒰, Q) ≅ Ȟ^{p+1}(𝒰, G) = 0 for p >= 1.
282	
283	*(c) Induction.*
284	- The long exact sequence gives H^1(U, G) = coker(I(U) -> Q(U)) = 0 for U ∈ 𝔅, by (a).
285	- It also gives H^p(U, G) ≅ H^{p-1}(U, Q) for p >= 2.
286	- Induction on p, applied to all sheaves satisfying the hypothesis at once, gives the claim using (b). ∎
287	
288	**Verification of the hypotheses in our situation.**
289	- C = (A_P^op, J); fibre products exist (§0).
290	- 𝔅 = the f.p. objects, a set in V; Cov as in 3.4, a set in V.
291	- (1) is Lemma 3.5(ii); Cov consists of covering families by Lemma 3.5(i).
292	- (2'), and hence (2), is Lemma 3.5(iii). This is where the non-f.p. members of covers are dealt with.
293	
294	## §7 Cohomology and the conclusion
295	
296	**7.1 The sheaves pi^{-1}I^k are acyclic on 𝔅.** By Cor. 5.3, Ȟ^p(𝒰, pi^{-1}I^k) = 0 for p > 0 and 𝒰 ∈ Cov. By §6, H^p(U, pi^{-1}I^k) = 0 for p > 0 and U ∈ 𝔅.
297	
298	**7.2 H^p(U, pi^{-1}F) for U ∈ 𝔅.**
299	- pi^{-1} is exact (1.6), so 0 -> pi^{-1}F -> pi^{-1}I^0 -> pi^{-1}I^1 -> ... is exact in Ab(A_P^op).
300	- Its terms are Γ(U, -)-acyclic for U ∈ 𝔅. By dimension shifting, H^p(U, pi^{-1}F) = H^p(pi^{-1}I^•(U)).
301	- By Cor. 5.3 this complex is I^•(Phi_U), naturally in k, and the augmented complex 0 -> F(Phi_U) -> I^0(Phi_U) -> ... is exact (Lemma 2.2).
302	- Hence **H^0(U, pi^{-1}F) = F(Phi_U), and H^p(U, pi^{-1}F) = 0 for p > 0, for all f.p. U.**
303	
304	**7.3 R^p pi_*.**
305	- pi_* = restriction to B_P (1.6). It is left exact, and preserves injectives as the right adjoint of the exact functor pi^{-1}. (The latter is not even needed below.)
306	- Let G -> J^• be an injective resolution in Ab(A_P^op). Then R^p pi_* G = H^p(J^•|_B).
307	- Cohomology in PSh(B_P) is objectwise, so (R^p pi_* G)(b) = H^p(J^•(b)) = H^p(b, G).
308	- **Thus R^p pi_* G is the presheaf b ↦ H^p(b, G).**
309	
310	**7.4 The derived unit.**
311	- Since pi^{-1} is exact, L pi^{-1} = pi^{-1}. The unit of the derived adjunction pi^{-1} ⊣ R pi_* on D^+ is, for a presheaf F in degree 0, the composite
312	 F --η--> pi_* pi^{-1} F --can--> R pi_* pi^{-1} F.
313	- Here η is the underived unit, and can is the canonical map. It is represented by pi_*(pi^{-1}F) -> pi_*(J^•), induced by the augmentation pi^{-1}F -> J^0 of an injective resolution J^•.
314	- The map can induces the identification pi_* = R^0 pi_* on H^0.
315	- Its source is concentrated in degree 0. Its target has H^0 = R^0 pi_* pi^{-1}F and H^p = R^p pi_* pi^{-1}F.
316	- On H^0 the composite is η, an isomorphism by Cor. 5.3.
317	- For p > 0 and b ∈ B_P, (R^p pi_* pi^{-1} F)(b) = H^p(b, pi^{-1}F) = 0 by 7.3 and 7.2, since b is f.p. (Lemma 0.1(c)).
318	- Hence the composite is an isomorphism on all cohomology presheaves, i.e. a quasi-isomorphism.
319	- The identification in 7.2–7.3 is that of the cohomology of the given map, not merely an abstract isomorphism R pi_* pi^{-1}F ≅ F. Concretely, H^0 of can∘η is the unit, which we showed is the composite of the two isomorphisms in 1.6.
320	
321	**Theorem.** Let P be any monoid (integral, saturated, sharp, commutative), and assume Results B and D. Then for every presheaf of abelian groups F on B_P^op, F -> R pi_* pi^{-1} F is a quasi-isomorphism.
322	
323	Moreover, H^p(U, pi^{-1}F) = 0 for p > 0 and pi^{-1}F(U) = F(Phi_U), for every f.p. object U of A_P.
324	
325	*(Remark.* By the way-out lemma, the statement extends to bounded-below complexes of presheaves, since both sides are triangulated functors on D^+ and agree on objects in a single degree.)
326	
327	## §8 Status
328	
329	**Proved here, from Results B and D**, with standard category theory and homological algebra:
330	- the whole sheaf-theoretic part, for arbitrary P;
331	- the categories (1.1–1.2);
332	- the Kan extension and its exactness (1.4–1.5), and the forms of pi^{-1} and pi_* (1.6);
333	- the injectives (§2);
334	- the cofinality of all-f.p. covers, which handles covers with non-f.p. members (3.2, 3.5);
335	- the Čech complexes, including repeated indices (§4);
336	- sheafification on f.p. objects (§5);
337	- Cartan's criterion, with a full proof (§6);
338	- the derived-unit computation (§7).
339	
340	**Used from the problem statement, not re-proved.** The birhizomic covers form a Grothendieck topology; in either reading, the property used is (★) of 3.3. If the intended topology were the one *generated* by birhizomic covers and the covers did *not* already form a topology, then (★) could fail, and Lemma 3.5(iii) would need a separate argument. The problem asserts this case does not arise.
341	
342	**Quoted from memory:**
343	- the standard sieve/plus-construction facts in 5.0;
344	- the equivalence of pretopology-sheaves and topology-sheaves in 3.3;
345	- the chain equivalence between ordered and oriented chain complexes (Spanier 4.3.8). This is needed only if Result D is read with "ordered" meaning tuples without repetition;
346	- the identification of Stacks tag 03F7. The lemma itself is proved in §6.
347	
348	**I found no false step** in the chain derivation as recorded. The corrections to the recorded chain are minor:
349	- Exactness of Lan for non-f.p. objects is used only to get pi^{-1} exact.
350	- Commutation of Lan with infinite products holds only on f.p. objects, and is used only there.
351	- "Repeated indices are harmless" is justified by the explicit maps of Lemma 4.1. A valuation description is not needed.
352	- In Cartan's criterion, the cofinality hypothesis is supplied by the witness-subfamily lemma 3.2 together with (★), rather than being trivial.
353	
354	**Open:** nothing within the sheaf-theoretic part. The overall answer YES rests on Results B and D, which were taken as given here.
355	
356	=== END OF ANSWER round5_q4 ===

\begin{document} \section{Problem statement} In the following, a monoid is an integral, saturated, sharp, commutative, unital semigroup.  Monoids are written additively.  A monoid $M$ induces a translation invariant partial order on its associated group $M^{\rm gp}$ such that $x \geq 0$ if and only if $x \in M$.  A valuative monoid is a monoid in which the associated partial order is a total order. If $M$ is a monoid, $x \in M^{\rm gp}$, and $y \in M$, we write $x \prec y$ to mean that there are integers $m$ and $n$ such that $my \leq x \leq ny$. A monoid homomorphism $f : M \to N$ is called \emph{infinitesimal} if the following condition holds: \begin{enumerate}[label=$\bullet$] \item If there are $x \in M^{\rm gp}$ and $y \in M$ such that $f(x) \in N$ and $x \prec y$ and $f(y) \prec f(x)$ then $x \in M$. \end{enumerate} If $P \xrightarrow f Q \xrightarrow g N$ are monoid homomorphisms, we say that $f$ is \emph{birhizomic} at $g$ if it is of finite presentation in the category of (integral, saturated, sharp) monoids and, for every factorization of $gf$ through monoid homomorphisms $P \xrightarrow h M \xrightarrow p N$ with $p$ infinitesimal, there is a unique monoid homomorphism $u : Q \to M$ with $pu = g$ and $uf = h$. A family of morphisms $P \rightarrow Q_i$ is called a birhizomic cover if, for every valuative monoid $V$ and every homomorphism $v : P \to V$, there is a factorization of $v$ through some $Q_i \to V$ such that $P \to Q_i$ is birhizomic at $Q_i \to V$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  Let $A_P$ be the category of monoid homomorphisms $P \to Q$.  The birhizomic covers form a Grothendieck topology on $A_P^{\rm op}$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  For any $x$ in $P$, there is an initial monoid homomorphism $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$ that sends $x$ to $0$.  Let $B_P$ be the full subcategory of $A_P$ consisting of homomorphisms $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$, for $x \in P$. We have given $A_P^{\rm op}$ the birhizomic topology and $B_P^{\rm op}$ the trivial topology in which all presheaves are sheaves.  The inclusion $B_P^{\rm op} \subset A_P^{\rm op}$ is left exact.  By left Kan extension and sheafification, it extends to a functor $\pi^{-1} : \operatorname{Sh}(B_P) \to \operatorname{Sh}(A_P)$ on the categories of sheaves.   Let $\pi_\ast$ be the right adjoint of $\pi^{-1}$. \paragraph{Question} \em Is it the case that, for all presheaves of abelian groups $F$ on $B_P^{\rm op}$, the morphism $$F \to \mathrm R \pi_\ast \pi^{-1} F$$ is a quasi-isomorphism? \end{document}

Problem statement (for reference — /data/output/logs/prob-001/work/math-proof-run/problem.md is the authoritative text; go by the file wherever this copy differs or looks garbled):
\begin{document} \section{Problem statement} In the following, a monoid is an integral, saturated, sharp, commutative, unital semigroup.  Monoids are written additively.  A monoid $M$ induces a translation invariant partial order on its associated group $M^{\rm gp}$ such that $x \geq 0$ if and only if $x \in M$.  A valuative monoid is a monoid in which the associated partial order is a total order. If $M$ is a monoid, $x \in M^{\rm gp}$, and $y \in M$, we write $x \prec y$ to mean that there are integers $m$ and $n$ such that $my \leq x \leq ny$. A monoid homomorphism $f : M \to N$ is called \emph{infinitesimal} if the following condition holds: \begin{enumerate}[label=$\bullet$] \item If there are $x \in M^{\rm gp}$ and $y \in M$ such that $f(x) \in N$ and $x \prec y$ and $f(y) \prec f(x)$ then $x \in M$. \end{enumerate} If $P \xrightarrow f Q \xrightarrow g N$ are monoid homomorphisms, we say that $f$ is \emph{birhizomic} at $g$ if it is of finite presentation in the category of (integral, saturated, sharp) monoids and, for every factorization of $gf$ through monoid homomorphisms $P \xrightarrow h M \xrightarrow p N$ with $p$ infinitesimal, there is a unique monoid homomorphism $u : Q \to M$ with $pu = g$ and $uf = h$. A family of morphisms $P \rightarrow Q_i$ is called a birhizomic cover if, for every valuative monoid $V$ and every homomorphism $v : P \to V$, there is a factorization of $v$ through some $Q_i \to V$ such that $P \to Q_i$ is birhizomic at $Q_i \to V$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  Let $A_P$ be the category of monoid homomorphisms $P \to Q$.  The birhizomic covers form a Grothendieck topology on $A_P^{\rm op}$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  For any $x$ in $P$, there is an initial monoid homomorphism $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$ that sends $x$ to $0$.  Let $B_P$ be the full subcategory of $A_P$ consisting of homomorphisms $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$, for $x \in P$. We have given $A_P^{\rm op}$ the birhizomic topology and $B_P^{\rm op}$ the trivial topology in which all presheaves are sheaves.  The inclusion $B_P^{\rm op} \subset A_P^{\rm op}$ is left exact.  By left Kan extension and sheafification, it extends to a functor $\pi^{-1} : \operatorname{Sh}(B_P) \to \operatorname{Sh}(A_P)$ on the categories of sheaves.   Let $\pi_\ast$ be the right adjoint of $\pi^{-1}$. \paragraph{Question} \em Is it the case that, for all presheaves of abelian groups $F$ on $B_P^{\rm op}$, the morphism $$F \to \mathrm R \pi_\ast \pi^{-1} F$$ is a quasi-isomorphism? \end{document}

# round3_q2: arbitrary P

Plan: (1) prove that kernel faces of f.p. maps are principal (done below, for every P). (2) The nerve-contractibility crux: not settled; I record what I have.

## Part (1). Theorem: for any monoid P and any f.p. f : P -> Q, Phi_Q = f^{-1}(0) is the face generated by a single element.

**Reduction to a finite presentation.** Q is a retract under P of Q' = (P (+) N^k / R)^{int,sat,sharp} with R finite. This is the standard description of compact objects in the under-category, which I cite from memory rather than prove. If maps Q -> Q' -> Q compose to id_Q under P, then ker(P->Q) = ker(P->Q'). Indeed, x killed in Q' implies x killed in Q. Conversely, if x is killed in Q, its image in Q' is the image of 0, which is 0.

**Kernel of P -> Q'.** Let G = (P^gp (+) Z^k)/L, where L is generated by l_j = r_j - s_j, j = 1..J. Let M0 be the image of P (+) N^k in G, and let M1 = {g : ng in M0 for some n >= 1} be its saturation. Then Q' = M1/M1^*. So x in P is killed iff its image is a unit of M1. This happens iff -nx in M0 for some n >= 1, i.e. iff -nx - p - m in L for some p in P and m in N^k (all taken in P^gp (+) Z^k). Write the element of L as sum c_j l_j with c in Z^J. The Z^k-component condition says c lies in K = {c in Z^J : Z^k-part of sum c_j l_j lies in -N^k}. K is the set of lattice points of a rational polyhedral cone, so it is a finitely generated monoid (Gordan). Let psi : K -> P^gp be the P^gp-part of c |-> -sum c_j l_j, and let Y = psi(K), a finitely generated submonoid of P^gp. Then x is killed iff nx + p in Y for some n >= 1 and p in P. Such an element y = nx + p lies in S := Y ∩ P, and nx <= y. Conversely, if nx <= y in S, then p := y - nx is in P. Hence

  Phi_Q = face of P generated by the submonoid S = Y ∩ P.

**Principality.** For s in S let F(s) be the face generated by s. Then F(s+t) is the join of F(s) and F(t), so the family {F(s)} is directed. I claim that a strictly increasing chain F(s_1) ⊊ F(s_2) ⊊ ... has length at most rk Y^gp + 1, which is finite.
- A face F of a saturated P satisfies F^gp ∩ P = F: if x = a - b with a, b in F, then x <= a, so x is in F.
- Put G_i = F(s_i)^gp ∩ Y^gp. Suppose some n s_{i+1} lies in G_i with n >= 1. Then n s_{i+1} is in F(s_i)^gp ∩ P = F(s_i), and since F(s_i) is a face, s_{i+1} is in F(s_i). That contradicts strictness.
- So the ranks of the G_i strictly increase.

Hence a maximal F(s) exists. By directedness it contains every F(t), so Phi_Q = F(s) with s in S. ∎

Consequence: Step 0 of Background B holds for every P. The comma category of b -> Q over B_P has the terminal object P[-s]^sharp, so (Lan F)(Q) = F(Phi_Q) on f.p. Q, and pi^{-1}F is the sheafification of F∘b. (For non-f.p. Q the kernel face need not be principal. Example: P valuative of infinite rank and P -> 0. These objects are irrelevant here because Cartan's criterion only uses the f.p. objects.)

Special case check: for P valuative, the faces are P ∩ (convex subgroups). The convex subgroups restricted to Y^gp form a chain of length <= rank + 1, which agrees with the theorem.

## Part (2): the crux. NOT resolved.

What remains open: for a birhizomic covering {Q -> Q_i} of an f.p. Q over arbitrary P, and a principal face tau, is N_tau = {sigma : Phi_{Q_sigma} ⊂ Phi_tau} contractible or empty?

Remarks (not proofs):
- By Part (1), Phi_{Q_sigma} is principal. So the condition "Phi_{Q_sigma} ⊂ Phi_tau" depends on finitely many elements. For each finite subcomplex, one can restrict to a finitely generated submonoid P_0 ⊂ P carrying the relevant generators s, the relation data and the generator of tau. This suggests candidate (iii): reduce to P_0 fine and use Background B. However, the covering of Q need not restrict to a birhizomic covering over P_0. The cover property refers to valuations of P, and the infinitesimality test maps change. So this reduction is unproved. This is exactly the gap.
- Background B's Step 4 for the fine case is itself unchecked by me.

## Part (3): conclusion

Proved here: Step 0 extends to all P (Part 1).

Open:
- (a) the contractibility of N_tau for non-finitely-generated P;
- hence (b) the headline claim (answer YES) for arbitrary P.

The claim holds for finitely generated P only conditionally on Background B, whose outline I have not re-verified. I found no counterexample.

=== END OF ANSWER round3_q2 ===
# round4_q7: proof of #19

**Plan (written first).** I prove #19 as stated, for every P. I do not use the suggested fine-model transfer; Section 7 explains why. The proof has four steps.
(a) Each locus E_i is cut out by finitely many non-strict sign conditions x ∈ W, with x in U := Q^gp ⊗ Q.
(b) The nerve condition Φ_σ ⊂ τ is a condition on the cone Q_Q + cone(X_σ).
(c) Compactness gives a finite subcover.
(d) An abstract acyclicity theorem, proved by induction on the number of "undecided" sign conditions. The induction step refines the cover by the two-member sign cover {z ≥ 0}, {z ≤ 0} and uses the standard double-complex comparison of Čech complexes.

Status: **all steps proved below.**

---

## 0. Result

**Theorem.** Let P be any monoid, f : P → Q any map in 𝒞 (the category of integral, saturated, sharp commutative monoids), and {Q → Q_i}_{i∈I} a family of f.p. maps under Q. Assume that every valuation v : Q → V factors through some Q_i. Let τ ⊂ P be any subset with Φ_Q := f^{-1}(0) ⊂ τ. Then:
- N_τ = {σ ⊂ I finite nonempty : Φ_σ ⊂ τ} is nonempty;
- its augmented ordered chain complex is exact, so its reduced integral homology vanishes;
- for every abelian group A, its augmented ordered cochain complex with coefficients A is exact.

In particular #19 holds. Three of its hypotheses are not needed: birhizomy (only "factors through some member" is used), f.p. of Q over P, and principality of τ.

"f.p." is read as: Hom_Q(Q_i, –) commutes with filtered colimits in 𝒞 under Q. If instead it means "presented by finitely many generators and relations", Lemma 1(i) below is immediate.

## 1. Cones and valuations

Put U = Q^gp ⊗ Q. Q^gp is torsion-free: if nx = 0, then x and −x lie in Q by saturation, so x = 0 by sharpness. So Q ⊂ U. Let Q_Q = Q_{≥0}·Q.

A *cone* is a subset K ⊂ U with 0 ∈ K, K + K ⊂ K and Q_{>0}K ⊂ K. Its lineality is lin K = K ∩ (−K). A cone is *total* if W ∪ (−W) = U.

- Q_Q has lineality 0. If x = q/n and −x = q'/n', then n'q + nq' = 0 in Q^gp, so q = q' = 0 by sharpness and torsion-freeness.
- A valuation v : Q → V gives the total cone W_v = {x ∈ U : v(x) ≥ 0 in V^gp ⊗ Q}, which contains Q_Q. (The divisible hull of an ordered group is ordered.)
- Conversely, a total cone W ⊃ Q_Q gives a valuation v_W : Q → V_W. Here V_W is the nonnegative part of the ordered Q-vector space H_W = U/lin W, with positive cone W/lin W. V_W is integral, saturated, sharp and totally ordered.

**Lemma Z.** Every cone K is contained in a total cone W with lin W = lin K.

*Proof.* Cones K' ⊃ K with lin K' = lin K are closed under unions of chains, so Zorn gives a maximal one, K'. Suppose x ∉ K' ∪ (−K'), and put K'' = K' + Q_{≥0}x. If y ∈ lin K'', write y = k_1 + ax and −y = k_2 + bx with a, b ≥ 0. Then k_1 + k_2 = −(a+b)x.
- If a + b > 0, then −x ∈ K', which is a contradiction.
- So a = b = 0, and y = k_1 ∈ lin K'.

Hence lin K'' = lin K'. Since K'' ⊋ K', this contradicts maximality, so K' is total. ∎

**Consequence (injective valuations).** Every M ∈ 𝒞 has a valuation ι : M → V with ι(m) = 0 only for m = 0. To see this, apply Lemma Z to M_Q ⊂ M^gp ⊗ Q, which has lineality 0 as shown above.

## 2. Lemma 1: loci are finite sign conditions

For each i let E_i be the set of total cones W ⊃ Q_Q such that v_W extends to Q_i, i.e. there is g : Q_i → V_W under Q.

**Lemma 1.** For each i there is a finite set X_i ⊂ U such that:
(a) E_i = {W : X_i ⊂ W};
(b) for any valuation v : Q → V, if v extends to Q_i, then X_i ⊂ W_v.

*Proof.*

(i) *Q_i is a retract under Q of a finitely presented object.* Write M = Q_i. For a finite S ⊂ M and a finite set R of relations r = s between elements of Q ⊕ N^S that hold in M, let T(S,R) be the image of (Q ⊕ N^S)/R after integralizing, saturating and sharpening.
- The pairs (S,R) form a directed poset.
- Filtered colimits of objects of 𝒞, computed in monoids, stay in 𝒞: integrality, nx = ny ⇒ x = y, saturation and sharpness are each witnessed at a finite stage.
- The map colim T(S,R) → M is surjective.
- It is injective. Let x, y lie at a common stage T and have the same image in M. Choose n with nx = [a] and ny = [b], where a, b ∈ Q ⊕ N^S; saturation gives this. Then (a,b) is a relation valid in M. Adding it to R makes nx = ny, hence x = y, because the groups are torsion-free.
- So M = colim T(S,R). By f.p., id_M factors through some T = T(S,R), and M is a retract of T under Q.

Maps out of a retract: v extends to M if and only if it extends to T. Compose with M → T → M in one direction and with T → M in the other.

(ii) *Extensions to T.* Let H be an ordered divisible group containing v(Q), with V ⊂ H_{≥0}. A map T → H_{≥0} under Q is the same as a vector y ∈ H^S with y ≥ 0 satisfying the relations. Indeed, a map from Q ⊕ N^S that respects R factors uniquely through integralization, saturation and sharpening, because H_{≥0} is integral, saturated and sharp.

Write the j-th relation as (a_j, α_j) = (b_j, β_j) with a_j, b_j ∈ Q and α_j, β_j ∈ N^S. It reads (α_j − β_j)·y = c_j, where c_j := v(b_j − a_j).

(iii) *Fourier–Motzkin.* Consider a finite system of rational linear inequalities in unknowns y and parameters c, over an ordered divisible group H. Eliminating one unknown replaces the system by the "lower bound ≤ upper bound" pairs together with the inequalities not involving that unknown. This preserves solvability in H: given the rest, take the unknown to be the maximum of its finitely many lower bounds (or the minimum of the upper bounds, or 0 if there are none).

Eliminating all y from {y ≥ 0, (α_j − β_j)·y = c_j} gives finitely many rational vectors u_m, independent of H, with:
solvable in H ⟺ u_m·c ≥ 0 for all m.

Put x_m = Σ_j u_{mj}(b_j − a_j) ∈ U and X_i = {x_m}. Then u_m·c = v(x_m).

Conclusion:
- For H = H_W this gives (a).
- For H = V^gp ⊗ Q, if v extends to Q_i then it extends to T inside H_{≥0}, so v(x_m) ≥ 0 for all m, i.e. X_i ⊂ W_v. This is (b). ∎

## 3. Lemma 2: the nerve condition as a cone condition

For finite σ ⊂ I put X_σ = ∪_{i∈σ} X_i and K_σ = Q_Q + cone(X_σ). For a cone K ⊃ Q_Q put f^{-1}(lin K) = {p ∈ P : f(p) ∈ lin K}.

Since f(p) ∈ Q_Q ⊂ K, this equals {p ∈ P : −f(p) ∈ K}.

**Lemma 2.** Φ_σ := ker(P → Q_σ) = f^{-1}(lin K_σ).

*Proof.* A map Q_σ → V_W under Q is the same as a family of maps Q_i → V_W under Q, i ∈ σ, because Q_σ is the pushout in 𝒞 and V_W ∈ 𝒞. So the set of W for which v_W extends to Q_σ is ∩_{i∈σ} E_i = {W ⊃ K_σ}.

(⊂) Suppose p ∈ Φ_σ. Take W ⊃ K_σ total with lin W = lin K_σ (Lemma Z). Then v_W extends to Q_σ and kills the image of p, so f(p) ∈ lin W = lin K_σ.

(⊃) Suppose f(p) ∈ lin K_σ. Let ι : Q_σ → V be injective (§1) and v = ι|_Q. Since v extends to every Q_i, i ∈ σ, Lemma 1(b) gives X_σ ⊂ W_v, so K_σ ⊂ W_v. Hence v(f(p)) = 0, i.e. ι(image of p) = 0, so the image of p is 0. ∎

Let 𝒢 = {cones K ⊃ Q_Q : f^{-1}(lin K) ⊂ τ}. Then:
- **N_τ = {σ : K_σ ∈ 𝒢}.**
- **(G0)** If Q_Q ⊂ K ⊂ K' and K' ∈ 𝒢, then K ∈ 𝒢.
- **(G1)** If K ∈ 𝒢 and W ⊃ K is total with lin W = lin K, then W ∈ 𝒢. The sets f^{-1}(lin ·) are equal.
- **(G2)** For any cone K ⊃ Q_Q and any z ∈ U, f^{-1}(lin(K + Qz)) = f^{-1}(lin(K + Q_{≥0}z)) ∪ f^{-1}(lin(K + Q_{≥0}(−z))). Indeed, write −f(p) = k + tz and split according to the sign of t. So if K ± z ∈ 𝒢, then K + Qz ∈ 𝒢.
- **(G3)** Q_Q ∈ 𝒢, because f^{-1}(lin Q_Q) = f^{-1}(0) = Φ_Q ⊂ τ. Here lin Q_Q = 0 and Q ⊂ U.

## 4. Lemma 3: finite subcover

The set 𝒯 of total cones W ⊃ Q_Q is closed in {0,1}^U. Each defining condition involves finitely many coordinates:
- z ∈ W or −z ∈ W;
- z, z' ∈ W ⇒ z + z' ∈ W;
- z ∈ W ⇒ rz ∈ W for r ∈ Q_{>0};
- q ∈ W for q ∈ Q_Q.

So 𝒯 is compact by Tychonoff. Each E_i = {X_i ⊂ W} is open. The E_i cover 𝒯: every W gives a valuation v_W, which factors through some Q_i by hypothesis. Hence a **finite J_0 ⊂ I has ∪_{i∈J_0} E_i = 𝒯.**

## 5. Theorem T: abstract acyclicity

Fix:
- a Q-vector space U and a cone K_0;
- a family 𝒢 of cones containing K_0, satisfying (G0), (G1) and (G2) for cones containing K_0;
- an abelian group A.

For a cone K ⊃ K_0 and a finite family (X_j)_{j∈J} of finite subsets of U, let C^•(K) be the augmented ordered Čech complex:
- C^p(K) = ∏_{(j_0,…,j_p) ∈ J^{p+1}} A(K + cone X_{j_0} + … + cone X_{j_p}) for p ≥ −1, where A(K') = A if K' ∈ 𝒢 and 0 otherwise;
- the maps between factors are the identity A → A or 0 (well defined by (G0));
- d is the alternating sum of the deletions.

When K ∈ 𝒢, this is the augmented ordered cochain complex of N(K) = {σ : K + cone X_σ ∈ 𝒢} with coefficients A.

**Theorem T.** If every total cone W ⊃ K contains some X_j, then C^•(K) is exact.

*Proof.* Induction on m(K) = #{z ∈ Z : z ∉ K and −z ∉ K}, where Z = ∪_j X_j is finite. If K ∉ 𝒢, then C^•(K) = 0 by (G0). So assume K ∈ 𝒢.

*Cone lemma.* Suppose there is j* such that σ ∈ N(K) ⇒ σ ∪ {j*} ∈ N(K), and {j*} ∈ N(K). Then (hc)(j_0,…,j_{p−1}) = c(j*, j_0,…,j_{p−1}) is well defined: if the tuple with j* added carries A, so does the tuple without it, by (G0). The usual computation gives dh + hd = id, including in degree −1. So C^• is contractible.

*Base case m(K) = 0.* Take W ⊃ K total with lin W = lin K (Lemma Z). Some X_{j*} ⊂ W. Let z ∈ X_{j*}.
- If z ∉ K, then −z ∈ K because z is decided, so z ∈ lin W = lin K ⊂ K, a contradiction.
- So X_{j*} ⊂ K, and K + cone X_{j*} = K. Hence j* is a cone point and the cone lemma applies.

*Row lemma.* For any cone K' ⊃ K_0 and z ∈ U, the augmented complex of the two-member family X_+ = {z}, X_− = {−z} on K' is exact. If K' ∉ 𝒢 it is zero. If K' ∈ 𝒢:
- By Lemma Z and (G1), some total W ∈ 𝒢 contains K'. Then W contains K' + z or K' − z, so at least one vertex lies in the nerve, by (G0).
- If both vertices lie in it, the edge does too, by (G2).

So the nerve is a vertex or an edge, and the cone lemma applies.

*Inductive step, m(K) > 0.* Pick an undecided z ∈ Z. Consider the double complex
D^{p,q} = ∏_{σ ∈ J^{p+1}, ρ ∈ {±}^{q+1}} A(K + cone X_σ + cone{ρ_0 z, …, ρ_q z}), for p, q ≥ −1,
with commuting deletion differentials in σ and in ρ.
- **Row p** is ∏_σ of the row-lemma complex on K + cone X_σ, hence exact.
- **Column q ≥ 0** is ∏_ρ of C^•(K_ρ), where K_ρ ∈ {K + Q_{≥0}z, K + Q_{≥0}(−z), K + Qz}. The cover hypothesis passes to K_ρ ⊃ K, and m(K_ρ) < m(K) because z is now decided. So these columns are exact by induction.
- **Column q = −1** is C^•(K).

Each total degree involves only finitely many (p, q). Exact rows make Tot D acyclic. The columns q ≥ 0 form a subcomplex whose total complex is acyclic, by filtering by q. The quotient by this subcomplex is column −1, so C^•(K) is exact. ∎

## 6. Proof of #19

1. Apply T with U = Q^gp ⊗ Q, K_0 = K = Q_Q, the family 𝒢 of §3, and the family (X_i)_{i∈J'} for any finite J' ⊃ J_0. The cover hypothesis holds by Lemma 3.
2. By Lemma 2, N(Q_Q) is the full subcomplex N_τ(J') of N_τ on J'. Hence the augmented ordered cochain complex of N_τ(J') with coefficients A is exact, for every A.
3. *Nonemptiness.* Take W_0 ⊃ Q_Q total with lin W_0 = 0. Then W_0 ∈ 𝒢 by (G3) and (G1). It contains some X_i, so K_i ⊂ W_0, so {i} ∈ N_τ by (G0).
4. *Exactness of the chain complex of N_τ(J').* Let C̃ be its augmented ordered chain complex, a complex of free abelian groups in degrees ≥ −1. The universal coefficient theorem gives a surjection H^n(Hom(C̃, A)) → Hom(H_n C̃, A). Taking A = H_n C̃ shows H_n C̃ = 0.
5. *Passage to the infinite complex.* The augmented ordered chain complex of N_τ is the directed union over finite J' ⊃ J_0 of these complexes, so it is exact. Its reduced homology, which is simplicial reduced homology, vanishes.
6. *Cochains of N_τ.* An exact complex of free abelian groups bounded below is split, since subgroups of free groups are free. So Hom(–, A) of it is exact, i.e. the augmented ordered cochain complex of N_τ is exact for every A.

This is what steps 3–6 of the chain use. ∎

## 7. Remarks

**Why I departed from the fine-model transfer.** Lemma 1 already turns everything into finitely many sign conditions inside the true cone Q_Q ⊂ Q^gp ⊗ Q. The proof never passes to the fine submonoids P_S. So the round3_q4 obstruction does not arise: no valuation of a smaller monoid that fails to extend ever needs to be covered.

Outer polyhedral models would in fact fail. Take the valuative Q_0 = {x > 0} ∪ {x = 0, y ≥ 0}. Every rational polyhedral cone containing it also contains −(0,1), which creates spurious lineality.

**Consistency with #15.** The argument reproves the fine case (#15, Steps 2–4) without Lemma K's tangent-cone induction and without the nerve theorem.

**Possible gap in the chain, outside #19 (flagged, not resolved).** A birhizomic cover need only have f.p. members among those that serve as birhizomic witnesses. Chain step 5 asserts that all members of a covering of an f.p. object are f.p. To support that, one should either restrict to the subfamily of witnesses, which is itself a birhizomic cover with all members f.p., and argue with sieves, or check this point separately.

## 8. Status

- **Proved:** #19 exactly as stated, in the stronger form of §0. Every step has its proof written out here, apart from the standard facts listed next.
- **Standard facts used, not reproved:**
  - Tychonoff's theorem;
  - the double-complex comparison (a double complex in the region p, q ≥ −1 with exact rows has an acyclic total complex);
  - the universal coefficient theorem for complexes of free abelian groups;
  - ordered chains compute simplicial homology.
- **Open within this file:** nothing for #19. The chain-level f.p.-membership point in §7 is outside the statement of #19 and is left unchecked here.

# Answer to round5_q4: the sheaf-theoretic part, for an arbitrary monoid P

**Plan.** I prove: *assuming Results B and D (taken as given), for every monoid P and every presheaf of abelian groups F on B_P^op, the derived unit F -> R pi_* pi^{-1} F is a quasi-isomorphism.* The sections are:
- §0 conventions;
- §1 the categories, the Kan extension and the adjunction;
- §2 the injectives I_{tau,A};
- §3 coverings and the cofinal system Cov;
- §4 Čech complexes;
- §5 sheafification on f.p. objects;
- §6 Cartan's criterion, proved in full;
- §7 the cohomology computation and the conclusion;
- §8 status.

I checked every step and found no false or unrepairable one. The one place where the problem's own assertion is used is flagged in §3.3: the birhizomic covers form a Grothendieck topology.

---

## §0 Conventions

- **Monoids.** "Monoid" means integral, saturated, sharp, commutative monoid. **Mon** is the category of these. For a map f : P -> Q, write Phi_Q := f^{-1}(0).
- **Faces.** For x in P, face(x) := {y in P : y <= nx for some n >= 1} is the smallest face containing x. A face is *principal* if it has this form.
- **Universes.** Fix universes U ∈ V with P ∈ U.
  - A_P is the category of maps P -> Q in Mon with Q ∈ U. It is V-small.
  - Presheaves and sheaves take values in V-small abelian groups. Every U-small group is one of these.
  - Then (A_P^op, birhizomic topology) is a V-small site. The usual theory applies inside V: sheafification by the plus construction, enough injectives in Ab(A_P^op), and derived functors.
  - B_P is essentially U-small, since its objects are indexed by the elements of P.
  - Nothing in the answer depends on the choice of U and V.
- **Filtered colimits in Mon.** These are computed on underlying sets. A filtered colimit of integral, saturated, sharp monoids is again integral, saturated and sharp: any equation x + y = 0, nz = w, or x + z = y + z already holds at some stage. Connected colimits in an under-category P/Mon are computed in Mon.
- **f.p.** A map f : P -> Q is f.p. if Hom_{P/Mon}(Q, -) commutes with filtered colimits in P/Mon.
- **Pushouts.** Pushouts exist in Mon: form the pushout of commutative monoids, then take the integral image, saturate it, and divide by units. Fibre products in A_P^op are pushouts under P.

**Lemma 0.1.**
- (a) If P -> Q and Q -> Q' are f.p., so is P -> Q'.
- (b) If Q -> Q' is f.p. and Q -> R is arbitrary, then R -> Q' ⊔_Q R is f.p.
- (c) Each P -> P[-x]^♯ is f.p.

*Proof.*

(b) Let X be an object under R. Then Hom_R(Q' ⊔_Q R, X) = Hom_Q(Q', X), and a filtered colimit under R is also a filtered colimit under Q.

(a) Let X = colim X_k be a filtered colimit under P. A map Q' -> X under P is a pair (a, c): a map a : Q -> X under P, and a map c : Q' -> X under Q, where X is viewed under Q via a.
- Since Q is f.p., a factors through some a_k : Q -> X_k, and two such factorizations agree further along.
- The X_{k'} for k' >= k, viewed under Q via a_k, form a filtered system with colimit (X, a). Since Q' is f.p. under Q, c factors through some X_{k'}, uniquely up to going further along.
- Hence colim_k Hom_P(Q', X_k) -> Hom_P(Q', X) is bijective.

(c) Hom_P(P[-x]^♯, X) is a point if x ↦ 0 in X, and empty otherwise. For X = colim X_k, x ↦ 0 in X iff x ↦ 0 in some X_k. ∎

Hence every finite iterated pushout over Q of f.p. maps Q -> Q_i, with Q f.p. under P, is f.p. under P.

## §1 The categories, the Kan extension, pi^{-1} and pi_*

**1.1 Kernel faces.** If f : P -> Q is in A_P, then Phi_Q is a face of P.
- It is a submonoid.
- If a + b ∈ Phi_Q, then f(a) + f(b) = 0, so f(a) = f(b) = 0 because Q is sharp.

So x ∈ Phi_Q iff face(x) ⊂ Phi_Q. If Q -> Q' is a map under P, then Phi_Q ⊂ Phi_{Q'}.

**1.2 The objects b_x := (P -> P[-x]^♯).**
- *Construction.* Let P[-x] = {p - nx} ⊂ P^gp. It is integral, and it is saturated: if m g + k x ∈ P, then m(g + kx) ∈ P, so g + kx ∈ P. Set P[-x]^♯ = P[-x]/P[-x]^*. Dividing a saturated integral monoid by its units keeps it saturated and integral, and makes it sharp.
- *Universal property.* For f : P -> Q in A_P, a map P[-x]^♯ -> Q under P exists iff f(x) = 0, and it is then unique.
  - If f(x) = 0, then f extends uniquely to P[-x], since P[-x] is generated by P and -x. The extension kills the units of P[-x], because Q is sharp.
  - Conversely, x becomes a unit in P[-x], so it maps to 0 in P[-x]^♯, and hence f(x) = 0.
  - Uniqueness holds because P -> P[-x]^♯ is surjective onto generators: every element is the class of p - nx.
- *Kernel.* Phi_{b_x} = face(x). Indeed, y ↦ 0 iff y is a unit of P[-x], iff -y = p - nx for some p, n, iff y + p = nx, iff y ∈ face(x).
- *Consequences.*
  - Hom_{A_P}(b_x, b_y) is a point if face(x) ⊂ face(y), and empty otherwise.
  - B_P is therefore a preorder, equivalent to the poset Pr(P) of principal faces under inclusion.
  - Pr(P) is directed, since face(x), face(y) ⊂ face(x + y). Its least element is face(0) = {0}, which corresponds to b_0 = P.
  - For tau ∈ Pr(P), let b_tau be any object of B_P with kernel face tau. For a functor F on B_P, write F(tau) := F(b_tau). Any two choices of b_tau are uniquely isomorphic.
  - Every b_x is f.p., by Lemma 0.1(c).

**1.3 Presheaves.** A presheaf on B_P^op (resp. A_P^op) is a functor B_P -> Ab (resp. A_P -> Ab). Write ι : B_P -> A_P for the inclusion.
- The trivial topology makes Sh(B_P^op) = PSh(B_P^op). In it, exactness is objectwise.
- Restriction is ι^* G = G∘ι.

**1.4 The left Kan extension.** The left adjoint of ι^* on presheaves (Stacks' u_p, SGA4 I.5) is
 (Lan F)(Q) = colim_{(b, b->Q) ∈ ι/Q} F(b),
where ι/Q is the comma category of pairs (b ∈ B_P, b -> Q in A_P).
- By 1.2, a pair (b_x, ·) exists iff x ∈ Phi_Q, and the map is then unique. Also b_x -> b_y over Q exists iff face(x) ⊂ face(y).
- Hence ι/Q is a preorder, equivalent to the poset Pr(P)_{⊂Phi_Q} = {face(x) : x ∈ Phi_Q}.
- This poset is nonempty, since it contains {0}, and directed, since x, y ∈ Phi_Q implies x + y ∈ Phi_Q.

So (Lan F)(Q) is a *filtered* colimit, for every Q. Filtered colimits in Ab are exact, and kernels and cokernels of presheaves are computed objectwise. **Therefore Lan is exact.**

**Lemma 1.5 (f.p. objects).** Let Q be f.p. under P. By Result B, Phi_Q = face(x_Q). Put b(Q) := b_{x_Q}.
- (b(Q), b(Q) -> Q) is terminal in ι/Q. So the canonical map F(b(Q)) = F(Phi_Q) -> (Lan F)(Q) is an isomorphism, natural in F.
- For a map Q -> Q' of f.p. objects, Phi_Q ⊂ Phi_{Q'}. Under these isomorphisms, Lan F(Q -> Q') becomes F(b(Q) -> b(Q')): both are the colimit map sending the summand of index b(Q) to the summand of index b(Q').
- For b ∈ B_P we have b(b) ≅ b. So the adjunction unit F(b) -> (Lan F)(b) is an isomorphism. (This is also the general fact that the unit is an isomorphism for fully faithful ι.)
- Consequently Lan commutes with arbitrary products *on f.p. objects*: (Lan ∏_j F_j)(Q) = ∏_j F_j(Phi_Q) = ∏_j (Lan F_j)(Q), naturally in Q f.p.

On non-f.p. objects this may fail, since filtered colimits do not commute with infinite products. It is never needed there.

**1.6 pi^{-1} and pi_*.**
- By definition pi^{-1} F = (Lan F)^#, where # denotes sheafification for the birhizomic topology J of §3.
- Lan and # are both exact, so **pi^{-1} is exact.**
- For a sheaf G: Hom_Sh((Lan F)^#, G) = Hom_PSh(Lan F, G) = Hom_{PSh(B)}(F, G∘ι). So **pi_* G = G∘ι = G|_B**, a left exact functor.
- The unit F -> pi_* pi^{-1} F is, at b ∈ B_P, the composite
  F(b) --(iso, 1.5)--> (Lan F)(b) --(sheafification map)--> (Lan F)^#(b).
  So it is an isomorphism as soon as the sheafification map is an isomorphism at f.p. objects. That is Corollary 5.3.

## §2 The injectives I_{tau,A}

Fix tau ∈ Pr(P) and an abelian group A.
- **Definition.** I_{tau,A}(b) = A if Phi_b ⊂ tau, and 0 otherwise. The map along b -> b' is id_A when both values are A, and 0 otherwise.
- **It is a functor.** Phi_b ⊂ Phi_{b'}, so the value A at b' forces the value A at b. The pattern 0 -> A never occurs, and composition is clearly respected.

**Lemma 2.1.** Hom_{PSh(B)}(F, I_{tau,A}) ≅ Hom_Ab(F(tau), A), via φ ↦ φ_{b_tau}. Hence I_{tau,A} is injective if A is.

*Proof.*
- *Uniqueness.* If Phi_b ⊂ tau, there is a unique map b -> b_tau. Naturality along it forces φ_b = φ_tau ∘ F(b -> b_tau).
- *Existence.* Given φ_tau, define φ_b by this formula when Phi_b ⊂ tau, and φ_b = 0 otherwise. Take a map b -> b'.
  - If both targets are A: φ_{b'} ∘ F(b -> b') = φ_tau ∘ F(b' -> b_tau) ∘ F(b -> b') = φ_b, by uniqueness of maps in B_P.
  - If the target at b' is 0: the square is trivially commutative.
- *Injectivity.* Hom(-, I_{tau,A}) = Hom(ev_{b_tau}(-), A). This is exact, because evaluation is exact and A is injective. ∎

**Lemma 2.2 (resolution).**
- Let E(-) denote an injective hull (or any injective embedding).
- The map F -> ∏_{tau ∈ Pr(P)} I_{tau, E(F(tau))}, whose tau-component corresponds via 2.1 to F(tau) ↪ E(F(tau)), is a monomorphism.
  - At b with Phi_b = sigma, its sigma-component is F(b) -> F(b_sigma) ≅ F(b) followed by F(b) ↪ E(F(b)).
  - The product is objectwise, and it is injective, as a product of injectives.
- Apply the same construction to the cokernel, and iterate. This gives an injective resolution
  0 -> F -> I^0 -> I^1 -> ...,  with each I^k = ∏_{tau ∈ Pr(P)} I_{tau, A_{k,tau}} for injective groups A_{k,tau}.
- The resolution is exact objectwise. The products may be infinite. ∎

## §3 Coverings and the cofinal system Cov

**3.1 Coverings of an object.** Let Q be an object of A_P. A *birhizomic cover of Q* is a family of maps {Q -> Q_i}_{i ∈ I} under P that is a birhizomic cover in the sense of the problem, with Q in the role of the base.
- Its *witness set* is I_0 = {i ∈ I : there are a valuative V and g : Q_i -> V such that Q -> Q_i is birhizomic at g}.
- By definition of "birhizomic at g", each Q -> Q_i with i ∈ I_0 is f.p.

**Lemma 3.2.** {Q -> Q_i}_{i ∈ I_0} is again a birhizomic cover of Q, and it refines {Q -> Q_i}_{i ∈ I}.

*Proof.*
- For a valuation v of Q, the cover property gives an i and a factorization Q -> Q_i -> V with Q -> Q_i birhizomic at Q_i -> V. That i lies in I_0 by definition, and the same factorization serves as the witness.
- Refinement holds because the new family is a subfamily (α = inclusion I_0 ⊂ I). ∎

**3.3 The topology; both readings.** Let J(Q) be the set of sieves on Q, in A_P^op, that contain the sieve generated by some birhizomic cover of Q.
- *Reading (a): the birhizomic covers form a pretopology.* They satisfy the isomorphism, base-change and composition axioms. The topology generated by a pretopology has exactly the sieves J(Q) as covering sieves, and the sheaves for the pretopology are the sheaves for J (SGA4 II.1.3–1.4; Stacks, Sites, section on sites and sieves, quoted from memory).
- *Reading (b): "the sieves generated by birhizomic covers form a Grothendieck topology."* Then this topology is J, again with covering sieves J(Q).
  - If one instead takes the *smallest* Grothendieck topology containing those sieves, it is again J. This uses the problem's assertion that J is already a topology.
  - **This assertion of the problem is used and not re-proved here.** The property actually used below is:

  (★) every covering sieve of every object Q contains the sieve generated by some birhizomic cover of Q.

So under both readings the site is (A_P^op, J), and (★) holds.

For uniformity, call a family {U_i -> U} a *covering family* if the sieve it generates lies in J. This is the class "Cov(C)" of the site in Stacks' sense (Stacks tag 00VH); it satisfies the site axioms since J is a topology and fibre products exist.

**3.4 The system Cov.** Let 𝔅 be the set of f.p. objects of A_P. Let **Cov** be the set of birhizomic covers {Q -> Q_i}_{i ∈ I} with Q ∈ 𝔅 and every Q -> Q_i f.p.

**Lemma 3.5.**
- (i) Every 𝒰 ∈ Cov is a covering family.
- (ii) For 𝒰 ∈ Cov, every member Q_i, and every iterated fibre product Q_{i_0...i_p} := Q_{i_0} ⊔_Q ... ⊔_Q Q_{i_p} (a pushout in Mon), lies in 𝔅.
- (iii) For Q ∈ 𝔅 and every covering sieve R of Q, there is 𝒰 ∈ Cov all of whose members lie in R. In particular, every covering family of Q is refined by a member of Cov.
- (iv) In 𝒰 ∈ Cov, every valuation of Q factors through some member.

*Proof.*
- (i) Immediate from the definition of J.
- (ii) Lemma 0.1(a)(b).
- (iii) By (★), R contains the sieve of a birhizomic cover 𝒰' of Q. By Lemma 3.2, its witness subfamily 𝒰 lies in Cov. Each member of 𝒰 is a member of 𝒰', so it lies in R. If R is generated by a covering family {V_j -> Q}, each member of 𝒰 factors through some V_j. Choosing such factorizations gives the refinement map.
- (iv) Each 𝒰 ∈ Cov is a birhizomic cover. ∎

So the coverings of f.p. objects with all members f.p. are cofinal among all coverings of f.p. objects, and their iterated fibre products are f.p.

## §4 Čech complexes on Cov

**Conventions.**
- For a presheaf G on A_P^op and 𝒰 = {Q -> Q_i}_{i ∈ I}, the Čech complex is that of Stacks, with *all* ordered tuples, repetitions allowed:
  Č^p(𝒰, G) = ∏_{t = (i_0..i_p) ∈ I^{p+1}} G(Q_t),  (ds)_{i_0..i_{p+1}} = Σ_j (-1)^j s_{i_0..î_j..i_{p+1}}|_{Q_{i_0..i_{p+1}}}.
- The *augmented* complex puts G(Q) in degree -1, with the restriction maps as augmentation.
- For a tuple t, write set(t) for its underlying set and Phi_t := ker(P -> Q_t).

**Lemma 4.1 (repeated indices).** Phi_t = Phi_{set(t)}, where for a finite set σ ⊂ I, Q_σ is the pushout over Q of the Q_i, i ∈ σ, as in Result D.

*Proof.* There are maps under P (indeed under Q) in both directions between Q_σ and Q_t:
- Q_σ -> Q_t sends the factor Q_i to the first slot of t equal to i.
- Q_t -> Q_σ sends the slot j to the coprojection of Q_{i_j}. Thus a repeated factor is mapped by the codiagonal.

By 1.1 the kernels are contained in each other. ∎

So for σ ⊂ σ' we have Phi_σ ⊂ Phi_{σ'}, and the sets N_tau = {σ : Phi_σ ⊂ tau} of Result D are simplicial complexes.

**Proposition 4.2.** Let Q ∈ 𝔅, 𝒰 ∈ Cov a covering of Q, tau ∈ Pr(P), A an abelian group, and G = Lan I_{tau,A}.
- (a) If Phi_Q ⊄ tau, the augmented Čech complex of G on 𝒰 is zero.
- (b) If Phi_Q ⊂ tau, it is isomorphic to the augmented ordered cochain complex of N_tau with coefficients A.

In both cases it is exact.

*Proof.* All the objects Q, Q_t lie in 𝔅 (Lemma 3.5(ii)). By Lemma 1.5, G(Q_t) ≅ I_{tau,A}(Phi_t). This is A if Phi_t ⊂ tau and 0 otherwise. Restriction maps between two nonzero terms are id_A.

(a) Each Q_t receives a map from Q under P, so Phi_Q ⊂ Phi_t ⊄ tau. Hence every term is 0.

(b) By Lemma 4.1, Č^p ≅ ∏_{t ∈ I^{p+1}, set(t) ∈ N_tau} A. With the differential above, this is exactly the ordered cochain complex C^p_ord(N_tau; A) = Hom(C^ord_p(N_tau), A). Here C^ord_p is free on the ordered (p+1)-tuples of vertices, repetitions allowed, spanning a simplex. The degree -1 term is G(Q) = A, and the augmentation is the diagonal A -> ∏_i A, i.e. the dual of the augmentation C^ord_0 -> Z.

*Exactness.* Result D applies:
- the members of 𝒰 are f.p. maps Q -> Q_i;
- every valuation of Q factors through one of them (Lemma 3.5(iv));
- tau ⊃ Phi_Q.

Result D's Q_σ and Phi_σ are ours. So the augmented ordered cochain complex of N_tau with coefficients A is exact.

*If "ordered" in Result D means tuples without repetition, or the oriented complex:* the ordered chain complex with repetitions and the oriented chain complex of a simplicial complex are naturally chain homotopy equivalent, compatibly with augmentations (Spanier, *Algebraic Topology*, Thm. 4.3.8, quoted from memory). So exactness of one augmented chain complex gives exactness of the other.
- An exact augmented chain complex of free abelian groups, bounded below, is split exact.
- Hence its Hom into A is exact.

So in every reading, (b) is exact. ∎

**Corollary 4.3.** Let 0 -> F -> I^0 -> I^1 -> ... be the resolution of Lemma 2.2. For Q ∈ 𝔅 and 𝒰 ∈ Cov over Q, the augmented Čech complex of each Lan I^k on 𝒰 is exact.

*Proof.* On 𝔅, Lan I^k ≅ ∏_tau Lan I_{tau,A_{k,tau}} naturally (Lemma 1.5), and only objects of 𝔅 occur in the complex. So the augmented Čech complex is the product of the complexes of Prop. 4.2, and a product of exact complexes of abelian groups is exact. ∎

## §5 Sheafification does not change values on f.p. objects

**5.0 Sieve facts.** These are standard (SGA4 II; Stacks, Sites), quoted from memory, and each is easily checked.
- Let R be the sieve on U generated by a family {U_i -> U} whose pairwise fibre products exist. Then Hom_PSh(R, G) is the equalizer of ∏_i G(U_i) ⇉ ∏_{(i,j)} G(U_i ×_U U_j). (A map R -> G is determined by its values on the generators. A compatible family defines one: given V -> U in R, factor it as V -> U_i -> U and take s_i|_V. Two factorizations yield a map V -> U_i ×_U U_j, so the value is well defined.)
- The plus construction is G^+(U) = colim_{R ∈ J(U)} Hom(R, G), over J(U) ordered by reverse inclusion.
- G^# = G^{++}, and G -> G^+ is natural.
- A sheaf satisfies the equalizer condition for every covering family.

**Lemma 5.1.** Let G be a presheaf on A_P^op such that, for every Q ∈ 𝔅 and every 𝒰 ∈ Cov over Q, the sequence
 0 -> G(Q) -> ∏_i G(Q_i) -> ∏_{(i,j)} G(Q_{ij})
is exact. Then:
- G(Q) -> G^+(Q) is an isomorphism for all Q ∈ 𝔅;
- G^+ satisfies the same hypothesis;
- hence G(Q) -> G^#(Q) is an isomorphism for all Q ∈ 𝔅.

*Proof.*
- By Lemma 3.5(iii), the sieves generated by members of Cov over Q are cofinal in J(Q). By 5.0 and the hypothesis, G(Q) -> Hom(R, G) is an isomorphism for each such R, compatibly with the transition maps (all are restrictions of the same element). So G(Q) -> G^+(Q) = colim Hom(R, G) is an isomorphism.
- For 𝒰 ∈ Cov over Q ∈ 𝔅, all the objects Q, Q_i, Q_{ij} lie in 𝔅 (Lemma 3.5(ii)). The natural map G -> G^+ is an isomorphism on all of them. So the sequence for G^+ is isomorphic to the one for G, and is exact.
- Apply the first point to G^+. ∎

**Corollary 5.2.** For every presheaf F on B_P^op, Lan F satisfies the hypothesis of Lemma 5.1.

*Proof.* Exactness of Lan gives an exact sequence 0 -> Lan F -> Lan I^0 -> Lan I^1 of presheaves.
- Lan I^0 and Lan I^1 satisfy the hypothesis of 5.1, by Cor. 4.3 in degrees -1, 0, 1.
- The functor G ↦ [the kernel of G(Q) -> ∏ G(Q_i) -> ∏ G(Q_ij), viewed as an equalizer] commutes with kernels of presheaves, since limits commute with limits.
- A diagram chase finishes the proof. Take s ∈ Lan F(Q) with all restrictions 0. Its image in Lan I^0(Q) has all restrictions 0, so it is 0, and hence s = 0. Next take a compatible family (s_i) for Lan F.
  - Its image in Lan I^0 glues to some t ∈ Lan I^0(Q).
  - The image of t in Lan I^1(Q) restricts to 0 on every Q_i, so it is 0.
  - Hence t comes from some s ∈ Lan F(Q), and s restricts to s_i by injectivity of Lan F(Q_i) -> Lan I^0(Q_i). ∎

**Corollary 5.3.**
- For Q ∈ 𝔅, F(Phi_Q) ≅ Lan F(Q) -> pi^{-1}F(Q) is an isomorphism, natural in F and in Q ∈ 𝔅.
- In particular the unit F -> pi_* pi^{-1} F is an isomorphism, since every b ∈ B_P is in 𝔅 (1.2, 1.6).
- For the same reason, pi^{-1}I^k(Q) ≅ Lan I^k(Q) ≅ I^k(Phi_Q) for Q ∈ 𝔅, naturally in k.
- Hence the Čech complexes of pi^{-1}I^k on members of Cov are those of Cor. 4.3. So **Ȟ^p(𝒰, pi^{-1} I^k) = 0 for p > 0 and every 𝒰 ∈ Cov.**

## §6 Cartan's criterion

**Statement.** This is Stacks Project, Cohomology on Sites, the lemma at tag 03F7, quoted from memory.
- *Setting.* Let C be a site with fibre products of the needed objects, 𝔅 a set of objects, and Cov a set of covering families such that:
  - (1) every 𝒰 = {U_i -> U} ∈ Cov has U, U_i and all U_{i_0} ×_U ... ×_U U_{i_p} in 𝔅;
  - (2) for each U ∈ 𝔅, the members of Cov covering U are cofinal: every covering of U is refined by one of them.
- *Conclusion.* If an abelian sheaf G has Ȟ^p(𝒰, G) = 0 for all p > 0 and all 𝒰 ∈ Cov, then H^p(U, G) = 0 for all p > 0 and all U ∈ 𝔅.

Here H^p(U, -) = R^pΓ(U, -) on Ab(C), with Γ(U, G) = G(U).

To be self-contained I prove it, using only the version (2') of (2) that I verified in Lemma 3.5(iii): every covering sieve of U ∈ 𝔅 contains all members of some 𝒰 ∈ Cov over U.

**Fact 6.1.** If I is an injective abelian sheaf and 𝒰 = {U_i -> U} is any family whose fibre products exist, then Ȟ^p(𝒰, I) = 0 for p > 0.

*Proof.*
- Let Z_V be the free abelian presheaf on h_V, and set K_p = ⊕_{t ∈ I^{p+1}} Z_{U_t}, with the alternating face differential. Then Hom_PSh(K_•, G) = Č^•(𝒰, G).
- Evaluate at W. Hom(W, U_t) is the set of tuples (φ_0..φ_p), φ_j : W -> U_{i_j}, with a common composite ψ : W -> U. So K_•(W) = ⊕_ψ Z[T_ψ^{•+1}], where T_ψ = {(i, φ) : φ : W -> U_i over ψ}.
- Each summand is the chain complex of the full simplex on T_ψ, with repetitions. It is acyclic in positive degrees: when T_ψ ≠ ∅, prepending a fixed element gives a contracting homotopy of the augmented complex. Its H_0 is Z if T_ψ ≠ ∅ and 0 otherwise.
- So K_• is a presheaf resolution of Z_R, where R is the sieve generated by 𝒰.
- Sheafification is exact, so K_•^# is a resolution of Z_R^#.
- Hence Č^•(𝒰, I) = Hom_PSh(K_•, I) = Hom_Sh(K_•^#, I) is exact in positive degrees, because Hom_Sh(-, I) is exact. ∎

**Proof of Cartan.** Let G satisfy the hypothesis. Choose an embedding G ↪ I with I an injective sheaf (Ab(C) is a Grothendieck category), and let Q = I/G be the sheaf quotient. Sections are left exact, so G(W) = ker(I(W) -> Q(W)) for every W.

*(a) I(V) -> Q(V) is onto for V ∈ 𝔅.*
- Take s ∈ Q(V). Since I -> Q is an epimorphism of sheaves, s lifts locally on some covering sieve R of V.
- By (2'), pick 𝒱 = {V_i -> V} ∈ Cov with members in R, and lifts t_i ∈ I(V_i) of s|_{V_i}.
- Put c_{ij} = t_j|_{V_ij} - t_i|_{V_ij}. It lies in G(V_ij), since it maps to s - s = 0 in Q. As c = dt in Č^•(𝒱, I), and Č^•(𝒱, G) ⊂ Č^•(𝒱, I), we get dc = 0 in Č^2(𝒱, G).
- Since Ȟ^1(𝒱, G) = 0, c = dg for some g ∈ Č^0(𝒱, G). Then (t_i - g_i) is compatible on all V_ij.
- I is a sheaf and 𝒱 is a covering family, so the family glues to t ∈ I(V). The image of t and s agree on every V_i, hence they are equal, because Q is a sheaf.

*(b) Q again satisfies the hypothesis.*
- For 𝒰 ∈ Cov, all the U_t lie in 𝔅 by (1). So 0 -> Č^•(𝒰, G) -> Č^•(𝒰, I) -> Č^•(𝒰, Q) -> 0 is exact, by (a) and since products are exact.
- By Fact 6.1, Ȟ^p(𝒰, Q) ≅ Ȟ^{p+1}(𝒰, G) = 0 for p >= 1.

*(c) Induction.*
- The long exact sequence gives H^1(U, G) = coker(I(U) -> Q(U)) = 0 for U ∈ 𝔅, by (a).
- It also gives H^p(U, G) ≅ H^{p-1}(U, Q) for p >= 2.
- Induction on p, applied to all sheaves satisfying the hypothesis at once, gives the claim using (b). ∎

**Verification of the hypotheses in our situation.**
- C = (A_P^op, J); fibre products exist (§0).
- 𝔅 = the f.p. objects, a set in V; Cov as in 3.4, a set in V.
- (1) is Lemma 3.5(ii); Cov consists of covering families by Lemma 3.5(i).
- (2'), and hence (2), is Lemma 3.5(iii). This is where the non-f.p. members of covers are dealt with.

## §7 Cohomology and the conclusion

**7.1 The sheaves pi^{-1}I^k are acyclic on 𝔅.** By Cor. 5.3, Ȟ^p(𝒰, pi^{-1}I^k) = 0 for p > 0 and 𝒰 ∈ Cov. By §6, H^p(U, pi^{-1}I^k) = 0 for p > 0 and U ∈ 𝔅.

**7.2 H^p(U, pi^{-1}F) for U ∈ 𝔅.**
- pi^{-1} is exact (1.6), so 0 -> pi^{-1}F -> pi^{-1}I^0 -> pi^{-1}I^1 -> ... is exact in Ab(A_P^op).
- Its terms are Γ(U, -)-acyclic for U ∈ 𝔅. By dimension shifting, H^p(U, pi^{-1}F) = H^p(pi^{-1}I^•(U)).
- By Cor. 5.3 this complex is I^•(Phi_U), naturally in k, and the augmented complex 0 -> F(Phi_U) -> I^0(Phi_U) -> ... is exact (Lemma 2.2).
- Hence **H^0(U, pi^{-1}F) = F(Phi_U), and H^p(U, pi^{-1}F) = 0 for p > 0, for all f.p. U.**

**7.3 R^p pi_*.**
- pi_* = restriction to B_P (1.6). It is left exact, and preserves injectives as the right adjoint of the exact functor pi^{-1}. (The latter is not even needed below.)
- Let G -> J^• be an injective resolution in Ab(A_P^op). Then R^p pi_* G = H^p(J^•|_B).
- Cohomology in PSh(B_P) is objectwise, so (R^p pi_* G)(b) = H^p(J^•(b)) = H^p(b, G).
- **Thus R^p pi_* G is the presheaf b ↦ H^p(b, G).**

**7.4 The derived unit.**
- Since pi^{-1} is exact, L pi^{-1} = pi^{-1}. The unit of the derived adjunction pi^{-1} ⊣ R pi_* on D^+ is, for a presheaf F in degree 0, the composite
 F --η--> pi_* pi^{-1} F --can--> R pi_* pi^{-1} F.
- Here η is the underived unit, and can is the canonical map. It is represented by pi_*(pi^{-1}F) -> pi_*(J^•), induced by the augmentation pi^{-1}F -> J^0 of an injective resolution J^•.
- The map can induces the identification pi_* = R^0 pi_* on H^0.
- Its source is concentrated in degree 0. Its target has H^0 = R^0 pi_* pi^{-1}F and H^p = R^p pi_* pi^{-1}F.
- On H^0 the composite is η, an isomorphism by Cor. 5.3.
- For p > 0 and b ∈ B_P, (R^p pi_* pi^{-1} F)(b) = H^p(b, pi^{-1}F) = 0 by 7.3 and 7.2, since b is f.p. (Lemma 0.1(c)).
- Hence the composite is an isomorphism on all cohomology presheaves, i.e. a quasi-isomorphism.
- The identification in 7.2–7.3 is that of the cohomology of the given map, not merely an abstract isomorphism R pi_* pi^{-1}F ≅ F. Concretely, H^0 of can∘η is the unit, which we showed is the composite of the two isomorphisms in 1.6.

**Theorem.** Let P be any monoid (integral, saturated, sharp, commutative), and assume Results B and D. Then for every presheaf of abelian groups F on B_P^op, F -> R pi_* pi^{-1} F is a quasi-isomorphism.

Moreover, H^p(U, pi^{-1}F) = 0 for p > 0 and pi^{-1}F(U) = F(Phi_U), for every f.p. object U of A_P.

*(Remark.* By the way-out lemma, the statement extends to bounded-below complexes of presheaves, since both sides are triangulated functors on D^+ and agree on objects in a single degree.)

## §8 Status

**Proved here, from Results B and D**, with standard category theory and homological algebra:
- the whole sheaf-theoretic part, for arbitrary P;
- the categories (1.1–1.2);
- the Kan extension and its exactness (1.4–1.5), and the forms of pi^{-1} and pi_* (1.6);
- the injectives (§2);
- the cofinality of all-f.p. covers, which handles covers with non-f.p. members (3.2, 3.5);
- the Čech complexes, including repeated indices (§4);
- sheafification on f.p. objects (§5);
- Cartan's criterion, with a full proof (§6);
- the derived-unit computation (§7).

**Used from the problem statement, not re-proved.** The birhizomic covers form a Grothendieck topology; in either reading, the property used is (★) of 3.3. If the intended topology were the one *generated* by birhizomic covers and the covers did *not* already form a topology, then (★) could fail, and Lemma 3.5(iii) would need a separate argument. The problem asserts this case does not arise.

**Quoted from memory:**
- the standard sieve/plus-construction facts in 5.0;
- the equivalence of pretopology-sheaves and topology-sheaves in 3.3;
- the chain equivalence between ordered and oriented chain complexes (Spanier 4.3.8). This is needed only if Result D is read with "ordered" meaning tuples without repetition;
- the identification of Stacks tag 03F7. The lemma itself is proved in §6.

**I found no false step** in the chain derivation as recorded. The corrections to the recorded chain are minor:
- Exactness of Lan for non-f.p. objects is used only to get pi^{-1} exact.
- Commutation of Lan with infinite products holds only on f.p. objects, and is used only there.
- "Repeated indices are harmless" is justified by the explicit maps of Lemma 4.1. A valuation description is not needed.
- In Cartan's criterion, the cofinality hypothesis is supplied by the witness-subfamily lemma 3.2 together with (★), rather than being trivial.

**Open:** nothing within the sheaf-theoretic part. The overall answer YES rests on Results B and D, which were taken as given here.

202	- Saturated: if x is in the colimit group and nx lies in the colimit, then both facts hold at some stage, so x lies in that stage.

\begin{document} \section{Problem statement} In the following, a monoid is an integral, saturated, sharp, commutative, unital semigroup.  Monoids are written additively.  A monoid $M$ induces a translation invariant partial order on its associated group $M^{\rm gp}$ such that $x \geq 0$ if and only if $x \in M$.  A valuative monoid is a monoid in which the associated partial order is a total order. If $M$ is a monoid, $x \in M^{\rm gp}$, and $y \in M$, we write $x \prec y$ to mean that there are integers $m$ and $n$ such that $my \leq x \leq ny$. A monoid homomorphism $f : M \to N$ is called \emph{infinitesimal} if the following condition holds: \begin{enumerate}[label=$\bullet$] \item If there are $x \in M^{\rm gp}$ and $y \in M$ such that $f(x) \in N$ and $x \prec y$ and $f(y) \prec f(x)$ then $x \in M$. \end{enumerate} If $P \xrightarrow f Q \xrightarrow g N$ are monoid homomorphisms, we say that $f$ is \emph{birhizomic} at $g$ if it is of finite presentation in the category of (integral, saturated, sharp) monoids and, for every factorization of $gf$ through monoid homomorphisms $P \xrightarrow h M \xrightarrow p N$ with $p$ infinitesimal, there is a unique monoid homomorphism $u : Q \to M$ with $pu = g$ and $uf = h$. A family of morphisms $P \rightarrow Q_i$ is called a birhizomic cover if, for every valuative monoid $V$ and every homomorphism $v : P \to V$, there is a factorization of $v$ through some $Q_i \to V$ such that $P \to Q_i$ is birhizomic at $Q_i \to V$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  Let $A_P$ be the category of monoid homomorphisms $P \to Q$.  The birhizomic covers form a Grothendieck topology on $A_P^{\rm op}$. Let $P$ be a monoid.  For any $x$ in $P$, there is an initial monoid homomorphism $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$ that sends $x$ to $0$.  Let $B_P$ be the full subcategory of $A_P$ consisting of homomorphisms $P \to P[-x]^\sharp$, for $x \in P$. We have given $A_P^{\rm op}$ the birhizomic topology and $B_P^{\rm op}$ the trivial topology in which all presheaves are sheaves.  The inclusion $B_P^{\rm op} \subset A_P^{\rm op}$ is left exact.  By left Kan extension and sheafification, it extends to a functor $\pi^{-1} : \operatorname{Sh}(B_P) \to \operatorname{Sh}(A_P)$ on the categories of sheaves.   Let $\pi_\ast$ be the right adjoint of $\pi^{-1}$. \paragraph{Question} \em Is it the case that, for all presheaves of abelian groups $F$ on $B_P^{\rm op}$, the morphism $$F \to \mathrm R \pi_\ast \pi^{-1} F$$ is a quasi-isomorphism? \end{document}# round4_q5: proof of statement #19

## Status and plan

I prove #19 exactly as stated, and in fact in a stronger form. Three hypotheses turn out to be unnecessary: that the members are birhizomic (only the covering property "every valuation of Q factors through some Q_i" is used), that tau is principal, and that Q is f.p. over P.

I depart from the named approach ("birhizomic openness + lexicographic nerve theorem"). ## §1 Conventions and elementary facts

**1.0 Notation.**
- 𝒞 is the category of integral, saturated, sharp commutative monoids ("monoids").
- For a monoid B, B/𝒞 is the category of maps B → M in 𝒞. Its morphisms are the maps under B, and Hom_B(M, N) denotes its Hom-sets.
- For f : P → Q, write Φ_Q := f^{-1}(0).
- For x ∈ P, face(x) := {y ∈ P : y ≤ nx for some n ≥ 1}. Here y ≤ z means z − y ∈ P.
- A *face* of P is a submonoid F with a + b ∈ F ⇒ a, b ∈ F. A face is *principal* if it equals face(x) for some x.
- **Size.** Fix universes U ∈ V with P ∈ U. A_P consists of the maps P → Q with Q ∈ U, and presheaves take values in V-small groups. The usual theory (plus construction, enough injectives, derived functors) then applies to the V-small site A_P^op. Nothing below depends on this choice.

**1.1 Torsion-freeness (F4).** For M ∈ 𝒞, M^gp is torsion-free. If nx = 0 then nx ∈ M, so x ∈ M by saturation; likewise −x ∈ M, so x = 0 by sharpness. Consequently nx = ny ⇒ x = y, and M ⊂ M^gp ⊂ M^gp ⊗ Q.

**1.2 Filtered colimits (F1).** A filtered colimit of objects of 𝒞, computed in commutative monoids, lies in 𝒞. Each axiom is witnessed at a finite stage:
- a + c = b + c in the colimit already holds at some stage, so a = b there;
- nx = m (with x in the group) already holds at some stage;
- x + y = 0 already holds at some stage.

So filtered colimits in 𝒞 and in B/𝒞 are computed on underlying sets.

**1.3 The int/sat/sharp reflection and pushouts.** Let N be a commutative monoid and E ⊂ N × N a set of relations. Form the quotient monoid N/E and let G be its group completion. Let M_0 be the image of N/E in G, let M_1 = {g ∈ G : ng ∈ M_0 for some n ≥ 1}, and put T = M_1/M_1^*.
- T ∈ 𝒞. It is integral as a submonoid of G/M_1^*, and it is sharp. It is saturated: if ng ∈ T for g ∈ G/M_1^*, then a lift g̃ has n g̃ ∈ M_1, so g̃ ∈ M_1.
- Every map N → X with X ∈ 𝒞 that respects E factors uniquely through T. It extends to G → X^gp. It sends M_1 into X, because X is saturated and X^gp is torsion-free. It kills M_1^*, because X is sharp.

We write T = (N/E)^{int,sat,sharp}. Pushouts in 𝒞 are formed this way from pushouts of commutative monoids. Fibre products in A_P^op are pushouts under P.

**1.4 Finite presentation.** A map B → M in 𝒞 is *f.p.* if Hom_B(M, −) commutes with filtered colimits in B/𝒞. This is the problem's "of finite presentation in the category of monoids".

**Lemma 1.5.**
- (a) Composites of f.p. maps are f.p.
- (b) If Q → Q' is f.p. and Q → R is arbitrary, then R → Q' ⊔_Q R is f.p.
- (c) Each P → P[−x]^♯ is f.p.

Hence every finite iterated pushout over Q of f.p. maps Q → Q_i, with Q f.p. under P, is f.p. under P.

*Proof.*
- (b) Hom_R(Q' ⊔_Q R, X) = Hom_Q(Q', X), and a filtered colimit under R is also one under Q.
- (a) Let P → Q → Q' be f.p. and X = colim X_k under P. A map Q' → X under P is a pair (a, c): a map a : Q → X under P, and a map c : Q' → X under Q, where X is viewed under Q via a.
  - a factors through some X_k, uniquely up to going further along.
  - The X_{k'} with k' ≥ k, viewed under Q, have colimit X, so c factors through some X_{k'}, again uniquely up to going further.
  - Hence colim_k Hom_P(Q', X_k) → Hom_P(Q', X) is bijective.
- (c) follows from 1.6: Hom_P(P[−x]^♯, X) is a point if x ↦ 0 in X and empty otherwise. In a filtered colimit, x ↦ 0 holds iff it holds at some stage (1.2). ∎

**1.6 The objects b_x = (P → P[−x]^♯).**

- *Universal property.* For f : P → Q in A_P, a map P[−x]^♯ → Q under P exists iff f(x) = 0, and it is then unique. - *Kernel.* Φ_{b_x} = face(x). Indeed y ↦ 0 iff y is a unit of P[−x], iff −y = p − nx for some p, n, iff y + p = nx, iff y ≤ nx.
- *Kernel faces in general.* For any f : P → Q, Φ_Q is a face, since f(a) + f(b) = 0 forces f(a) = f(b) = 0 in sharp Q. A map Q → Q' under P gives Φ_Q ⊂ Φ_{Q'}. Also x ∈ Φ_Q iff face(x) ⊂ Φ_Q.
- *Consequences.*

  - So B_P is a preorder, equivalent to the poset Pr(P) of principal faces.
  - Pr(P) is directed, since face(x), face(y) ⊂ face(x + y), and has least element face(0) = {0}, with b_0 = P.
  - For τ ∈ Pr(P), write b_τ for any b_x with face(x) = τ, and F(τ) := F(b_τ).

*Proof.* Consider pairs (S, R): S ⊂ M finite, and R a finite set of pairs (a, b) of elements of B ⊕ N^S having the same image in M under the obvious map. These pairs are directed by inclusion. - L → M is surjective: m ∈ M is the image of the generator of T({m}, ∅).

So M = colim T(S,R) in B/𝒞. Since M is f.p., id_M factors through some T = T(S,R): there is s : M → T under B whose composite with T → M is id_M. ∎

**1.8 The site.**
- *Covers of an object.* For an object Q of A_P, a *birhizomic cover of Q* is a family {a_i : Q → Q_i} of maps under P that is a birhizomic cover in the sense of the problem, with Q as base. (A map under P out of Q is just a map out of Q.)

**Lemma 1.9 (pretopology axioms).** Birhizomic covers satisfy the following:
- isomorphisms are covers;
- base change: if {a_i : Q → Q_i} is a cover and c : Q → Q', then {Q' → Q'_i := Q' ⊔_Q Q_i} is a cover;
- composition: if {a_i : Q → Q_i} is a cover and each {b_ij : Q_i → Q_ij} is a cover, then {b_ij a_i} is a cover.

*Proof.*
- *Isomorphisms.* Let φ : Q → Q' be an isomorphism and v a valuation of Q. Then v = (vφ^{-1})φ, and φ is f.p. Given h : Q → M and an infinitesimal p : M → V with ph = v, the map u = hφ^{-1} is the unique one with uφ = h, and pu = vφ^{-1}.
- *Base change.* Let v' be a valuation of Q'. Then v'c = g_i a_i with a_i birhizomic at g_i. Put g' = (v', g_i) : Q'_i → V. The map Q' → Q'_i is f.p. by 1.5(b).
  - Let h : Q' → M and an infinitesimal p : M → V satisfy ph = v'. Then (hc, p) factors g_i a_i, so there is a unique u_i : Q_i → M with p u_i = g_i and u_i a_i = hc.

  - Uniqueness: any such u restricts on Q_i to a map with the defining properties of u_i.
- *Composition.* Let v be a valuation of Q. Write v = g_i a_i with a_i birhizomic at g_i, and g_i = g_ij b_ij with b_ij birhizomic at g_ij. The composite b_ij a_i is f.p. by 1.5(a).
  - Given (h, p) with p infinitesimal and ph = v, take the unique u_i with p u_i = g_i and u_i a_i = h.
  - Then take the unique u with pu = g_ij and u b_ij = u_i. It satisfies u b_ij a_i = h.
  - Uniqueness: if u' has these properties, then u' b_ij has those of u_i, so u' b_ij = u_i, and then u' = u. ∎

Its sheaves are the presheaves satisfying the sheaf condition for birhizomic covers. This agrees with the problem's assertion that the birhizomic covers form a Grothendieck topology. The property used below is:

(★) every covering sieve of every object Q contains all members of some birhizomic cover of Q.

**Lemma 1.10 (witness subfamily).** {Q → Q_i}_{i ∈ I_0} is a birhizomic cover of Q, all of whose members are f.p.

*Proof.* For a valuation v of Q, the cover property gives i and a factorization through Q_i at which a_i is birhizomic. Then i ∈ I_0. ∎

## §2 Theorem B: kernel faces of f.p. maps are principal

**Theorem B.** For every monoid P and every f.p. f : P → Q, Φ_Q = face(s) for some s ∈ P.

*Proof.*

*Step 1: reduction.* By 1.7 with B = P, Q is a retract under P of Q' = ((P ⊕ N^k)/R)^{int,sat,sharp}, with R finite. Then ker(P → Q) = ker(P → Q'):
- if x dies in Q', it dies in Q, which is the image of Q' under the retraction;
- if x dies in Q, apply the section Q → Q', which is a map under P.

*Step 2: the kernel of P → Q'.* Write the relations as pairs (r_j, s_j) in P ⊕ N^k, for j = 1..J, and put l_j = r_j − s_j ∈ P^gp ⊕ Z^k. Let L be the subgroup they generate and G = (P^gp ⊕ Z^k)/L. As in 1.3, M_0 is the image of P ⊕ N^k in G, M_1 is its saturation in G, and Q' = M_1/M_1^*.

x ∈ P dies in Q' iff its image is a unit of M_1, iff −x ∈ M_1, iff −nx ∈ M_0 for some n ≥ 1, iff (−nx − p, −m) ∈ L for some p ∈ P and m ∈ N^k. Write the element of L as Σ c_j l_j with c ∈ Z^J.
- The Z^k-component condition says c lies in K := {c ∈ Z^J : the Z^k-part of Σ c_j l_j lies in −N^k}.
- K is the set of lattice points of a rational polyhedral cone, so it is a finitely generated monoid (Gordan's lemma).
- Let ψ : K → P^gp be the P^gp-part of c ↦ −Σ c_j l_j. It is additive, so Y := ψ(K) is a finitely generated submonoid of P^gp.
- The condition reads nx + p = ψ(c). Conversely, for c ∈ K with ψ(c) = nx + p, put m := −(Z^k-part of Σ c_j l_j) ∈ N^k.

Hence x dies iff nx + p ∈ Y for some n ≥ 1 and p ∈ P, i.e. iff nx ≤ y for some y ∈ S := Y ∩ P. Since x ≤ nx, this is iff x ≤ y for some y ∈ S. So Φ_Q is the face generated by the submonoid S, namely ∪_{t ∈ S} face(t).

*Step 3: principality.* The family {face(t) : t ∈ S} is directed, since face(t + t') ⊃ face(t), face(t'). Consider a strictly increasing chain face(s_1) ⊊ face(s_2) ⊊ … with s_i ∈ S, and put G_i := face(s_i)^gp ∩ Y^gp.
- For any face F of P, F^gp ∩ P = F: if x = a − b with a, b ∈ F and x ∈ P, then x + b = a ∈ F, so x ∈ F.
- If n s_{i+1} ∈ G_i for some n ≥ 1, then n s_{i+1} ∈ face(s_i)^gp ∩ P = face(s_i), so s_{i+1} ∈ face(s_i), contradicting strictness.
- So s_{i+1} ∈ G_{i+1} has infinite order modulo G_i. Since G_i ⊂ G_{i+1}, the ranks strictly increase inside the finitely generated free group Y^gp (P^gp is torsion-free).

Hence chains have length ≤ rk Y^gp + 1, and there is a maximal face(s) with s ∈ S, starting from s = 0. By directedness it contains every face(t), t ∈ S, so Φ_Q = face(s). ∎

**Corollary 2.1.** For f.p. Q, (b_s, b_s → Q) is terminal in the comma category of objects of B_P over Q (§4.1).

**Theorem D.** Let P be any monoid, f : P → Q any map in 𝒞, and {Q → Q_i}_{i ∈ I} a family of f.p. maps under Q such that every valuation v : Q → V (V valuative) factors through some Q_i. - N_τ is a nonempty simplicial complex, i.e. closed under nonempty subsets, since Q_{σ'} → Q_σ for σ' ⊂ σ;
